docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 6 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Tantra–Āgama: Tantric and Āgamic Traditions. It surveys the scriptures, doctrines and practices of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta Āgamas and Tantras, the Śrīvidyā and Kashmiri Śaiva traditions, the theory and practice of mantra, yantra and ritual, Buddhist and Jain Tantra, the temple religion that the Āgamas still govern in South India, the patronage of Tantric Śaivism by the kings of the early medieval “Śaiva Age”, and the regional Tantric traditions of Kerala, Bengal, Assam, Odisha, Nepal, western India and the Tamil country, together with the Nātha and Siddha orders that moved between them. It also considers the lesser-known Tantras of healing and exorcism, the roles of women as practitioners, partners and gurus, and, in its last chapter, the ethics of the traditions and the history of how “Tantra” has been condemned, defended and studied in colonial India and the modern West.

The word “Tantra” has attracted both romantic fantasy and hostile caricature. This volume tries to avoid both. It follows the findings of historical and philological scholarship — that the surviving Tantric scriptures date from about the fifth century CE onwards, that their traditions are many rather than one, and that they include both sublime philosophy and practices of power and transgression — while presenting the traditions’ own self-understanding with respect. Traditional dates and attributions are reported as such; quotations from Sanskrit texts are given only where their wording and source could be checked, and many unattested verses found in earlier drafts have been removed. Questions of caste, gender and access, which the traditions themselves debated, are discussed openly.

The volume is an introduction, not a substitute for the critical editions and specialist studies listed in the bibliography, to which readers are referred for further study. Every primary-text quotation should be checked against a critical edition before citation.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Transliteration and Pronunciation
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). A macron marks a long vowel: ā is pronounced as in “father”, ī as in “machine”, ū as in “rule”, while short a is like the u of “but”. The vowels e and o are always long, ai is pronounced as in “aisle” and au as in “how”. The vowel ṛ is a syllabic r, close to the ri of “rig”. Consonants written with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ) are retroflex, pronounced with the tip of the tongue turned back; ś and ṣ both sound roughly like English sh; c is always the ch of “church”; and an h after a consonant marks aspiration, so that th is the t of “hothouse” and ph the p of “uphill”, never English th or f. Ṃ marks nasalisation of the preceding vowel, ḥ a light echo of it, and ṅ and ñ are the nasals of “sing” and “canyon”.

Tamil words follow the transliteration of the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras, which distinguishes short e and o from long ē and ō and writes the distinctively Tamil sounds as ḻ (as in Āḻvār), ṟ and ṉ. Tibetan, Chinese and Japanese terms are given in simplified or standard romanisations without diacritics. Modern place names (Thanjavur, Bhubaneswar, Guwahati) and the names of modern persons are spelled in their customary English forms, and Sanskrit titles of texts are printed in italics.

docs.title: 1.1 The Meaning of Tantra and Āgama
docs.text:
Few words in Indian religious history have been as widely misunderstood as tantra. In modern popular usage the term has been narrowed to suggest exotic sexuality or vague occultism, a reduction that owes as much to nineteenth-century colonial polemic as to twentieth-century Western marketing. The Sanskrit word derives from the root tan, “to stretch, extend, weave”, with the instrumental suffix -tra: a tantra is literally a loom or the warp on a loom, and by extension a framework, system, doctrine or treatise. In classical Sanskrit the word is used for any systematic work (the Pañcatantra is a collection of fables; the Mīmāṃsākas speak of tantra as a ritual principle). Only gradually did it come to denote a particular class of revealed scriptures and the traditions based on them (Padoux 2017; Goudriaan and Gupta 1981).

Tantric authors also offered devotional “etymologies” (nirukti) of the word. A verse widely quoted as coming from the Kāmikāgama explains tantra as that which “extends” (tanoti) many matters concerning tattva (principles of reality) and mantra, and “protects” (trāṇaṃ kurute). It is given here as later authors cite it; its place in the surviving Kāmika has not been checked against an edition:

Attributed to the Kāmikāgama

tanoti vipulān arthān tattvamantrasamanvitān | trāṇaṃ ca kurute yasmāt tantram ity abhidhīyate ||

Because it extends many matters joined with tattva and mantra, and because it gives protection, it is called tantra.

Such explanations are plays on sound, not historical etymology: the element -tra is an ordinary instrumental suffix and has nothing to do with trā “to protect”. They show, all the same, what the tradition took its scriptures to be: comprehensive revelations of the structure of reality, of the mantras that act upon it, and of the means of salvation.

The word āgama means “that which has come down” (from ā-gam, “to come towards”), that is, a teaching received through transmission. In the Tantric traditions it denotes scripture revealed by a deity. A popular verse of uncertain origin plays on the three syllables ā-ga-ma: the teaching has “come” (āgata) from the mouths of Śiva, “gone” (gata) to the Goddess, and been “approved” (mata) by Vāsudeva. Some Śākta texts distinguish āgama, a teaching spoken by Śiva to the Goddess, from nigama, one spoken by the Goddess to Śiva; elsewhere nigama simply denotes the Veda.

docs.title: 1.1.1 What Counts as “Tantra”?
docs.text:
Modern scholars use “Tantra” in two senses. In the narrow sense it refers to the scriptures called tantra, āgama or saṃhitā and the traditions that regard them as revelation. In the wider sense (“Tantrism”) it is a label for a cluster of practices and ideas found across Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Buddhist and Jain religion from about the fifth or sixth century CE onwards. Padoux and Flood both stress that “Tantrism” is a scholarly category rather than a self-description, and that no single feature is shared by every tradition so labelled (Padoux 2017; Flood 2006).

The features most often listed form a recognisable family. Practice begins with initiation (dīkṣā) by a guru, which in many systems is itself a cause of liberation. The initiate receives mantras, including monosyllabic “seed” (bīja) mantras, which are understood as the deity’s own form in sound. Worship is elaborate, and before he worships the deity the worshipper purifies and divinises his own body (bhūtaśuddhi, nyāsa); the deity and its retinue are installed in diagrams (maṇḍala, yantra). The cosmos is mapped as a graded hierarchy of principles (tattvas) through which the soul is bound and through which it ascends. The goals are both liberation (mukti) and supernatural power or worldly benefit (bhukti, siddhi). And the teaching is secret: in some traditions it includes the ritual use of substances and acts that orthodox Brahmanical norms forbid. None of these features is unique to Tantra, and not every Tantric tradition has all of them; it is the combination that is distinctive. The approach adopted in this volume, which starts from the scriptures themselves, is discussed again at the end of the book (Section 14.7).

docs.title: 1.2 Tantra and Veda
docs.text:
The relationship between the Tantric and Vedic traditions was contested from the beginning, and it shaped how the Tantric scriptures defended their authority. In a philosophical culture that took the Veda as the norm of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), the Mīmāṃsā position was severe: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (7th century) held that only the authorless Veda has intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya), so that texts composed by persons, even divine ones, are reliable only insofar as they agree with it. Kumārila placed the Pāñcarātra and Pāśupata scriptures outside the Veda, and several Dharmaśāstra and Purāṇa passages treat Tantric initiates as heretical or impure.

The Tantric traditions answered in three ways. Many Śaiva Siddhānta and Pāñcarātra authors presented their scriptures as consistent with the Veda, adding a higher and more specific teaching to the general Vedic one, and South Indian temple priests (ādiśaivas, bhaṭṭācāryas) have long insisted on their Vedic credentials. A second line defended the scriptures’ independent authority: the Vaiṣṇava teacher Yāmuna (10th–11th century) argued in his Āgamaprāmāṇya that the Pāñcarātra, revealed by the omniscient Lord, is as authoritative as the Veda and does not contradict it, and Rāmānuja adopted his position (van Buitenen 1971); Siddhānta authors such as Sadyojyotis and Rāmakaṇṭha argued in the same way from Śiva’s omniscience. A third line claimed superiority: the Bhairava and Kaula scriptures, and Abhinavagupta after them, placed Vedic religion low in an ascending hierarchy of revelations — Vedic, Siddhānta, Bhairava, Kaula — with their own teaching at the summit, and some texts deliberately inverted Vedic purity rules (Sanderson 1988).

Meanwhile Tantric ritual steadily entered orthodox practice. Much of the pūjā performed by “Smārta” Brahmins today, including nyāsa and bīja mantras, is Tantric in origin (Bühnemann 1988; Sanderson 2009). The Tantric theory of language, which treats the phonemes as forms of power and mantras as the deity’s body rather than as conventional signs, also defined itself against both the Mīmāṃsā doctrine of the eternal Veda and the Buddhist view of language as convention (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 1.3 Genres of Tantric Literature
docs.text:
Readers of Tantric literature meet several kinds of text, which carry different kinds of authority. Scriptures (āgama, tantra, saṃhitā, yāmala, mata) present themselves as revealed by a deity, usually in dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess, Bhairava and Bhairavī, or the Lord and a sage; their Sanskrit is often irregular, and they were revised and expanded over centuries. Commentaries (vṛtti, ṭīkā, vivaraṇa, viveka) are the work of named human authors, such as Rāmakaṇṭha on the Kiraṇa or Jayaratha on the Tantrāloka. Independent treatises argue a philosophical case, as Utpaladeva’s Īśvara­pratyabhijñā­kārikā or Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam do. Ritual manuals (paddhati), such as those of Somaśambhu and Aghoraśiva, guide the officiant step by step and in practice often shaped ritual more than the scriptures did. Digests (nibandha, saṁgraha), such as the Śāradātilaka, the Mantramahodadhi and Kṛṣṇānanda’s Tantrasāra, compile material from many scriptures. Finally there are hymns (stotra) and vernacular poetry: the Saundaryalaharī, Utpaladeva’s hymns, the Tamil Tēvāram and Āḻvār hymns, the Kannada vacanas, the Buddhist dohās and the Bengali Śākta songs.

Much of what is popularly attributed to “the Tantras” comes in fact from late digests, from modern manuals or from oral tradition. Wherever possible this volume identifies which kind of source a statement rests on.

docs.title: 1.4 Canons and Classes of Scripture
docs.text:
Each Tantric stream gives conventional canonical numbers: twenty-eight Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas, 108 Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās and sixty-four Bhairava or Śākta Tantras. These numbers are ideal, not descriptive: some texts on the lists are lost, others survive only in later redactions, and many important texts are not on the lists at all (Goudriaan and Gupta 1981; Flood 2006). Figure 1.1 sets out the main Hindu streams in simplified form.

Figure 1.1. A simplified classification of the major Hindu Tantric traditions. Real boundaries were fluid; the Śākta traditions grew out of the Śaiva Bhairava and Kaula scriptures.

The Śaiva Āgamas. The Siddhānta canon recognises twenty-eight principal Āgamas (mūlāgamas), traditionally divided into ten Śivabheda texts, from the Kāmika to the Suprabheda, and eighteen Rudrabheda texts, from the Vijaya to the Vātula, each with subsidiary scriptures (upaāgamas). Tradition assigns them to the five faces of Śiva; the full list is given in Table 2.1. Research since the 1990s, much of it based on early Nepalese manuscripts, has shown that the oldest Siddhānta scriptures — the Niśvāsa, the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha, the Rauravasūtrasaṅgraha, the Kiraṇa, the Pārameśvara, the Mataṅgapārameśvara, the Sarvajñānottara and others — were composed in North India and were the texts quoted by the Kashmiri commentators of the tenth and eleventh centuries. Many of the South Indian texts that now bear names from the list, such as the Kāmika and the Kāraṇa, are much later compilations, often later than the twelfth century, which absorbed material from the ritual manuals (Goodall et al. 2015; Sanderson 2009). The Śaiva canon and its four-part ideal structure — doctrine, yoga, ritual and conduct — are described in Chapter 2.

The Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās. The Pāñcarātra claims 108 Saṃhitās, though later lists name over two hundred titles. Three early works, the Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya, are honoured as the “three gems”; Chapter 3 shows that still earlier works survive in Nepalese manuscripts.

The Bhairava and Śākta Tantras. The scriptures of the Bhairava class, which are the matrix of the later Śākta traditions, are listed in the Śrīkaṇṭhīya Saṃhitā (as quoted by Jayaratha) as sixty-four texts in eight groups of eight. The best known surviving works of this family include the Svacchanda, the Brahmayāmala (also called Picumata), the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, the Mālinīvijayottara, the Jayadrathayāmala and the Kubjikāmata. Later Śākta works include the Vāmakeśvarīmata, the Yoginīhṛdaya, the Kulārṇava, the Tantrarāja and many Bengali and Assamese Tantras of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries, among them the Mahānirvāṇa, a work of the late eighteenth century (Section 4.5) (Sanderson 1988; Goudriaan and Gupta 1981).

Buddhist and Jain Tantra. Buddhist Tantra, the Mantranaya or Vajrayāna, has its own scriptures, from the early ritual Tantras to the Guhyasamāja, Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra and Kālacakra. They were studied at Nālandā, Vikramaśīla and other monasteries and transmitted to Tibet, where they remain central to all schools. Jain authors adopted mantra, diagram and the worship of protective goddesses within a framework that rejected blood offering and transgressive rites. Both are treated in Chapter 10. The boundaries were porous: the Buddhist Yoginītantras borrowed whole passages from Śaiva scriptures, and the Buddhist goddess Tārā entered the Hindu lists of the Mahāvidyās (Sanderson 2009; Shaw 2006).

docs.title: 1.4.1 Saura and Gāṇapatya Traditions
docs.text:
Later Smārta Brahmins worship five deities together — Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, the Sun (Sūrya) and Gaṇeśa — in the pañcāyatana rite, and hagiography credits Śaṅkara with reconciling six cults (ṣaṇmata), adding Skanda. Two of these, the Saura and the Gāṇapatya, also had Tantric forms, though on a much smaller scale than the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta traditions.

A distinctive cult of the Sun, served by priests called Magas or Śākadvīpī Brahmins, is described in the Sāmba and Bhaviṣya Purāṇas. Their legend tells how Sāmba, son of Kṛṣṇa, was cured of a skin disease by the Sun, built his temple at Mūlasthāna (Multan) and brought Maga priests from Śākadvīpa to serve it; the names and some practices of these priests reflect Iranian influence (Stietencron 1966). Great Sun temples were built at Modhera in Gujarat (1026–27) and Koṇārka in Odisha (13th century). Saura Tantric scriptures existed but are largely lost, known chiefly from quotations. Their legacy survives inside Śaivism: in the Siddhānta manuals, the daily worship of Śiva is preceded by a worship of the Sun (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998; Sanderson 2009).

Images of Gaṇeśa become common from about the fifth century. In Tantric ritual of every tradition the elephant-headed god, as Vināyaka, the remover of obstacles, is worshipped first, and he appears in the outer enclosures of many maṇḍalas. A separate Gāṇapatya tradition, treating him as the supreme deity, produced the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Purāṇas and the late Gaṇapati Upaniṣad, and took root above all in Maharashtra, where the saint Morayā Gosāvī of Chinchwad and the circuit of eight shrines (aṣṭavināyaka) became its centres. Tantric forms of the god include Mahāgaṇapati, worshipped with his consort in Śrīvidyā, and Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati, whose left-handed cult was conducted in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa, “with the remnants of food in the mouth”). Buddhist Tantra also adopted Gaṇapati, who reached Japan as Kangiten (Section 10.16) (Courtright 1985).

docs.title: 1.5 Historical Overview
docs.text:
Table 1.1 gives a schematic periodisation, which the chapters that follow fill in. Dates follow mainstream scholarship; traditional dates, where they differ, are noted in the chronology at the end of the volume.

Table 1.1. A Schematic Periodisation of the Tantric Traditions Period Development Before c. 450 CE Vedic mantra and ritual; Śaiva ascetic movements (Pāśupatas, attested by the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE); goddess cults; no surviving Tantric scripture c. 450–700 CE Earliest surviving Śaiva Tantra (Niśvāsa); Devīmāhātmya; early Buddhist ritual Tantras; the Tamil poet-saints, Nāyaṉmārs and Āḻvārs (c. 6th–9th century) c. 700–1200 CE The “Śaiva Age” (Sanderson): royal patronage of Śaiva initiation across South and Southeast Asia; Bhairava and Kaula scriptures; early Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās; Buddhist Yoginītantras; Kashmiri exegesis (Abhinavagupta, c. 950–1016); Siddhānta manuals c. 1200–1800 CE Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta (Meykaṇṭār, 13th century); South Indian Āgamic compilations; Śrīvidyā in the South (Bhāskararāya, 18th century); Bengali and Assamese Śākta Tantras; decline of Buddhism in India 19th century Colonial and missionary polemic against “Tantrism”; first printed editions 20th–21st century Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe); Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies; critical editions of the Institut Français de Pondichéry; historical and philological research; living temple traditions

The systematised Tantric scriptures appear only from about the fifth or sixth century CE, but they drew on older material. The Ṛgveda’s reflections on sacred speech (Vāc), for instance in the hymn ṚV 10.125, were later read as anticipations of the Tantric theology of the Word. The healing, protective and aggressive rites of the Atharvaveda form a typological, if not a direct historical, bridge to Tantric ritual for worldly ends. The Śrīsūkta, a hymn to Śrī-Lakṣmī among the supplementary khila hymns appended to the fifth book of the Ṛgveda, was widely used in later goddess worship. The Śatarudrīya of the Yajurveda (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5) and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad supplied the vocabulary of later Śaiva theology, and the five mantras of Śiva in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (10.43–47) became the basis of the Āgamic doctrine of Śiva’s five faces. Above all, the ascetic orders of the Pāśupatas and their successors — the “Atimārga” in Sanderson’s terminology — preceded and shaped the Tantric Śaiva “Mantramārga” (Section 2.1).

Scholarly Note: Is Tantra Prehistoric?

Popular books often claim that Tantra goes back to the Indus Civilisation of the third millennium BCE, citing the so-called “proto-Śiva” seal from Mohenjo-daro, which shows a horned figure seated among animals, and the female figurines found at Harappan sites. These claims cannot be sustained. The Indus script is undeciphered; the identification of the seated figure with Śiva, first proposed by John Marshall in the 1930s, is one interpretation among several; and there is no textual or archaeological evidence linking Harappan religion to the specific doctrines and rituals of the Tantras, which appear in the historical record only from about the fifth century CE. Tantric traditions certainly drew on older Indian religious elements — Vedic mantra, ascetic practice, goddess cults and folk ritual — but “Tantra” as a body of scripture and practice is a product of the early medieval period (Samuel 2008; Sanderson 2009).

The formative period, from about 450 to 700, saw the composition of the oldest layer of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, dated by its editors to about 450–550 (Goodall et al. 2015); the Devīmāhātmya, the first sustained Sanskrit theology of the Great Goddess (Coburn 1984); and the first Buddhist ritual Tantras, followed in the seventh century by the Mahāvairocana and the Tattvasaṅgraha. The centuries from about 700 to 1200 produced the greater part of the surviving Śaiva and Buddhist Tantric literature and its most sophisticated commentaries: the Siddhānta exegesis of Sadyojyotis, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and Rāmakaṇṭha; the non-dual synthesis of Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja in Kashmir; the ritual manuals of Somaśambhu (1095) and Aghoraśiva (12th century); the Vaiṣṇava defence of the Pāñcarātra by Yāmuna and Rāmānuja; and, in eastern India under the Pālas, the Buddhist Yoginītantras and the Kālacakra (early 11th century). The Kulārṇava and Tantrarāja probably belong to the following two centuries, and the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta took its classical form with Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam in the thirteenth century.

docs.title: 1.6 Guru, Lineage and Initiation
docs.text:
The Āgamic traditions give great weight to transmission through a lineage (paramparā) of teachers. Knowledge of the scriptures is not supposed to be acquired by private reading; it must be received through initiation from a qualified guru. The lineage may be personal, from master to disciple; hereditary, as among the South Indian temple priests (ādiśaivas, bhaṭṭācāryas); monastic, as in the medieval Siddhānta maṭhas and the Tamil ātīṉams; or visionary, as when Kaula and Śrīvidyā lineages trace their teaching through divine, perfected and human streams (divya, siddha, mānava oghas). A verse from the Guru Gītā (traditionally assigned to the Skanda Purāṇa) expresses the devotional attitude to the teacher common to many later traditions:

Guru Gītā, short recension 32

gurur brahmā gurur viṣṇur gurur devo maheśvaraḥ | gurur eva paraṃ brahma tasmai śrīgurave namaḥ ||

The guru is Brahmā, the guru is Viṣṇu, the guru is the god Maheśvara. The guru alone is the supreme Brahman: to that glorious guru, salutation.

In common recitation the third quarter usually reads guruḥ sākṣāt paraṃ brahma. All the traditions treated in this volume agree that the guru is indispensable, but they understand the relationship in different ways, and the differences say much about each tradition.

In the Śaiva Siddhānta the guru is the instrument through which Śiva acts in initiation. What matters is his ritual competence and his consecration as ācārya, not his personal holiness: the liberating power of initiation lies in the rite, which the guru performs while identified with Śiva. The manuals accordingly describe the qualifications of teacher and pupil largely in terms of birth, conduct and ritual knowledge, and they regulate the relationship after initiation by the rules (samayas) that bind the initiate to honour the guru, his family and his lineage (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998). Entitlement (adhikāra) follows the grade of initiation: the samayin may attend worship and receive mantras; the putraka, having received the liberating initiation, performs the daily worship of Śiva; the sādhaka propitiates a mantra to obtain powers; and the ācārya initiates others and performs consecrations (Table 2.6). In the South this conception allowed the role to become hereditary in priestly and monastic lineages.

The Kashmiri non-dualists placed the weight elsewhere. For Abhinavagupta the true guru is one in whom the nature of consciousness has been fully recognised, and the transmission of that recognition can, in the highest case, take place without elaborate ritual; later Kaula manuals such as the Kulārṇava speak of initiation by touch, by a glance or by thought alone. Ritual initiation remains necessary for those of lesser receptivity, graded according to the intensity of the “descent of power” (śaktipāta) in the disciple (Section 2.14), and Abhinavagupta even allows that a person may be initiated directly by the deity (Sanderson 1988; Törzsök 2014). The Kaula and Krama lineages, with their stress on oral transmission and on lines of teachers that include women (Section 4.14), belong to this side of the spectrum.

Later Śākta and Kaula manuals combine both conceptions with an intense devotion to the guru. They require teacher and pupil to test each other before initiation, often for a year; they forbid the disclosure of the mantra and of the guru’s instructions to the uninitiated; and they prescribe the daily worship of the guru and of the lineage of teachers, often in the form of the guru’s sandals (pādukā) visualised on the crown of the head. The Kulārṇava Tantra combines the most exalted claims — the guru is Śiva himself in human form — with warnings against teachers interested only in their pupils’ wealth, and the tension between absolute devotion and the need to discern a true teacher runs through the whole literature. Buddhist Tantra developed the same ideal of devotion to the master (vajrācārya), codified in the Gurupañcāśikā (“Fifty Verses on the Guru”), traditionally attributed to Aśvaghoṣa, which also advises the disciple to examine a teacher before accepting him. In the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition the ācārya who confers the five sacraments becomes, especially for the Teṉkalai school, a mediator whose acceptance of the disciple is itself a ground of salvation (Section 3.7), and the Gauḍīya ritual code opens with the qualifications of guru and disciple (Section 3.14) (Broo 2023).

The authority that all these traditions give the guru has been a source both of their continuity and of their vulnerability. It has preserved oral teachings and lineages for centuries, and it has also, in modern times, been exploited by teachers who claimed Tantric sanction for abuse (Section 14.2).

docs.title: 1.7 Manuscripts and the Modern Recovery of the Āgamas
docs.text:
Unlike the Vedic corpus, preserved by oral recitation of extraordinary fidelity, most Āgamic texts survived in manuscripts. In the Tamil country they were written on palm leaf in the Grantha script and are now held in collections such as those of the Institut Français de Pondichéry, the Sarasvati Mahal at Thanjavur, the Adyar Library and the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library in Chennai; Kashmiri works were copied in the Śāradā script, on birch bark and later paper; Kerala’s ritual manuals in Malayalam script; and the scriptures of the Bhairava, Śākta and Buddhist traditions in the scripts of Nepal, whose National Archives in Kathmandu hold many of the oldest witnesses. The dry climate of the Kathmandu Valley and the continuity of Tantric practice there preserved palm-leaf manuscripts from as early as the ninth century; several fundamental works survive nowhere else.

The Āgamas present themselves as eternal revelation and give no dates. Scholars date them by manuscript evidence (the oldest manuscript of the Niśvāsa is a Nepalese palm-leaf copy of about the ninth century), by citations in datable authors, by internal cross-references and linguistic features, and by inscriptions. The resulting picture places the composition of the surviving Śaiva scriptures between roughly the fifth and the twelfth centuries, with substantial South Indian compilations thereafter (Goodall et al. 2015; Sanderson 2009).

The modern recovery of this literature has been the work of a few institutions. The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, published in Srinagar from 1911 under the patronage of the Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir, issued the principal Kashmiri Śaiva texts, including the complete Tantrāloka with Jayaratha’s commentary (1918–1938) (Abhinavagupta 1918–1938). Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe, 1865–1936) and his collaborators published the Tantrik Texts series and English studies that did much to rehabilitate Tantra in the eyes of educated readers, though from a strongly apologetic, Vedāntic standpoint (Section 14.4) (Avalon 1919; Urban 2003). The Institut Français de Pondichéry, founded in 1955, whose manuscript collection of Śaiva texts was inscribed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2005, published N.R. Bhatt’s critical editions of the Rauravāgama, Ajitāgama, Mṛgendrāgama and Mataṅgapārameśvarāgama, Hélène Brunner’s edition and translation of the Somaśambhupaddhati and, more recently, the work of Dominic Goodall and colleagues on the Kiraṇa and the Niśvāsa (Bhatt 1961–1988; Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998; Goodall et al. 2015). The Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation Project (1970–2002) and its successor microfilmed and described a very large number of Nepalese manuscripts, and the Muktabodha Indological Research Institute has made e-texts and manuscript images widely available.

Editing these texts is difficult. Manuscripts vary widely, reflecting centuries of regional adaptation by practising communities; the technical ritual vocabulary is often missing from the standard dictionaries (the Tāntrikābhidhānakośa was begun to fill this gap: (Brunner et al. 2000)); the Sanskrit of the scriptures frequently departs from Pāṇinian norms, a “divine” usage (aiśa) that editors must not “correct”; and many works exist in several recensions. The editorial practice developed at Pondicherry, Oxford and Hamburg combines strict philology with attention to living ritual.

docs.title: 1.8 Temples, Kings, Caste and Gender
docs.text:
The Āgamas are not only historical documents. Many major temples of South India — for example the Śiva temples of Madurai and Tiruvaṇṇāmalai and the Viṣṇu temples of Śrīraṅgam and Tirupati — regulate their worship according to Āgamic manuals (Śaiva, Pāñcarātra or Vaikhānasa), and court cases over temple administration and priestly appointment routinely turn on what “the Āgamas” require (Fuller 2003). Great temples were also major economic institutions: the inscriptions of Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014) on the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur, consecrated about 1010, record endowments of villages and treasure and list hundreds of employees, including four hundred temple women, musicians, priests, accountants and craftsmen (Chapter 11).

Behind these institutions lies a long history of royal patronage. Alexis Sanderson has argued that between about the fifth and the thirteenth centuries initiatory Śaivism became the dominant religion of much of South and Southeast Asia, chiefly because its officiants could serve kings: with a form of initiation adapted to rulers, with rites of consecration, protection and victory, with royal temples, and with networks of monasteries that supplied trained preceptors to distant courts. Competing for the same patronage, the Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain traditions adopted many features of Śaiva ritual, which in Sanderson’s view is why so much of later Indian religious practice is Tantric in form (Sanderson 2009). Through the same channels Tantric ritual and texts reached Cambodia, Champa, Java and Bali, and Buddhist Tantra travelled to Tibet, China and Japan. The thesis, its evidence and the qualifications other historians have offered are examined in Chapter 12; the transmission of Buddhist Tantra beyond India in Section 10.14.

The Tantric traditions are often described as egalitarian. The record is mixed. Many Śaiva and Śākta scriptures declare initiation open to all four varṇas and, in some cases, to women; the Siddhānta held that initiation destroys the initiate’s caste in a spiritual sense, and several Kaula sources declare caste distinctions void within the ritual circle. The Pāñcarātra and the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition likewise accepted devotees of all castes. Here the Tantras differed sharply from Vedic religion, from which Śūdras and women were excluded (Sanderson 2009; Flood 2006). But openness to initiation did not abolish caste in social life. Siddhānta manuals prescribe different procedures and mantras for initiates of different castes; most texts reserve the role of ācārya, and especially of temple priest, for Brahmins; and in South India temple priesthood became the hereditary preserve of the ādiśaiva and bhaṭṭācārya communities. Kaula texts that abolish caste “inside the circle” often require that it be observed outside it. Women appear as initiates, as partners in Kaula ritual and, occasionally, as gurus, but nearly all Tantric texts were written by and for men (Section 4.14). The temples governed by the Āgamas also enforced untouchability until the temple-entry movements and legislation of the 1930s and 1940s, and who may serve as an Āgamic priest remains contested in the courts today (Section 11.10). The most radical social critiques associated with Śaiva devotion came largely from outside the Āgamic priesthood: the Nāyaṉmār hagiographies include devotees of low and “untouchable” birth such as Nandanār, and the Vīraśaiva poets of twelfth-century Karnataka rejected both caste and temple ritual (Section 2.10).

docs.title: 1.9 The Approach and Plan of This Volume
docs.text:
This volume ties statements about doctrine and ritual, as far as possible, to identifiable texts, and it quotes them only where their wording and source are reasonably secure. Where a tradition gives a date or an authorship that differs from the scholarly consensus, both are reported and labelled. The traditions are set in their social and political setting, including royal patronage, caste and gender; the transgressive rites of some lineages are described as the sources describe them; and the Āgamic and Tantric traditions are treated throughout as living religions, not as relics.

The chapters that follow begin with the scriptural traditions: the Śaiva Āgamas, including the lesser streams of healing and exorcism (Chapter 2); the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas and their temple liturgies (Chapter 3); the Śākta Tantras and the place of women in them (Chapter 4); Śrīvidyā (Chapter 5); and the non-dual Śaivism of Kashmir with the Krama (Chapter 6). Three chapters then treat the shared practices of mantra, yantra and maṇḍala, and ritual (Chapters 7–9). Buddhist and Jain Tantra follow (Chapter 10), and then the institutions and places in which Tantra lived: the temple (Chapter 11), the royal courts of the “Śaiva Age” (Chapter 12), and the regions from Kerala and the Tamil country to Bengal, Assam and Nepal, with the Nātha and Siddha orders that crossed them (Chapter 13). The last chapter turns to the ethics of the traditions and to the history of how “Tantra” has been condemned, defended, marketed and studied since the colonial period (Chapter 14).

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Śaiva Āgamas
docs.text: The Śaiva Āgamas or Tantras are the scriptures of the initiatory Śaiva religion that, in Alexis Sanderson’s phrase, dominated the religious landscape of South and Southeast Asia in the early medieval “Śaiva Age” (Sanderson 2009). They form the scriptural foundation of the Śaiva Siddhānta, the dualist Śaivism that survives today in the temples of Tamil Nadu, and of the Bhairava, Trika and Kaula traditions that culminated in the non-dual Śaivism of Kashmir. Revealed, according to tradition, from the five faces (pañcamukha) of Śiva, these texts govern initiation, daily worship, temple building and consecration, and much of the living temple religion of South India.

docs.title: 2.1 Origin and Authority of the Śaiva Āgamas
2.1.1 The Five Faces of Śiva
docs.text:
The Śaiva Āgamas claim to issue from the five faces of Śiva, each associated with a direction and with one of the five “Brahma” mantras of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. The South Indian tradition distributes the twenty-eight principal Āgamas among the five faces and correlates the faces with Śiva’s five cosmic acts (Table 2.1); both correlations are traditional.

Table 2.1. The Five Faces of Śiva and the Āgamas Traditionally Assigned to Them Face Direction Cosmic act Associated Āgamas Sadyojāta West Creation Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, Ajita Vāmadeva North Preservation Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumat, Suprabheda Aghora South Dissolution Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, Āgneya, Vīra Tatpuruṣa East Concealment Raurava, Makuṭa, Vimala, Candrajñāna, Mukhabimba Īśāna Zenith Grace Prodgīta, Lalita, Siddha, Santāna, Sarvokta, Pārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Vātula

The five mantras themselves, recited daily in Śaiva worship, are:

The Pañcabrahma Mantras (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.43–47)

Sadyojāta: sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi sadyojātāya vai namo namaḥ | bhave bhave nātibhave bhavasva mām | bhavodbhavāya namaḥ || Vāmadeva: vāmadevāya namo jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ śreṣṭhāya namo rudrāya namaḥ kālāya namaḥ … sarvabhūtadamanāya namo manonmanāya namaḥ || Aghora: aghorebhyo ’tha ghorebhyo ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ | sarvataḥ śarva sarvebhyo namas te astu rudrarūpebhyaḥ || Tatpuruṣa: tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi | tan no rudraḥ pracodayāt || Īśāna: īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatir brahmaṇo ’dhipatir brahmā śivo me astu sadāśivom ||

(Sadyojāta) I take refuge in Sadyojāta; homage to Sadyojāta. Do not consign me to birth after birth; guide me beyond birth. Homage to the source of being. (Aghora) To those forms of Rudra that are not terrible, to those that are terrible, to those more terrible than the terrible, to all, O Śarva, in all places: homage to your Rudra-forms. (Tatpuruṣa) May we know that Supreme Person; may we meditate on the Great God; may Rudra inspire us. (Īśāna) May the lord of all knowledge, the ruler of all beings, the overlord of Brahman, Brahmā, be gracious to me: may he be Sadāśiva. (Vāmadeva: a litany of homage to the god’s names and powers.)

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Āgamas and the Vedas
docs.text: The Siddhānta theologians did not reject the Veda. They regarded it as a valid but lower revelation, also spoken by Śiva, suited to the uninitiated; the Āgamas were the higher, specific teaching for initiates. Temple priests (ādiśaivas) recite Vedic mantras alongside Āgamic ones, and Tamil Siddhāntins later spoke of the Veda as the “general” and the Āgama as the “special” scripture. Orthodox Brahmins, for their part, long regarded Śaiva initiates with suspicion (Chapter 1).

docs.title: 2.1.3 Atimārga and Mantramārga
docs.text:
Sanderson’s influential classification divides early Śaivism into two great branches (Sanderson 1988):

The Branches of Early Śaivism

(1) The Atimārga (“outer” or “transcendent path”): orders of ascetics seeking liberation alone — the Pāśupatas, the Lākulas (known in the inscriptions of Karnataka as Kālāmukhas) and the Kāpālikas with their “observance of the skull”. (2) The Mantramārga (“path of mantras”): the Tantric Śaivism open to householders as well as ascetics, seeking both liberation and powers through initiation and mantra. It comprises the Śaiva Siddhānta and the more esoteric Bhairava Tantras (the Mantrapīṭha, centred on Svacchandabhairava, and the Vidyāpīṭha, centred on goddesses and including the Trika), from which the Kaula and Kālī-centred Krama traditions developed. Each system tended to regard those below it as valid but limited.

docs.title: 2.1.4 The Pāśupata Tradition
docs.text:
The Pāśupatas are the earliest Śaiva order for which we have substantial evidence. Their founder, Lakulīśa, probably lived in the second century CE: the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE names a teacher in the line of his disciple Kuśika. The Pāśupatasūtra, with the commentary (Pañcārthabhāṣya) of Kauṇḍinya, teaches:

  1. Five categories (pañcārtha): effect (kārya, the world and souls), cause (kāraṇa, the Lord), union (yoga), observance (vidhi) and the end of suffering (duḥkhānta);

  2. Deliberate dishonour: in an advanced stage the ascetic courts public contempt by feigning madness, making lewd gestures or snoring in public, so that those who abuse him take on his demerit and he receives their merit;

  3. Bathing in ash: smearing the body with ash and lying in ash, a practice that became a mark of Śaivism generally.

docs.title: 2.1.5 Lakulīśa in Art and Memory
docs.text: Lakulīśa, the founder of the Pāśupatas, is shown in sculpture as a naked, seated ascetic holding a club (lakuṭa, from which his name derives) and a citron, often with an erect phallus signifying his continence and mastery. Images of him are common in temples of Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Karnataka from about the sixth to the twelfth century. Tradition places his birth or manifestation at Kāyārohana (modern Karvan, near Vadodara in Gujarat), which remained a Pāśupata centre. Inscriptions record Lakula and Pāśupata teachers across western, central and southern India, showing how widely these ascetic orders spread before the Tantric Mantramārga became dominant (Lorenzen 1972).

docs.title: 2.1.6 The Atimārga in the Sources
docs.text:
Because the Atimārga orders left few texts of their own, they were long known chiefly from their opponents. Research on early Nepalese manuscripts, above all the Niśvāsamukha, has made it possible to see them as the Tantric scriptures saw them. These sources describe the Atimārga in three tiers, which Sanderson has reconstructed as stages of a single development (Sanderson 2009):

  1. The Pāñcārthika Pāśupatas, who followed the Pāśupatasūtra and its five categories, and whose practice culminated in the courting of dishonour described above.

  2. The Lākulas, who adopted the more extreme “great observance” (mahāvrata): the ascetic carried a skull as a begging bowl and a staff topped by a skull (khaṭvāṅga), wore ornaments of human bone and smeared himself with the ash of cremation grounds. The Lākulas also elaborated a cosmology of many worlds through which the liberated soul ascends, an intermediate stage between the Pāśupata system and that of the Tantras.

  3. The Kāpālikas (“skull-bearers”), who called their system the “Soma doctrine” (Somasiddhānta), lived in cremation grounds and worshipped Bhairava with his consort, with offerings of meat and alcohol and rites involving women. Their practice leads directly to the Bhairava Tantras of the Mantramārga (Section 2.5), and they are often regarded as precursors of the later Aghorīs.

Lākulas and Kālāmukhas. The two names refer to one order, not two. In the inscriptions of Karnataka the Lākulas of the second tier appear as “Kālāmukhas” (“black-faced”), the spelling used by Lorenzen and by most historians of the region; Sanderson, who identifies the inscriptional Kālāmukhas with the Lākulas of the scriptures, writes the name “Kālamukha” (Lorenzen 1972; Sanderson 2009). This volume uses the conventional form Kālāmukha for the order as it appears in the inscriptions.

The penance of the skull. The skull observance had a Brahmanical model. The Dharmaśāstras prescribe that a man who has killed a Brahmin should live for twelve years in a hut in the forest, begging, and carrying the skull of a dead man as his emblem (e.g. Manusmṛti 11.73). Śaiva myth told that Bhairava, having cut off one of Brahmā’s heads, had to wander with the skull stuck to his hand until he reached Vārāṇasī, where it fell away. The Kāpālika ascetic imitated the god’s penance, but transformed its meaning: what for the Dharmaśāstra was the expiation of the worst of sins became, for the Śaiva, an identification with Śiva in his most terrible form (Lorenzen 1972). Stella Kramrisch’s study of Śiva’s mythology traces the many tellings of this myth of the god’s own transgression and penance (Kramrisch 1981).

Hostile portraits. Literary sources from the seventh century onwards present the skull-bearers as figures of fear or ridicule:

  • in Mahendravarman I’s farce Mattavilāsa (7th century) a drunken Kāpālika, Satyasoma, and his female companion lose their skull bowl and accuse a Buddhist monk of stealing it;

  • in the play Mālatīmādhava by Bhavabhūti (early 8th century), the Kāpālika Aghoraghaṇṭa and his female pupil Kapālakuṇḍalā abduct the heroine to sacrifice her to the goddess Karālā at a shrine beside the cremation ground of the city, while another adept of the play has won her powers on the mountain Śrīparvata (Śrīśailam);

  • in Kṛṣṇamiśra’s allegorical drama Prabodhacandrodaya (late 11th century) a Kāpālika expounds the “Soma doctrine” and wins over a Jain and a Buddhist with wine and the embrace of his female partner.

The Vaiṣṇava theologians Yāmuna and Rāmānuja, refuting the Śaivas, report that the Kāpālikas wore six insignia — necklace, neck ornament, earrings, crest jewel, ash and sacred thread — and that the Kālāmukhas ate from skulls, smeared themselves with the ash of corpses and worshipped the god in a pot of wine. These reports are polemical, but their details match the scriptures’ own descriptions of the skull observance closely enough to show that they were not invented (Lorenzen 1972).

The inscriptional Kālāmukhas. The inscriptions of Karnataka present an entirely different picture. There the Kālāmukhas, whose ascetics’ names often end in -rāśi or -śakti, appear as heads of richly endowed temple-monasteries, such as the Koḍiya monastery at Baḷḷigāve (Belgami) in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The inscriptions praise them as masters of grammar, logic, Mīmāṃsā and poetry, and as providers of food, medicine and teaching; they record grants from kings and local lords and describe the ascetics as followers of the Lākula doctrine. Lorenzen argued that the order lost its monasteries and much of its following to the Vīraśaivas in the thirteenth century (Lorenzen 1972). The contrast between the skull-bearing ascetic of the scriptures and the scholarly abbot of the inscriptions shows how far an order founded on renunciation could be drawn into the institutional religion of the early medieval kingdoms (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 2.2 The Four Pādas
docs.text: The ideal Siddhānta Āgama consists of four sections (pādas); in practice the ritual section is usually by far the longest and some texts lack one or more of the others.

docs.title: 2.2.1 The Vidyāpāda or Jñānapāda
docs.text:
The doctrinal section sets out the three categories (padārthas) of the Siddhānta:

  • Pati, the Lord Śiva: omniscient, omnipotent, eternally free, who performs five acts (creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment and grace) for the sake of souls;

  • Paśu, the soul (“bound beast”): innumerable, eternal and distinct from Śiva. Souls are by nature conscious agents, but their powers of knowledge and action are obscured;

  • Pāśa, the bonds: the innate impurity (āṇavamala), karma, māyā (the material cause of bodies and worlds), and Śiva’s own concealing power (tirodhānaśakti).

Because impurity is understood as a real substance, the Siddhānta holds that knowledge alone cannot remove it: only a ritual act — initiation — can. The Siddhāntins describe these bonds as three impurities (malas): the beginningless innate impurity (āṇavamala), which obscures the soul’s powers of knowledge and action and makes it “atomic” (aṇu) or limited; the bond of māyā (māyīyamala), the bodies, faculties and worlds that partly reveal the soul’s powers even as they bind it; and karma (kārmamala), the residue of past action that determines birth and experience.

The cosmos in which souls are bound is described as a hierarchy of thirty-six principles (tattvas), from Śiva down to earth, which extends the twenty-five tattvas of Sāṁkhya by eleven higher ones. The scheme is common to the Siddhānta and the non-dual Kashmiri schools, and it is set out once, for the whole volume, in Table 2.2. The two schools interpret it differently: for the Siddhānta the lower tattvas are the real evolutes of māyā, distinct from souls and from the Lord; for the non-dualists the whole series describes the stages by which a single consciousness contracts itself (Section 6.4). They also group the intermediate levels differently, as the table notes.

Table 2.2. The Thirty-Six Tattvas of the Śaiva Traditions Tattvas Description Pure (śuddha), 1–5 Śiva Pure consciousness Śakti The power of consciousness Sadāśiva Lord of the pure creation; in Kashmiri non-dualism, “I am this” with stress on “I” Īśvara In Kashmiri non-dualism, “I am this” with stress on “this” Śuddhavidyā Pure knowledge Mixed (śuddhāśuddha), 6–12 Māyā Principle of limitation; material cause of the impure worlds Five kañcukas Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati: limited agency, knowledge, attachment, time and causal order Puruṣa The soul as limited experiencer Impure (aśuddha), 13–36 Prakṛti Primal matter Buddhi, ahaṅkāra, manas The inner faculties Five jñānendriyas Cognitive senses Five karmendriyas Faculties of action Five tanmātras Subtle elements Five mahābhūtas Gross elements

The grouping 5 + 7 + 24 is that of the Siddhānta, which counts Puruṣa with Māyā and its coverings. Kashmiri presentations commonly treat Māyā and the five coverings (6–11) as the intermediate level and place Puruṣa at the head of the impure level (12–36).

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Yogapāda
docs.text:
The yoga of the Śaiva Āgamas is not Patañjali’s eight-limbed yoga but usually a “six-limbed” yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) consisting of breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), fixation (dhāraṇā), reasoning or discernment (tarka) and absorption (samādhi). Meditations on the tattvas, on mantras and on luminous forms of Śiva, and techniques for gaining yogic powers, are typical (Mallinson and Singleton 2017).

The fullest early account of this yoga is found in the Mālinīvijayottara, the scripture on which Abhinavagupta built his Trika (Chapter 6), whose yogic chapters Somadeva Vasudeva has edited and translated (Vasudeva 2004). Its yoga is organised around the hierarchy of the cosmos itself. The yogin fixes his mind successively on the levels of reality, beginning with the element earth and rising through the higher tattvas, and each successful fixation is said to give him mastery over that level and over the beings and powers that belong to it. The fixations (dhāraṇās) on the five elements are central: for each element the text prescribes its own visualisation and describes the signs by which progress is recognised and the powers that follow. The yogin’s ascent through the tattvas thus mirrors the ritual ascent through the same levels that the guru performs for the candidate in initiation (Section 2.12); yoga and ritual are two ways of travelling the one map of the cosmos.

Two further features distinguish this yoga from Patañjali’s. The first is the place of “reasoning” (tarka), which in the Mālinīvijayottara and in Abhinavagupta’s reading of it is not logical argument but a discriminating insight that separates what is to be rejected from what is to be accepted on the path; Abhinavagupta ranked it highest among the limbs. The second is that the goal is not the isolation of the soul from matter but a progressive identification with ever higher levels of Śiva’s power, culminating in a state of “absorption” (samāveśa) into Śiva. The scripture’s threefold classification of such absorption became the basis of Abhinavagupta’s doctrine of the “means” (upāyas) to liberation (Section 6.8) (Vasudeva 2004; Sanderson 1988). The yoga of the Śaiva scriptures, and the subtle-body practices that grew out of it (Section 2.13), are also the background of the later haṭha yoga treated in Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī.

docs.title: 2.2.3 The Kriyāpāda
docs.text:
The ritual section covers:

  • initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (abhiṣeka);

  • daily obligatory worship (nityapūjā) and fire offering (homa);

  • temple building (vāstu), from testing the site to the finial;

  • the making and installation of images (pratiṣṭhā);

  • occasional and optional rites, festivals (utsava) and expiations (prāyaścitta);

  • funerary and ancestral rites for initiates.

docs.title: 2.2.4 The Caryāpāda
docs.text: The section on conduct prescribes the observances of initiates: purity, conduct towards the guru, the rules (samayas) of each grade of initiate, expiations for breaking them, and the outward marks of the Śaiva. Sacred ash (vibhūti, bhasma) is applied in three horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts of the body. It recalls Śiva’s ash-smeared ascetic form and the Pāśupata bath in ash; theologically it is read as what remains when all else is burnt away, and it marks both purification and membership of the Śaiva community. Rudrākṣa (“eye of Rudra”) beads, the seeds of Elaeocarpus species of the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia, are worn and used for counting mantras. Later Purāṇic texts and popular manuals associate beads with different numbers of natural divisions (mukhas) with different deities and benefits; these lists vary, and the benefits claimed for them are matters of devotion.

docs.title: 2.3 The Śaiva Siddhānta
docs.text: The Siddhānta arose in North India; its great early exegetes, such as Sadyojyotis (c. 675–725) (Sanderson 2006), Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and his son Rāmakaṇṭha (10th century), worked in Kashmir. By the eleventh and twelfth centuries its centre of gravity had moved south: the ritual manual of Somaśambhu (1095 CE) and the works of Aghoraśiva of Chidambaram (12th century) became standard in Tamil temples (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998; Davis 1991). From the thirteenth century a distinct Tamil school developed, combining the Sanskrit Āgamas with the Tamil devotional hymns.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Canonical Literature
docs.text:
The main sources of the Śaiva Siddhānta are summarised in Table 2.3.

Table 2.3. Sources of the Śaiva Siddhānta Stream Language Key texts Āgamas Sanskrit The twenty-eight Āgamas and their upaāgamas (in practice especially the Kāmika, Kāraṇa, Ajita, Suprabheda and the Mṛgendra) Exegesis and manuals Sanskrit Sadyojyotis’s Nareśvaraparīkṣā; Bhoja’s Tattvaprakāśa; Rāmakaṇṭha’s commentaries; the paddhatis of Somaśambhu and Aghoraśiva Tēvāram Tamil Hymns of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (7th–9th century) Tiruvācakam Tamil Hymns of Māṇikkavācakar (c. 9th century) Tirumantiram Tamil About 3,000 verses ascribed to Tirumūlar; date disputed Periyapurāṇam Tamil Lives of the 63 Nāyaṉmārs by Cēkkiḻār (12th century) Meykaṇṭa Śāstras Tamil Fourteen doctrinal works headed by Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th century)

The Tamil hymns were later collected in the twelve-part canon of the Tirumuṟai.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Meykaṇṭār and the Tamil School
docs.text: Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th century) consists of twelve short Tamil sūtras with brief explanatory notes (vārttikas). The twelve Sanskrit verses known as the Śivajñānabodha and said to come from the Rauravāgama closely parallel them; whether they are the source or a later back-translation is debated. Meykaṇṭār and his successors, notably Aruḷnanti and Umāpati Śivācārya (14th century), produced the fourteen Meykaṇṭa Śāstras. The Tamil school retains the eternal distinction of souls from Śiva but describes liberation as a state of “non-duality” (advaita) in the sense of inseparability, in which the soul is united with Śiva as a sound is with a letter or a body with its soul.

docs.title: 2.3.3 The Structure of the Civañāṉapōtam
docs.text:
The twelve sūtras of Meykaṇṭār’s work are traditionally grouped in four sets of three. The first set offers proofs: that the world, which appears as “he”, “she” and “it” and undergoes origination and dissolution, must have a Lord as its cause; that the Lord is one with souls in the sense of being inseparable from them, yet distinct; and that the soul exists as something other than body, senses and mind. The second set defines the nature of soul, bonds and Lord. The third describes the means: the soul’s realisation of its own nature through the Lord’s grace, which comes in the form of the guru. The fourth describes the fruit: the liberated soul’s union with Śiva, the removal of the bonds, and the life of the liberated in the company of Śiva’s devotees, worshipping the guru’s form and the temple image as Śiva himself.

The Tamil school’s major later works include Aruḷnanti’s Civañāṉacittiyār (13th century), a long verse exposition that also refutes rival schools, and Umāpati Śivācārya’s works of the fourteenth century, which completed the canon of fourteen treatises. The ātīṉams, monasteries headed by non-Brahmin Śaiva ascetics such as those at Tiruvāvaṭutuṟai and Dharmapuram, became the main institutional home of this Tamil theology and of the study of the hymns.

docs.title: 2.3.4 The Sixty-Three Nāyaṉmārs
docs.text: The sixty-three Śaiva saints of the Tamil country include kings and peasants, women and men, Brahmins and devotees of low and “untouchable” birth. Their lives are told in Cēkkiḻār’s Periyapurāṇam (12th century), and their images, among them those of the hymnists Appar, Campantar and Cuntarar, the woman poet Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār and the king Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ, stand in many Tamil temples. The hagiographies celebrate extreme devotion that overrides social convention — the hunter Kaṇṇappar offering his own eyes, the Pulaiyar devotee Nandanār passing through fire to enter Chidambaram — even as the stories also reflect the caste order they describe (Peterson 1989).

docs.title: 2.4 The Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā
docs.text:
The Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, preserved in a single Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript of about the ninth century, is the oldest surviving Śaiva Tantra. It is not a unified work but a collection of five books composed over a period of perhaps two centuries: the Mūlasūtra, the oldest, whose core its editors date to about 450–550 CE; the Uttarasūtra; the Nayasūtra, which deals with doctrine and yoga; the Guhyasūtra, the longest; and the Niśvāsamukha, an introduction that places the Mantramārga in relation to the lay Śaivism of the Purāṇas, the Vedic religion and the ascetic Atimārga (Goodall et al. 2015).

The text shows Tantric Śaivism at an early stage. It already teaches initiation that liberates, mantras extracted in code, the worship of Śiva with his five faces, the tattvas and the yoga of the Mantramārga, but much of its ritual is simpler than that of the later Siddhānta, and it draws heavily on Vedic and Purāṇic material. It also includes extensive sections on rites for worldly ends, showing that the pursuit of powers was part of Tantric Śaivism from the beginning. Its critical edition, whose first volume appeared in 2015, has transformed our understanding of the origins of the Āgamas.

docs.title: 2.5 The Bhairava Tantras
docs.text:
Beside the Siddhānta, the Mantramārga comprised a second and more esoteric body of scripture, the Tantras of Bhairava, the fierce form of Śiva. Their followers regarded them as a higher revelation than the Siddhānta; Siddhānta authors, for their part, treated them as meant chiefly for initiates who sought supernatural powers (Sanderson 1988, 2009). They fall into two main groups.

The Mantrapīṭha (“seat of the mantras”) centres on Svacchandabhairava, a five-faced form of Bhairava, and his consort Aghoreśvarī. Its principal scripture, the Svacchandatantra, with the commentary (Uddyota) of Kṣemarāja, became the basis of the ordinary Śaiva ritual of Kashmir. Closely related is the Netratantra, devoted to Amṛteśvara, the “Lord of the nectar of immortality”, also called Mṛtyujit, “conqueror of death”; it provides rites of protection and healing, including rites for the protection of kings, and was likewise commented on by Kṣemarāja.

The Vidyāpīṭha (“seat of the female mantras”) is centred on goddesses. Its scriptures are divided into the Yāmala (“union”) Tantras, of which the Brahmayāmala or Picumata is the oldest surviving, and the Śakti Tantras, which include the scriptures of the Trika (the Siddhayogeśvarīmata and the Mālinīvijayottara) and the vast, Kālī-centred Jayadrathayāmala in four books. In the Brahmayāmala the deity is Kapālīśabhairava with the goddess Caṇḍā Kapālinī, surrounded by goddesses and their attendant yoginīs. The text prescribes the “great observance” (mahāvrata) of the skull-bearing ascetic, worship in cremation grounds, offerings of blood, meat and alcohol, ritual with female partners and the propitiation of yoginīs, with the aim of gaining powers such as flight and, ultimately, liberation (Hatley 2018).

These scriptures are the common source of the Kaula traditions (Chapter 4), of the Trika and Krama of Kashmir (Chapter 6) and, as Sanderson has shown, of much of the Buddhist Yoginītantras (Chapter 10). Their cult of the yoginīs is also reflected in the open-air yoginī temples of central and eastern India (Section 4.10).

docs.title: 2.6 The Other Streams: Gāruḍa, Bhūta and Vāma Tantras
docs.text:
The Siddhānta and the Bhairava Tantras were not the whole of the Mantramārga. Several scriptures and their exegetes describe the Śaiva revelation as flowing in five “streams” (srotas), each issuing from one of the five faces of Sadāśiva (Table 2.4). In this scheme the Siddhānta comes from the upper face, Īśāna, and the Bhairava Tantras from the southern face, Aghora, which is why they are also called the “southern” (dakṣiṇa) Tantras; the eastern, northern and western faces reveal three further classes of scripture, the Gāruḍa, the Vāma and the Bhūta Tantras (Sanderson 1988). The Brahmayāmala devotes a whole chapter (its thirty-ninth) to a myth of the origin of the streams, which shows that the scheme was already current among the authors of the Vidyāpīṭha (Hatley 2018). It should be distinguished from the later South Indian practice, described above (Table 2.1), of distributing the twenty-eight Siddhānta Āgamas themselves among the five faces: in the older scheme each face reveals a different kind of scripture, and only one of them is the Siddhānta.

Table 2.4. The Five Streams (Srotas) of the Mantramārga Stream Face and direction Concern What survives Siddhānta Īśāna, upper Liberation through initiation; the regular worship of Śiva Many Āgamas, ritual manuals and commentaries (this chapter) Gāruḍa Tatpuruṣa, east Snakebite and poison Scriptures lost; quotations, the digest Kriyākālaguṇottara, later compendia Vāma Vāmadeva, north Tumburu and his four sisters; protection and magic The Vīṇāśikhatantra Bhūta Sadyojāta, west Possessing spirits and their exorcism Scriptures lost; digests and quotations Bhairava (Dakṣiṇa) Aghora, south Fierce deities; powers and liberation Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha Tantras (Section 2.5)

The three middle streams have fared badly. Their scriptures were concerned less with liberation than with protection, healing and power, they were not adopted by the monastic and temple institutions that copied and commented on the Siddhānta, and almost all of them are lost. Yet they were once widely known: early Śaiva scriptures, the Buddhist Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa and later Purāṇas cite or absorb their teachings, and some of their mantras are still used.

docs.title: 2.6.1 The Gāruḍa Tantras and Tantric Medicine
docs.text:
Michael Slouber’s study of the Gāruḍa Tantras, the first book-length treatment of this literature, places them within a wider body of “Tantric medicine” with three branches: the exorcism of possessing beings, taught in the Bhūta Tantras; the treatment of illnesses of pregnancy and childhood, taught in the Bāla Tantras; and the treatment of snakebite and other poisons, the domain of the Gāruḍa Tantras (Slouber 2017). The healer in this system is not a physician in the Āyurvedic sense but an initiate (mantrin, gāruḍika) who, by identifying himself in meditation with a mantra-deity, acquires that deity’s power over the poison. The Āyurvedic branches of toxicology (agadatantra) and of the “science of spirits” (bhūtavidyā) are described in Volume 13, Āyurveda; the Tantric literature treated here ran parallel to them and borrowed from them.

The deity of the Gāruḍa Tantras is Garuḍa, the eagle who is the enemy of snakes. Contrary to what one might expect, he is not here the mount of Viṣṇu but an independent deity, conceived as a form of Śiva in the same way as Bhairava; the practitioner visualises Garuḍa as filling the cosmos and transforms himself into him. In the goddess-centred Tvaritāmūlasūtra Garuḍa even fights and defeats Viṣṇu. The central mantra is a five-syllable formula of Garuḍa, which Slouber traces in at least thirty premodern texts and finds still in use from Kerala to Tibet; another cycle centres on Śiva as Nīlakaṇṭha, the “blue-throated” god who swallowed the poison churned from the ocean, with a three-syllable mantra. A further group of rites is addressed to “snakebite goddesses” such as Tvaritā and the Buddhist Kurukullā, figures who move freely between Śaiva, Śākta, Buddhist and Jain settings (Slouber 2017).

The scriptures themselves are lost, but much of their content survives in later works. The most important is the Kriyākālaguṇottara, a digest of the Bhūta and Gāruḍa Tantras composed by about the eleventh century, of which Slouber edited and translated ten chapters from Nepalese manuscripts; it incorporates long passages from otherwise lost scriptures. Gāruḍa material also passed into the Agni, Nārada and Garuḍa Purāṇas, into Jain and Buddhist literature — the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa openly announces that it incorporates Gāruḍa teachings and makes Garuḍa a bodhisattva — and into the late medieval compendia of Kerala, where the treatment of snakebite (viṣavaidyam) remained a recognised specialism. Slouber argues that the Gāruḍa Tantras were not a marginal magical appendix to Śaivism: they taught a complete Tantric system with initiation and a soteriological goal, and the modern habit of contrasting a “rational” Āyurveda with “magical” healing misrepresents both (Slouber 2017).

Health and Safety Note

Snakebite is a medical emergency. The mantras and rites described in this section are reported as history; neither they nor traditional antidotes are a substitute for immediate transport to a hospital and treatment with antivenom by trained staff.

docs.title: 2.6.2 The Bhūta Tantras and Possession
docs.text: The Bhūta Tantras dealt with the many classes of beings — bhūtas, grahas (“seizers”), piśācas and others — held to cause illness and madness by possessing human beings, and with the rites by which a mantra-master could identify, propitiate or expel them. Like the Gāruḍa Tantras they are known chiefly through the Kriyākālaguṇottara and through quotation. Material of the same kind entered the Bhairava Tantras: the Netratantra, whose protective rites for kings were mentioned above, contains a long treatment of possessing beings and their expulsion by the mantra of Amṛteśvara. Frederick Smith’s survey of possession in Sanskrit literature shows how this Tantric material connects with the Āyurvedic doctrine of the seizers that afflict children and the insane, with Purāṇic and narrative literature, and with the possession and exorcism that remain part of religious life at goddess shrines and healing temples across South Asia (Smith 2006).

docs.title: 2.6.3 The Vāma Tantras: Tumburu and His Sisters
docs.text:
The northern, “left” (vāma) stream centred on Tumburu, a four-faced form of Śiva, and his four sisters, the goddesses Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī (or Ajitā) and Aparājitā. Its only surviving scripture is the Vīṇāśikhatantra, edited and translated by Teun Goudriaan, which prescribes initiation, the worship of the five deities of the system, meditations on the subtle body and a range of rites for subjugating, attracting and harming (Goudriaan 1985). In this cult goddesses already hold a prominent place, though subordinate to Tumburu; it is one of the earliest Śaiva systems in which they do. The Vīṇāśikha is one of the four Tantras that the Sdok Kak Thom inscription says were taught at the Khmer court in the ninth century (Section 12.7), and the four sisters were also known to Buddhist literature. The cult nevertheless seems to have faded early in India, and the stream survives mainly as a name in the classifications.

Taken together, the lost streams show that early Tantric Śaivism was not only a religion of liberation and temple worship but also a broad repertory of services — healing, protection, exorcism — offered to kings and ordinary people alike. This helps to explain the success of the Śaiva traditions in the early medieval centuries (Chapter 12), and why the figure of the mantra-healer, often called a “tāntrik”, has outlived much of the scriptural tradition that produced it.

docs.title: 2.7 The Mṛgendra Āgama
docs.text: The Mṛgendra, which presents itself as a supplement to the Kāmika, is among the most studied Siddhānta scriptures. It contains doctrinal, yogic, ritual and conduct sections, and its vidyāpāda sets out Siddhānta doctrine with unusual clarity. Its commentary (vṛtti) by the Kashmiri Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha (10th century) was in turn commented on by Aghoraśiva, and the text was edited by N.R. Bhatt, with a French translation of its ritual and conduct sections by Hélène Brunner, at Pondicherry.

docs.title: 2.8.1 The Kāmika
docs.text: The Kāmika stands first in the traditional list and is one of the most frequently cited authorities in South Indian temple practice. The text now known under this name, printed in Madras from 1975, is a large South Indian compilation dealing with temple construction, consecration, daily worship, festivals and expiations; it is considerably later than the Kāmika quoted by early Kashmiri authors and borrows from the twelfth-century manuals.

docs.title: 2.8.2 The Kiraṇa
docs.text: The Kiraṇa is one of the early Siddhānta scriptures; a Nepalese manuscript of it is dated 924 CE. Its doctrinal section was commented on by Rāmakaṇṭha (10th century), who used it to defend the dualist Siddhānta against both non-Śaiva schools and the emerging non-dualist exegesis of the Trika. The commentary has been critically edited and translated by Dominic Goodall (Goodall 1998).

docs.title: 2.8.3 The Raurava
docs.text: The Raurava takes its name from the sage Ruru, to whom it is said to have been taught. An early Rauravasūtrasaṅgraha survives; the much longer South Indian Rauravāgama edited by N.R. Bhatt deals principally with ritual, temple building and image installation (Bhatt 1961–1988).

docs.title: 2.8.4 The Svāyambhuva
docs.text: An early Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha, with doctrinal, ritual, yogic and conduct sections, is quoted by the Kashmiri exegetes and survives in Nepalese manuscripts; its doctrinal section was edited and translated by Pierre-Sylvain Filliozat. As with other titles on the list, later South Indian works also circulate under the name.

docs.title: 2.8.5 The Ajita
docs.text:
The Ajita is a South Indian ritual compendium of the later type, edited in four volumes by N.R. Bhatt at the IFP. It deals at length with temple construction, consecration, worship and festivals.

Scholarly Note: The Upaāgamas

Each of the twenty-eight principal Āgamas is said to have subsidiary texts (upaāgamas), traditionally numbered at 207, most of them lost. Some have independent importance: the Pauṣkara, counted as an upaāgama of the Pārameśvara, has a significant doctrinal section, and the Mṛgendra presents itself as part of the Kāmika.

docs.title: 2.9 The Daily Worship of the Temple
docs.text:
A large Tamil Śaiva temple performs worship up to six times a day. The Tamil names of the services are (Table 2.5):

Table 2.5. The Six Daily Services in Large Tamil Śaiva Temples No. Tamil name Time Character 1 Tiruvaṉantal Dawn Awakening of the deity 2 Kālacanti Early morning Morning worship 3 Uccikālam Noon Midday worship 4 Cāyarakṣai (Skt. sāyarakṣā) Dusk Evening worship 5 Iraṇṭāṅkālam Night Second evening service 6 Arttajāmam (Skt. ardhayāma) Late night Final service; the deity is put to rest

Each service follows the sequence laid down in the manuals: the priest’s own purification and divinisation of his body, the worship of the doorkeepers and attendant deities, invocation of Śiva into the liṅga, offerings (upacāras) of water, bathing, clothing, ornaments, food, lamps and incense, recitation of mantras, and dismissal or “retention” of the deity (Davis 1991). The temple’s architecture is also interpreted as a body, with the sanctum as the heart or womb and the superstructure as the head; Chapter 11 discusses this homology.

docs.title: 2.9.1 The Daily Worship of Śiva in the Siddhānta Manuals
docs.text:
The Siddhānta manuals, above all that of Somaśambhu (1095), lay down a daily worship of Śiva (śivapūjā) that every initiate of the higher grades was obliged to perform, whether at home or, in the case of temple priests, on behalf of a temple. Its sequence, studied in detail by Hélène Brunner and Richard Davis, is the skeleton of the temple services described above (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998; Davis 1991):

  1. Bath (snāna): a bath with water and with ash, accompanied by mantras, followed by the twilight rites (sandhyā).

  2. Entry and the doorkeepers: the worshipper enters the place of worship after honouring the door and its guardians (dvārapālas) and expelling obstacles with the weapon mantra.

  3. The fivefold purification (pañcaśuddhi): purification of the place (sthāna), of the self (ātman), of the substances (dravya), of the mantras (mantra) and of the liṅga. Purification of the self includes the destruction and re-creation of the body (bhūtaśuddhi) and the placing of mantras on it, so that the worshipper becomes a “Śiva” fit to worship Śiva.

  4. Inner worship: Śiva is worshipped mentally in the heart, and in some manuals in the fire of the navel and at the crown.

  5. The throne: the seat of Śiva is worshipped as a series of cosmic supports — the divine power of support, the cosmic tortoise and serpent, the four legs of virtue, knowledge, detachment and sovereignty, and a lotus — installed over the liṅga.

  6. Invocation: Śiva, in the form of Sadāśiva with five faces and ten arms, is visualised and invoked from the heart into the liṅga with his root mantra; his five Brahma mantras and six “limb” mantras are installed on the form.

  7. Offerings: water for the feet and for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), bathing, garments, unguents, flowers, incense, lamp and food, each with its mantra and gesture.

  8. The retinue: the attendant deities in the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas) — the “limb” mantras, the eight Vidyeśvaras, the guardians of the directions and their weapons — are worshipped in turn.

  9. Recitation and surrender: the root mantra is recited and the merit of the recitation is offered to Śiva; praise and prostration follow.

  10. Fire offering and conclusion: in the full form a fire offering follows; at the end the remains of the offerings are given to Caṇdeśa, the guardian of Śiva’s leftovers, and Śiva is dismissed or asked to remain in the liṅga, with a request for forgiveness for errors.

The structure — purification and divinisation of the worshipper, installation of the deity, hospitality, and dismissal — is common to almost all Tantric worship, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta and Buddhist.

docs.title: 2.10 The Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata Tradition
docs.text:
The Liṅgāyata or Vīraśaiva movement of twelfth-century Karnataka, associated above all with Basava (Basaveśvara), a minister at the Kalacuri court of Kalyāṇa, was a radical current within Śaivism:

  • The personal liṅga: every Liṅgāyata wears a small iṣṭaliṅga on the body, making the body itself the place of worship.

  • Rejection of temple religion: the poets mocked temple building, pilgrimage, sacrifice and priestly ritual. In one of Basava’s best-known vacanas the poor devotee, unable to build a temple, declares his legs the pillars, his body the shrine and his head the golden cupola (Ramanujan 1973).

  • Social critique: the movement rejected caste hierarchy, ideas of ritual pollution and the subordination of women; tradition holds that a marriage between a Brahmin and an “untouchable” family within the community provoked the violence that ended the early movement.

  • The vacanas: Basava, Akka Mahādēvi, Allama Prabhu, Dēvara Dāsimayya and many others, including women and men of artisan and low-caste backgrounds, composed free-verse “sayings” in Kannada, one of the great bodies of Indian devotional literature.

  • Doctrine and practice: the later theology systematised the path as six stages (ṣaṭsthala) and defined Liṅgāyata identity by eight “coverings” (aṣṭāvaraṇa: guru, liṅga, the wandering teacher or jaṅgama, sacred water, consecrated food, ash, rudrākṣa and mantra) and five codes of conduct (pañcācāra). The ideal of kāyaka, dignified work as worship, is central.

Whether Liṅgāyatism is a branch of Śaivism or a distinct religion has been debated in Karnataka since the nineteenth century and remains politically live.

docs.title: 2.11 Liberation in the Siddhānta and in Kashmiri Non-dualism
docs.text: The two great Śaiva theologies agree that liberation is the work of Śiva’s grace, but they disagree about what it is and how it comes. For the Siddhānta, liberation is “equality with Śiva” (śivasāmya): the soul’s innate omniscience and omnipotence become fully manifest, but it remains a distinct soul, equal to Śiva and not identical with him. Since its bondage is a real impurity, the means is a real act — initiation, followed by lifelong worship — and knowledge alone is insufficient; the soul is finally released from its bonds at death. Siddhānta authors such as Sadyojyotis and Rāmakaṇṭha defended this realist and pluralist position in sustained debate with Buddhists, Mīmāṃsakas and the Śaiva non-dualists (Goodall 1998). For the Kashmiri non-dualists, by contrast, liberation is the recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one’s identity with Śiva, who alone exists. It is reached through grace and insight, by the “means” (upāyas) that culminate in the “means-less” (anupāya); ritual is valued as an expression of insight rather than as its cause; and one may be “liberated while living” (jīvanmukta), experiencing everything as the play of one’s own consciousness (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 2.12 The Theory of Initiation
docs.text: Initiation (dīkṣā) is the central transformative event of the Śaiva religion. For the Siddhānta, since impurity is a substance, only the ritual action of initiation, in which Śiva acts through the guru, can remove it. A frequently cited traditional explanation derives the word dīkṣā from “giving” (dā) knowledge and “destroying” (kṣi) bondage.

docs.title: 2.12.1 The Grades of Initiation
docs.text:
The Siddhānta distinguishes a preliminary initiation, a liberating initiation and two further consecrations, each of which confers a grade with its own entitlements (adhikāra) and obligations (Table 2.6). Other traditions have their own sequences: the Śrīvaiṣṇava five sacraments (Section 3.7), the Buddhist consecrations (Table 10.2) and the “full consecration” (pūrṇābhiṣeka) of later Śākta lineages. A form of the liberating initiation that releases the initiate from its obligations, the “seedless” initiation given to kings, children and others, is discussed in Section 12.4.
