Table 2.6. The Grades of Śaiva Initiation and Their Entitlements Rite Grade Nature, purpose and entitlement Samayadīkṣā Samayin Preliminary initiation, which purifies the candidate, imposes the rules (samayas) and qualifies him or her to hear the scriptures, receive mantras and attend worship Nirvāṇadīkṣā Putraka Liberating initiation, in which the guru, through fire offerings, ritually purifies the candidate’s soul through all levels of the cosmos and destroys the karma that would cause future births; the putraka (“son”) performs the daily worship of Śiva Sādhakābhiṣeka Sādhaka Consecration, after the liberating initiation, of one who will propitiate a mantra-deity to gain powers (siddhi) Ācāryābhiṣeka Ācārya Consecration, after the liberating initiation, conferring authority to initiate others and to consecrate images and temples; in South India the temple priesthood came to be restricted to hereditary ādiśaiva lineages

docs.title: 2.12.2 The Ritual of the Liberating Initiation
docs.text:
The nirvāṇadīkṣā is described in detail in the Āgamas and especially in the manuals of Somaśambhu and others (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998):

  1. Preliminaries (adhivāsa): purifications of the candidate the day before; the guru interprets the candidate’s dreams as omens.

  2. Fire: the guru establishes and consecrates the sacrificial fire in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and invokes Śiva in it.

  3. The cord: a cord (pāśasūtra) is hung from the candidate’s crown to his toe, and the bonds and the levels of the cosmos are ritually “placed” in it.

  4. Purification of the paths (adhvaśodhana): the guru draws the candidate’s soul out and leads it through the six “paths” of the cosmos — including the thirty-six tattvas and the 224 worlds (bhuvanas) of the Siddhānta — purifying each with oblations.

  5. Destruction of karma: all karma except the portion that has begun to bear fruit in the present life (prārabdha) is burnt; this present body remains until death.

  6. Union with Śiva: the soul is joined to Śiva and returned to the candidate’s body; the cord is cut and burnt.

docs.title: 2.13.1 Channels (Nāḍīs)
docs.text: Śaiva and later yogic texts describe a network of subtle channels, conventionally 72,000, through which the breath or vital force (prāṇa) moves. Three are paramount: the central channel (suṣumnā), through which the yogin’s breath or kuṇḍalinī is made to rise, and the channels to its left (iḍā), associated with the moon and the left nostril, and to its right (piṅgalā), associated with the sun and the right nostril. Tantric traditions value the body as the instrument and site of liberation rather than an obstacle to it, and this map of the body is the ground of much of their yoga.

docs.title: 2.13.2 Systems of Centres (Cakras)
docs.text:
The early Siddhānta scriptures describe various sets of centres in the body — ādhāras (supports), granthis (knots), lakṣyas (targets of meditation) — and there was no single canonical list. Different Tantras teach four, five, six or more cakras. The Kubjikā scriptures of the tenth century or later are among the earliest to teach a system of six centres resembling the later standard one (Section 4.11); Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka treats kuṇḍalinī not as a physical force but as the contracted power of consciousness, whose awakening is the recognition of one’s own nature; the Nātha Gorakṣaśataka (c. 13th–14th century) and the Haṭhapradīpikā (c. 15th century) give the early haṭha-yoga accounts of its awakening; and the system of six cakras with the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown that is now familiar worldwide was given its classic form in Pūrṇānanda’s Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (1577), the work through which Arthur Avalon’s The Serpent Power made it known in the West (Avalon 1919; Flood 2006). Table 2.7 summarises that scheme.

Table 2.7. The Six Cakras and the Crown in the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa Cakra Location Petals Element Bīja Deities Mūlādhāra Perineum 4 Earth laṃ Brahmā; Ḍākinī Svādhiṣṭhāna Genital region 6 Water vaṃ Viṣṇu; Rākinī Maṇipūra Navel 10 Fire raṃ Rudra; Lākinī Anāhata Heart 12 Air yaṃ Īśa; Kākinī Viśuddha Throat 16 Ether haṃ Sadāśiva; Śākinī Ājñā Between the brows 2 Mind oṃ Śambhu; Hākinī Sahasrāra Crown 1000 — — Śiva and Śakti in union

Earlier texts teach many different systems, and this scheme should not be read back into them. The association of the cakras with endocrine glands, nerve plexuses, rainbow colours or psychological qualities derives from twentieth-century Theosophical and New Age writing, not from the Sanskrit sources (White 2003; Mallinson and Singleton 2017). The place of the cakras in haṭha yoga is treated in Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī.

Health and Safety Note

Intensive breath-retention and kuṇḍalinī practices are described in the texts as dangerous without expert guidance. Modern reports associate such practices, especially when undertaken without supervision, with psychological disturbance. They should not be attempted on the basis of a book, and they are not a substitute for medical or psychological care.

docs.title: 2.14 Grace (Anugraha)
docs.text: Grace is the fifth of Śiva’s five acts (creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment and grace) and, for the Śaiva theologians, the purpose of the other four. Its descent upon a soul is called śaktipāta, “the falling of power”. Signs of śaktipāta include devotion to Śiva, desire for initiation, and faith in the guru. Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 13) classifies it in nine grades, from the most intense, which liberates at once, to the mildest, which produces a gradual turning towards the path. The guru is regarded as the channel through which Śiva’s grace reaches the disciple, and the mantra as Śiva’s power in the form of sound.

docs.title: 2.15 Festivals
docs.text:
The Śaiva year is punctuated by festivals of the temple and of the household. The great night of Śiva (Mahāśivarātri, in Māgha or Phālguna, February–March) is kept with fasting and a night-long vigil. Each large temple has its own great annual festival (mahotsava, brahmotsava) of about ten days, with the hoisting of a flag, daily processions and a chariot festival. In the Tamil country Ārudrā Darśana (Tiruvātirai, in Mārkaḻi, December–January) celebrates the dance of Naṭarāja, above all at Chidambaram; Paṅkuṉi Uttiram (March–April) the divine marriages, including that of Śiva and Pārvatī; and Kārttikai Dīpam (November–December) is a festival of lights, whose great beacon on the hill at Tiruvaṇṇāmalai recalls Śiva’s appearance as a column of fire. The festivals of Gaṇeśa (Vināyaka Caturthī) and of Murukaṉ’s victory over Sūrapadman (Skanda Ṣaṣṭhī) belong to the same calendar.

In festival processions the movable festival image (utsavamūrti), distinct from the fixed image in the sanctum (mūlamūrti), is carried through the streets on a sequence of mounts (vāhanas) — the bull Nandi, a chariot, silver and golden mounts and others — bringing the deity to devotees who might not enter the sanctum. The theology of the festival as a re-enactment of Śiva’s five acts is set out in twelfth-century manuals such as Aghoraśiva’s Mahotsavavidhi (Davis 2010).

docs.title: 2.16 Nyāsa: Ritual Placing of Mantras
docs.text: Nyāsa (“placing”) is the ritual installation of mantras on the body of the worshipper. Through it the worshipper is understood to replace his ordinary body with a body made of mantras, becoming fit to worship Śiva — a principle often summarised in the dictum that only one who has become Śiva may worship Śiva. In Śaiva worship the six “limb” mantras of Śiva are placed on the heart, head, topknot, shoulders, eyes and the space around the body, and on the fingers and palms; the fifty phonemes of the alphabet may be placed on fifty points of the body; and in some rites the levels of the cosmos are mapped onto it, so that it becomes a microcosm. The kinds of nyāsa common to the Tantric traditions are described in Section 9.2.2.

docs.title: 2.17.1 Śiva Naṭarāja
docs.text:
The bronze image of Śiva as Naṭarāja, “King of Dancers”, dancing the ānandatāṇḍava within a ring of flames, was perfected in the Chōla period (10th–12th centuries). Its iconography is traditionally read as follows:

  • the upper right hand holds the drum (ḍamaru), the sound of creation;

  • the upper left hand holds fire, the power of dissolution;

  • the lower right hand shows the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā);

  • the lower left hand points, like an elephant’s trunk (gajahasta), to the raised foot, the refuge of devotees;

  • the right foot stands on the dwarf Apasmāra, ignorance;

  • the raised left foot (kuñcitapāda) signifies grace and release;

  • the ring of flames (prabhāmaṇḍala) signifies the cosmos and its cycles.

The Chidambaram temple, where Naṭarāja is the presiding deity, identifies its golden hall (citsabhā) with the “space of consciousness” (cidākāśa) in the heart. The Kashmiri Śaiva tradition contributed in another way: Abhinavagupta’s account of aesthetic experience (rasa) in his commentaries on the Nāṭyaśāstra and Dhvanyāloka draws on his Śaiva theology of consciousness (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 2.18 Epigraphic and Archaeological Evidence
docs.text: The history of the Śaiva traditions rests to an unusual degree on inscriptions. The Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 names Pāśupata teachers in the line of Kuśika (Section 2.1); the inscriptions of Karnataka from the eleventh to the thirteenth century document the Kālāmukha monasteries and their teachers; and those of Rājarāja I at Thanjavur (c. 1010) record the endowments and personnel of the Bṛhadīśvara temple. Beyond India, the temples and inscriptions of My Son in Champa, the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 from Prambanan in Java and the Sdok Kak Thom inscription of 1052 from the Thai–Cambodian border show Śaiva initiation and royal religion at work in Southeast Asia. Taken together, this evidence shows that Śaiva initiation and temple worship formed the framework of an extensive institutional network across the subcontinent and beyond; it is examined in Chapter 12 (Sanderson 2009).

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Vaiṣṇava Āgamas: Pāñcarātra and Vaikhānasa
docs.text:
sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi saṃniviṣṭo mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṃ ca | vedaiś ca sarvair aham eva vedyo vedāntakṛd vedavid eva cāham ||

— Bhagavad Gītā 15.15: “I am seated in the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge and their loss. I am what is to be known through all the Vedas; I am the maker of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda.”

The Vaiṣṇava Āgamic traditions — above all the Pāñcarātra and the Vaikhānasa — are the ritual and theological systems of the worshippers of Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa. Just as the Śaiva Āgamas provide the foundation of Śaiva temple worship, the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas govern worship in the great Viṣṇu temples of South India, among them Śrīraṅgam, Kāñcīpuram and Tirumala-Tirupati, and the shrines celebrated by the Tamil Āḻvār poets.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Origins and the Name
docs.text:
The Pāñcarātra is one of the oldest named Vaiṣṇava traditions: the Nārāyāṇīya section of the Mahābhārata (Śāntiparvan) already refers to it, together with Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Veda and the Pāśupata, as a body of doctrine. Its surviving Saṃhitās, however, are Tantric scriptures composed from about the sixth or seventh century onwards, first in Kashmir and North India and later, in very large numbers, in South India (Schrader 1916; Matsubara 1994).

The meaning of the name (“five nights”) was uncertain even to the tradition. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (13.6.1) describes a five-day sacrifice performed by Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa, by which he became all beings; later texts offer several explanations of their own, for instance that the doctrine was taught over five nights, or that it outshines five other systems as the sun outshines the night. None of these can be confirmed.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Para, Vyūha, Vibhava, Antaryāmin and Arcā
docs.text:
The central theological doctrine of the Pāñcarātra is that the supreme Lord manifests in five modes, which become progressively more accessible to devotees:

  1. Para: the transcendent Vāsudeva, possessing all six divine qualities (Section 3.1.3).

  2. Vyūha (“emanations”; Table 3.1): Vāsudeva and the three further emanations Saṁkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, who govern creation, maintenance and dissolution and the teaching of the path. Each of the three later emanations manifests two of the six qualities prominently.

  3. Vibhava (“manifestations”): the descents (avatāras); the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā lists thirty-nine, while the Purāṇic list of ten became standard.

  4. Antaryāmin: the Lord as the inner controller dwelling in the heart of every being.

  5. Arcā: the consecrated image in the temple or home, in which the Lord voluntarily makes himself present and accessible.

Table 3.1. The Four Vyūhas in Pāñcarātra Theology Vyūha Qualities stressed Traditional role Vāsudeva All six The supreme Lord, source of the other emanations Saṁkarṣaṇa Knowledge, strength Presides over individual souls; associated with dissolution and with teaching the scriptures Pradyumna Lordship, virility Presides over mind; associated with creation and with teaching right conduct Aniruddha Power, splendour Presides over the ego-principle; associated with maintenance and with granting the fruit of practice

Divine Accessibility (Saulabhya)

The fivefold scheme expresses a theology of divine condescension (saulabhya): the infinite Lord becomes progressively more accessible to finite devotees, culminating in the arcā form in which, in later Śrīvaiṣṇava theology, he places himself at the mercy of his worshippers. This doctrine underpins the importance of temple worship in Vaiṣṇavism.

docs.title: 3.1.3 The Six Divine Qualities
docs.text: The supreme Vāsudeva possesses six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), which the Pāñcarātra texts define in characteristic terms: knowledge (jñāna), an omniscience that comprehends all things at once; lordship (aiśvarya), independent sovereignty over all; power (śakti), the capacity to be the material cause of the world; strength (bala), the ability to support the universe without fatigue; virility (vīrya), the capacity to remain unchanged though the cause of change; and splendour (tejas), a self-sufficiency that needs no auxiliary cause. Together these qualities constitute bhaga, and the one who possesses them is bhagavat, “the Lord”.

docs.title: 3.2 The Principal Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
docs.text: Later lists name between 108 and over two hundred Saṃhitās, many of them lost. Three early works, the Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya, are honoured as the “three gems” (ratnatraya); later South Indian works were regarded as dependent on them: the Īśvara Saṃhitā on the Sātvata (it governs worship at Melkote), the Pārameśvara on the Pauṣkara (Śrīraṅgam), and the Pādma on the Jayākhya (associated with Kañcīpuram).

docs.title: 3.2.1 Before the “Three Gems”: The Nepalese Pāñcarātras
docs.text:
The “three gems” are not, as was long assumed, the earliest Pāñcarātra scriptures. In cataloguing the Nepalese manuscripts microfilmed by the Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation Project, Diwakar Acharya identified three works of an earlier stage, which he published in 2015: the Svāyambhuvapañcarātra, whose palm-leaf manuscript was copied in 1027; the Devāmṛtapañcarātra, preserved in a single incomplete manuscript of about the twelfth century; and the Aṣṭādaśavidhāna, a ritual manual of the first, transmitted in the same manuscript of 1027 (Acharya 2015). The oldest of them shows affinities with two of the later books of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (Section 2.4), so that it must postdate them. Acharya proposes no precise date, but on this reckoning the texts could go back to about 700 CE.

What makes these works important is the stage of development they reveal. Their deity is a single-headed Viṣṇu with two, four or eight arms — the eight-armed form is pan-Indian and very old — and their theology still treats Rudra, Brahmā and Janārdana as aspects of one Lord, in the manner of the Bhagavadgītā. The Devāmṛta prescribes the worship of five images, Narasiṃha, Varāha, Vāmana, Trivikrama and Vāsudeva in his cosmic form. At the same time the texts already follow a Śaiva model: they impose on the worshipper’s body a Vaiṣṇava version of the five “Brahma” mantras that the Śaivas had inherited from the Pāśupatas, and their ritual is organised around a maṇḍala of mantra-deities in concentric enclosures. They also distinguish the Vaiṣṇavas of the Pāñcarātra from the Bhāgavatas, which may reflect an older distinction between the worshippers of Nārāyaṇa and those of Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa that the later tradition forgot. The goddess, who is central to the Lakṣmītantra, hardly appears: these are Tantras of an unfeminised kind, comparable to the early Siddhānta (Acharya 2015).

docs.title: 3.2.2 The Jayākhya Saṃhitā
docs.text:
The Jayākhya, in thirty-three chapters, is among the oldest and most systematic surviving Saṃhitās; it was known in Kashmir by the ninth or tenth century. It treats the extraction (uddhāra) of mantras, initiation, daily worship, fire offering, yoga and the pursuit of powers, in a manner closely parallel to contemporary Śaiva scriptures.

The parallel is not accidental. Sanderson has shown that the ritual system of the Jayākhya is modelled on that of the Śaiva Mantramārga, from the grades of initiation to the structure of the daily worship (Sanderson 2009), and Acharya has argued that it is a reworking of an earlier scripture, the Jayottaratantra (Acharya 2015). It already knows a fourfold classification of initiates that the earliest Śaiva sources lack, which rules out the very early date (about the fifth century) once proposed for it in the foreword to its first edition (Gaekwad’s Oriental Series, 1931); it is now placed later, though before its use by the Kashmiri authors of the tenth century. Its theology centres on Vāsudeva accompanied by his powers. The same theology underlies a form of the Lord that dominated the art of Kashmir between the eighth and the tenth centuries: Vaikuṇṭha, a four-faced image whose human front face is flanked by the heads of a lion and a boar, with a fierce face at the back, often identified with the sage Kapila. Whether the side faces were understood as Narasiṃha and Varāha or, more abstractly, as the three further vyūhas grouped around Vāsudeva, is debated; the four-faced form expresses in a single image the doctrine of Table 3.1. The Jayākhya’s influence outlasted Kashmir: in South India the Pādma Saṃhitā was regarded as dependent on it.

docs.title: 3.2.3 The Sātvata Saṃhitā
docs.text: The Sātvata is centred on the worship of Vāsudeva and the vyūhas and was commented on in South India by Alasiṅgabhaṭṭa. It was quoted, along with the Jayākhya and Pauṣkara, by Yāmuna and Rāmānuja’s school as authoritative.

docs.title: 3.2.4 The Pauṣkara Saṃhitā
docs.text:
The Pauṣkara is valued for its treatment of worship and of ritual diagrams (maṇḍalas), and through the Pārameśvara Saṃhitā it is the basis of worship at Śrīraṅgam.

The Pārameśvara itself shows how a scripture could be rewritten for a single temple. Marion Rastelli’s study places its composition in the twelfth or thirteenth century in the milieu of the Raṅganātha temple, and reads it as a record of the Pāñcarātra as it was practised there: it takes over much of the older Pauṣkara, but adapts the daily and festival worship to the needs of a great temple with a large staff, a public of non-initiated devotees and an established Śrīvaiṣṇava community (Rastelli 2006). In this sense the South Indian Saṃhitās are not merely late copies of northern originals but documents of a living temple liturgy, and they are still cited when the procedures of particular temples are disputed.

docs.title: 3.2.5 The Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
docs.text: The Ahirbudhnya, in sixty chapters and named after the Vedic serpent-deity Ahirbudhnya (here identified with Śiva, who receives the teaching), is the most philosophically elaborate of the Saṃhitās. It is especially concerned with the worship of Sudarśana, Viṣṇu’s discus, as the Lord’s power, and contains an account of other doctrinal systems. Schrader’s study of it (1916) was the foundation of modern Pāñcarātra scholarship (Schrader 1916). Sudarśana here is more than a weapon: he is the Lord’s will (saṁkalpa) and active power, and the text gives rites with a diagram of Sudarśana for the protection of the king and his realm, a Vaiṣṇava counterpart to the Śaiva services to kings described in Chapter 12. Sudarśana shrines, with an image of the discus personified, often backed by Narasiṃha, are still a feature of South Indian Viṣṇu temples.

docs.title: 3.2.6 The Lakṣmītantra
docs.text: The Lakṣmītantra is unusual in that the teaching is given by the goddess Lakṣmī to Indra. Lakṣmī is presented as the Lord’s inseparable power (śakti), the agent of creation and the active principle in the universe; she is also the compassionate mediator (puruṣakāra) between souls and the Lord. The text is an important source for the theology of Śrī and for the doctrine of surrender discussed below (Gupta et al. 1979).

docs.title: 3.3 The Vaikhānasa Tradition
docs.text:
The Vaikhānasa tradition is a distinct stream of Vaiṣṇava temple worship that presents itself as Vedic rather than Tantric. Its priests belong to a hereditary community of Brahmins of the Taittirīya branch of the Black Yajurveda, who follow the Vaikhānasa Gṛhyasūtra and Dharmasūtra. According to tradition the sage Vikhanas received the teaching from Viṣṇu and passed it to four disciples, Atri, Bhṛgu, Marīci and Kāśyapa, to whom the principal ritual texts are attributed:

  1. Atri: the Samūrtārcanādhikaraṇa, on worship with images;

  2. Bhṛgu: several “sections” (adhikaraṇas) on ritual;

  3. Marīci: the Vimānārcanakalpa, on temples and worship;

  4. Kāśyapa: the Jñānakāṇḍa, which includes doctrine.

The Vaikhānasas do not undergo a separate Tantric initiation: a boy is held to be consecrated to Viṣṇu before birth through the viṣṇubali rite performed during his mother’s pregnancy. Their liturgy gives Vedic mantras a larger place, and their theology distinguishes the “partless” (niṣkala) and “with parts” (sakala) aspects of Viṣṇu and five forms (Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha) rather than the Pāñcarātra vyūhas. Their texts also give the classification of images as standing, seated or reclining, and as of “yoga”, “enjoyment” (bhoga), “heroic” or “fierce” type, which is widely used in iconographic writing (Table 3.2).

Table 3.2. Pāñcarātra and Vaikhānasa Compared Aspect Pāñcarātra Vaikhānasa Self-understanding Revelation of Nārāyaṇa; Tantric Vedic, derived from a Yajurvedic Kalpa tradition Priesthood Initiated priests (bhaṭṭācāryas); initiation (dīkṣā) open to devotees Hereditary Vaikhānasa Brahmins only; no separate initiation Theology Para, vyūha, vibhava, antaryāmin, arcā Niṣkala and sakala aspects; five forms of Viṣṇu Key texts Saṃhitās (Jayākhya, Sātvata, Pauṣkara, Pārameśvara, Īśvara, Pādma) Gṛhya- and Dharmasūtra; texts attributed to Atri, Bhṛgu, Marīci and Kāśyapa Examples of temples Śrīraṅgam; Varadarāja, Kāñcīpuram; Melkote Tirumala-Tirupati; many temples of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu

Kerala’s great Viṣṇu temples, such as Guruvāyūr and the Padmanābhasvāmi temple in Thiruvananthapuram, follow neither system strictly but the regional Kerala Tantric ritual codified in works such as the Tantrasamuccaya (15th century).

docs.title: 3.4 Images and Fires: The Vaikhānasa Temple
docs.text:
The Vaikhānasa claim to be Vedic rather than Tantric is not only a matter of self-description; it shapes the whole design of their worship. Gérard Colas has shown that the Vaikhānasa texts conceive temple worship as a transformation of the Vedic domestic and solemn fire rituals that their priests, as Taittirīya Brahmins, also maintained. Where the Vedic sacrificer made offerings into the fire, the Vaikhānasa priest makes offerings to Viṣṇu in the image, and the texts explicitly treat the offering to the image (arcanā) and the offering into the fire (homa) as two forms of the same act (Colas 1996). The image is the place where the “partless” (niṣkala) Viṣṇu, who pervades everything, is made present in a form “with parts” (sakala) that can be worshipped; the priest draws the god into it by meditation and mantra, as fire is kindled from the sticks.

The five images. A fully equipped Vaikhānasa temple has not one image of the deity but a set of up to five, each with its own function (Table 3.3). The great stone image in the sanctum, the “fixed” (dhruva) image, is too large and too sacred to be moved or bathed every day; the daily services are therefore performed on a small metal “power” image (kautuka), which is linked to the fixed image and receives its power. Other images are used for the bath (snapana), for processions and festivals (utsava) and for the daily distribution of food offerings to the attendant spirits (bali). The Vaikhānasa texts also correlate the five images with the five sacred fires of the Vedic fire ritual — the three fires of the solemn rites and the two further fires of the fivefold scheme — so that the set of images reproduces the set of fires; the details of the correspondence, which vary between texts, are studied by Colas (Colas 1996). Smaller temples may have only some of the five, and the texts allow for this.

Table 3.3. The Five Images (Pañcabera) of a Vaikhānasa Temple Image Function At Tirumala Dhruva (fixed) Principal image in the sanctum, usually of stone; source of the power of the others The main image of Veṅkaṭeśvara Kautuka (power) Daily worship, bathing rites and the night rest Bhoga Śrīnivāsa Utsava (festival) Processions and festivals; the form seen in the streets Malayappa Svāmī Snapana (bathing) Special ablutions Ugra Śrīnivāsa Bali (offering) Daily food offerings to the guardian deities and spirits Koluvu Śrīnivāsa

The system has practical as well as theological consequences. Because the fixed image is the permanent seat of the god and its power is extended to the others, the movable images can be taken out, bathed, dressed and carried in procession without disturbing the sanctum; and because the god is understood to be present in all of them at once, a single deity can appear simultaneously as the motionless Lord of the shrine and as the king who holds court, receives accounts and rides out among his people. At Tirumala, the most famous Vaikhānasa temple (Section 3.12), the “court” held each morning before the bali image, at which the day’s calendar and the temple accounts are read out, gives ritual form to this royal conception of the god.

Consecration. The general sequence of image consecration — the selection of the stone, the carving according to proportional rules, the opening of the eyes, the “sleeping” of the image in water, grain and on a couch, the fire offerings and the installation of the god’s power — is common to Śaiva, Pāñcarātra and Vaikhānasa practice and is described in Section 11.4. The Vaikhānasa versions differ in giving Vedic mantras and fire rituals the leading role, and in their elaborate provision for the relationship between the fixed and the movable images. In Pāñcarātra temples, by contrast, the presence of the god is established by Tantric mantras and by the placing (nyāsa) of the principles (tattvas) on the image, in close parallel to Śaiva practice.

Rivalry. The two systems competed for temples. Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography and temple chronicles credit Rāmānuja with introducing Pāñcarātra worship at Śrīraṅgam and elsewhere, and Vaikhānasa authors responded by insisting on the Vedic purity of their own birth-based priesthood against the initiatory credentials of the Pāñcarātrins (Section 3.9). The details of the hagiographic accounts cannot be verified, but the division of South Indian Viṣṇu temples between the two systems, and the litigation it has occasionally produced, are well documented (Colas 1996; Matsubara 1994).

docs.title: 3.5 The Āḻvārs and the Sacred Geography of Viṣṇu
3.5.1 The Twelve Āḻvārs
docs.text:
The twelve Āḻvārs (“those immersed” in the Lord) were Tamil poet-saints who lived between about the sixth and ninth centuries CE (the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition assigns them far earlier dates). Their hymns, about four thousand verses, were collected by Nāthamuni (10th century) as the Nālāyira Tivviyappirapantam (“Four-Thousand Divine Compositions”), which the Śrīvaiṣṇava community regards as a Tamil Veda and recites in temples alongside the Sanskrit Veda. The Āḻvārs included a woman, Āṇṭāḷ, and a poet of the low-status Pāṇar community, Tiruppāṇ, whose reception into the Śrīraṅgam sanctum is celebrated in hagiography (Table 3.4).

Table 3.4. The Twelve Āḻvārs and Their Principal Works No. Āḻvār Principal work(s) 1 Poykai Mutal Tiruvantāti 2 Pūtattāḻvār Iraṇṭām Tiruvantāti 3 Pēyāḻvār Mūṉṟām Tiruvantāti 4 Tirumaḻicai Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti; Tiruccanta Viruttam 5 Nammāḻvār Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses) and three shorter works 6 Maturakavi Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu 7 Kulacēkarar Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi 8 Periyāḻvār Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi, including Tiruppallāṇṭu 9 Āṇṭāḷ Tiruppāvai; Nācciyār Tirumoḻi 10 Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Tirumālai; Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci 11 Tiruppāṇ Amalaṉātipirāṉ 12 Tirumaṅkai Periya Tirumoḻi and other works

docs.title: 3.5.2 The 108 Divya Deśams
docs.text:
The temples praised in the Āḻvārs’ hymns are known as the 108 divyadeśas (“divine places”). Tradition groups them by the old regions of the Tamil country and beyond (Table 3.5):

Table 3.5. Traditional Regional Grouping of the 108 Divya Deśams Region Count Examples Chōḷa country (Kaveri delta) 40 Śrīraṅgam; Kumbakonam Pāṇṭiya country (far south) 18 Tirumāliruñcōlai (Alagar Kovil); Srivilliputtur Malai country (Kerala) 13 Thiruvananthapuram (Padmanābhasvāmi) Middle country 2 Tiruvahīndrapuram Toṇṭai country (north Tamil Nadu) 22 Kāñcīpuram (Varadarāja and others) Northern country 11 Tirumala; Ahobilam; Ayodhyā; Mathurā; Dvārakā; Badarīnāth; Muktināth (Nepal) Celestial 2 Vaikuṇṭha; the Ocean of Milk Total 108

The opening verse of Nammāḻvār’s Tiruvāymoḻi (1.1.1), recited daily in Śrīvaiṣṇava worship, begins by praising the Lord “who possesses the highest good, beyond which there is nothing higher” and who “graciously gave clear understanding, free of confusion”, and ends by urging the poet’s own heart to rise and worship his radiant feet that dispel sorrow.

docs.title: 3.6 The Sixteen Offerings of Worship
docs.text:
Hindu image worship in general, Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva alike, treats the deity as an honoured guest and offers a sequence of “services” (upacāras). A widely used list of sixteen (ṣoḍaśopacāra) is given below; the exact list varies between texts and traditions (Table 3.6; Bühnemann 1988).

Table 3.6. A Common List of Sixteen Upacāras No. Name Meaning 1 Āvāhana Invocation of the deity 2 Āsana Offering a seat 3 Pādya Water for the feet 4 Arghya Respectful water offering 5 Ācamana Water for sipping 6 Snāna Bath 7 Vastra Garment 8 Yajñopavīta Sacred thread 9 Gandha Sandal paste 10 Puṣpa Flowers 11 Dhūpa Incense 12 Dīpa Lamp 13 Naivedya Food offering 14 Tāmbūla Betel 15 Pradakṣiṇa and namaskāra Circumambulation and prostration 16 Mantrapuṣpa / visarjana Final flower offering with mantras; dismissal

docs.title: 3.7 The Śrīvaiṣṇava Synthesis
docs.text:
The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition of South India united three streams: the Vedānta of the Upaniṣads, the Brahmasūtra and the Gītā; the Tamil devotion of the Āḻvārs; and the ritual of the Pāñcarātra temples.

  • Nāthamuni (10th century) is credited with recovering and arranging the Āḻvār hymns and introducing their recitation in temples.

  • Yāmuna (Yāmunācārya, 10th–11th century) wrote the Āgamaprāmāṇya, a defence of the Pāñcarātra’s validity against Mīmāṃsā and other critics, arguing that its revelation by the omniscient Lord makes it as authoritative as the Veda (van Buitenen 1971).

  • Rāmānuja (traditionally 1017–1137; many scholars prefer c. 1077–1157) gave the tradition its Vedāntic theology, Viśiṣṭādvaita (“non-dualism of the qualified”), in his Śrībhāṣya and other works. In commenting on the Brahmasūtra’s section on the Bhāgavata doctrine (2.2.42–45 in Śaṅkara’s numbering), which Śaṅkara read as a refutation of the Pāñcarātra, he argued that the passage in fact upholds it. Hagiography credits him with reorganising temple administration and worship at Śrīraṅgam.

docs.title: 3.7.1 The Five Daily Observances
docs.text:
The Pāñcarātra divides the devotee’s day into five periods (pañcakāla), each with its observance:

  1. Abhigamana (approach): morning purification, prayer and preparation;

  2. Upādāna (gathering): collecting flowers and materials for worship;

  3. Ijyā (worship): the performance of pūjā;

  4. Svādhyāya (study): recitation and study of scripture;

  5. Yoga (meditation): contemplation of the Lord at night.

docs.title: 3.7.2 Initiation: The Five Sacraments
docs.text: Śrīvaiṣṇava initiation, called samāśrayaṇa (“taking refuge”) or pañcasaṃskāra, comprises five elements: branding of the shoulders with the discus and conch (tāpa), the sectarian forehead mark (puṇḍra), a new devotional name (nāma), the mantra (mantra), and instruction in worship (yāga). It is given to men and women of all castes by an ācārya.

docs.title: 3.7.3 The Three Mantras
docs.text:
Śrīvaiṣṇava teaching centres on three mantras, the “three secrets” (rahasyatraya):

  1. The tirumantra or eight-syllable mantra, oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya, interpreted as expressing the soul’s essential dependence on and service to Nārāyaṇa;

  2. The dvaya (“pair”), śrīman nārāyaṇa caraṇau śaraṇaṃ prapadye | śrīmate nārāyaṇāya namaḥ — “I take refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa with Śrī; homage to Nārāyaṇa with Śrī”, expressing the means and the goal;

  3. The caramaśloka (“final verse”), Bhagavad Gītā 18.66.

Bhagavad Gītā 18.66

sarvadharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja | ahaṃ tvā sarvapāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ ||

Abandoning all duties, take refuge in me alone. I shall free you from all sins; do not grieve.

docs.title: 3.8 Surrender (Prapatti)
docs.text: The doctrine of prapatti or śaraṇāgati, surrender to the Lord, is the distinctive soteriological contribution of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition. Prepared in the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās and in Rāmānuja’s Śaraṇāgatigadya, it was developed by his successors into an independent means of liberation, open to all, as an alternative to the demanding discipline of bhaktiyoga. The Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā and the Lakṣmītantra describe six components of surrender: the resolve to act in accordance with the Lord’s will (ānukūlyasya saṁkalpaḥ); the abandonment of what is opposed to it (prātikūlyasya varjanam); the confidence that the Lord will protect (rakṣiṣyatīti viśvāsaḥ); the choice of the Lord as one’s protector (goptṛtvavaraṇam); the placing of oneself in his charge (ātmanikṣepaḥ); and the humility of one who knows himself helpless (kārpaṇyam).

docs.title: 3.8.1 The Role of Śrī
docs.text: In Śrīvaiṣṇava theology Lakṣmī (Śrī) is inseparable from Nārāyaṇa and acts as the mediator (puruṣakāra) who intercedes for erring souls, softening the Lord’s justice with her compassion. The name of the tradition, “Śrīvaiṣṇava”, and the dvaya mantra both give her a central place.

docs.title: 3.8.2 Vaṭakalai and Teṉkalai
docs.text:
From the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the Śrīvaiṣṇavas divided into two schools, whose main differences are summarised in Table 3.7.

Table 3.7. Vaṭakalai and Teṉkalai Compared Issue Vaṭakalai (“northern”) Teṉkalai (“southern”) Grace and effort “Monkey-and-young” analogy (markaṭakiśoranyāya): the devotee must cling to the Lord, as a young monkey clings to its mother; surrender is an act required of the soul “Cat-and-kitten” analogy (mārjārakiśoranyāya): the Lord carries the soul as a cat carries its kitten; grace alone saves Status of Śrī Infinite like the Lord and, with him, both means and goal The supreme mediator, but not herself the means of salvation Language Greater weight on Sanskrit sources Greater weight on the Tamil hymns and their commentaries Leading teachers Vedānta Deśika (1268–1369, traditional dates) Piḷḷai Lokācārya (13th–14th century); Maṇavāḷa Māmuṉi (1370–1443)

The two schools also differ in social attitudes, sectarian marks and temple privileges, and their rivalry has led to long-running litigation over temple rights.

docs.title: 3.9 Defending and Regulating Pāñcarātra Practice
docs.text:
The status of the Pāñcarātra remained contested long after Yāmuna. Its priests were sometimes regarded by orthodox Brahmins as of lower standing, because their eligibility rested on Tantric initiation rather than on Vedic birth alone, and the rival Vaikhānasa priests stressed their own exclusively Vedic credentials. In the fourteenth century Vedānta Deśika wrote the Pāñcarātrarakṣā (“Protection of the Pāñcarātra”), which defends the tradition’s orthodoxy and regulates its practice on the basis of the Saṃhitās, including the five daily observances, the initiatory rites and the conduct of worship.

In the temples, the Saṃhitās prescribe the daily worship of the image in several services, the great festival with its flag-hoisting, processions on the vehicles of the Lord (Garuḍa, the serpent Śeṣa, the elephant and others), the bath and the chariot, and the periodic reconsecration of the temple. They also regulate who may enter which part of the temple and who may touch the image. As in the Śaiva temples, these prescriptions have been the subject of modern litigation, both between Vaṭakalai and Teṉkalai over ritual precedence and recitation, and between temple priests and the state over appointments.

docs.title: 3.9.1 Initiation and Caste in the Pāñcarātra
docs.text: Several Saṃhitās allow initiation of members of all four classes, and the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition prides itself on teachers of low birth: the Āḻvār Nammāḻvār was of a cultivator caste, and hagiography tells how Rāmānuja proclaimed the eight-syllable mantra from the temple tower at Tirukkoṭṭiyūr so that all might hear it. At the same time, the Saṃhitās often prescribe different mantras and ritual roles according to caste, and temple priesthood remained restricted to Brahmins (Matsubara 1994).

docs.title: 3.10 Cosmogony
docs.text: The Pāñcarātra describes creation as a real, divinely willed emanation, not an illusion. It distinguishes a “pure creation” (śuddhasṛṣṭi), consisting of the vyūhas and the eternal heaven (Vaikuṇṭha) made of a pure, non-material substance (śuddhasattva), from the “impure creation” of matter (prakṛti) and time, which follows a Sāṃkhya-like sequence of principles. Time (kāla) is treated as a real instrument of the Lord, operating in the material world but not in the eternal realm.

docs.title: 3.11 Iconography
docs.text:
The Vaiṣṇava Āgamas contain detailed iconographic prescriptions (mūrtilakṣaṇa) (Smith 1969; Rao 1914–1916). Two features are especially characteristic:

  • Posture and type: Vaikhānasa and śilpa texts classify images of Viṣṇu as standing (sthānaka), seated (āsana) or reclining (śayana), and each as of the yoga, bhoga, vīra or ābhicārika type. The reclining Raṅganātha on the serpent Śeṣa at Śrīraṅgam and the standing Veṅkaṭeśvara at Tirumala are famous examples.

  • The twenty-four forms (caturviṃśatimūrti): the twenty-four ways of distributing conch, discus, mace and lotus among four hands (\(4! = 24\)) are each given a name (Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda and so on); different texts assign the names differently.

docs.title: 3.12 Śrīraṅgam and Tirumala
docs.text:
The Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam, on an island in the Kāverī near Tiruchirappalli, is often described as the largest functioning Hindu temple complex. Its seven concentric enclosures (prākāras) contain streets and houses as well as shrines. Worship follows the Pārameśvara Saṃhitā; the Lord is awakened with Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār’s Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci, and the temple maintains both Sanskrit Vedic recitation and the dramatised Tamil recitation of the Āḻvār hymns by the araiyars.

The Veṅkaṭeśvara temple at Tirumala above Tirupati, by contrast, follows the Vaikhānasa Āgama and has hereditary Vaikhānasa priests. It is among the most visited and wealthiest religious institutions in the world. The Lord is awakened each morning with the Sanskrit Veṅkaṭeśa Suprabhātam composed by Prativādi Bhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṉ (15th century), and a nine-day brahmotsava is celebrated annually.

docs.title: 3.13 Vaiṣṇava Temples, Bronzes and Art
docs.text:
The Vaiṣṇava Āgamas, like their Śaiva counterparts, prescribe the temple plan, the flag-staff (dhvajastambha) bearing Garuḍa before the sanctum, the offering platform (balipīṭha) on the main axis, and subsidiary shrines for Śrī, Bhūdevī, the Āḻvārs and the ācāryas. South Indian bronze processional images (utsavamūrtis), cast by the lost-wax process by hereditary sculptors (sthapatis), are among the great achievements of Indian art.

Each South Indian dynasty left its mark on Vaiṣṇava art. The Pallavas (7th–9th centuries) carved the Varāha and Trivikrama panels of Māmallapuram and built the Vaikuṇṭhaperumāḷ temple at Kāñcīpuram; the Chōḷa period (9th–13th centuries) was the classic age of bronze casting and of the expansion of Śrīraṅgam and other shrines; the Hoysaḷas (12th–14th centuries) built the temples of Belur and Halebidu and patronised Rāmānuja’s tradition at Melkote; and under Vijayanagara and the Nāyakas (14th–18th centuries) the great temples acquired their towering gopuras, pillared halls, further enclosures and painted ceilings.

docs.title: 3.14 Mantra Manuals of Kṛṣṇa Worship
docs.text:
Outside the temple Saṃhitās, Tantric methods also shaped the personal worship of Kṛṣṇa in northern and eastern India. From about the fifteenth century a group of ritual manuals taught the worship of Kṛṣṇa, above all as the cowherd Gopāla of Vṛndāvana, by the same means that Śaiva and Śākta manuals used for their deities: initiation by a guru, the conferral of a mantra, the purification of the elements of the body, the placing of mantras on the limbs (nyāsa), the visualisation of the deity in his paradise, worship with the sixteen offerings and recitation of the mantra.

The most influential of these manuals was the Kramadīpikā of Keśava, whom tradition identifies with Keśava Kāśmīrī, a teacher of the Nimbārka school, probably of the fifteenth century. It sets out, in a compact series of chapters, the mantras of Kṛṣṇa and the procedures for their worship, and it circulated widely. Texts of this kind made a Vaiṣṇava “mantraśāstra” available to devotees who had no connection with the temple priesthoods of the South.

The Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas of Bengal and Vṛndāvana, followers of Caitanya, gave this tradition its most elaborate form in the Haribhaktivilāsa, a ritual code in twenty chapters composed in Vṛndāvana about 1540. Its authorship is disputed between the two Gosvāmīs Sanātana and Gopāla Bhaṭṭa; its first critical edition, by Måns Broo, attributes it to Sanātana. The work is largely a compilation: it quotes more than two hundred earlier texts, but Broo has shown that most of these quotations were taken from about twenty works of the same kind, among them Tantric manuals and Purāṇas. Its first five chapters treat the qualities of guru and disciple, the choice of mantras, initiation and the preparations for worship (Broo 2023). The Haribhaktivilāsa thus gave a devotional movement that stressed the singing of the divine name a fully Tantric framework of initiation and daily worship, and it remains the normative ritual handbook of the Gauḍīya tradition. Its emphasis on the guru, who confers the mantra and on whom the disciple’s progress depends, is shared with the Śaiva and Śākta traditions (Section 1.6); its exclusion of transgressive rites shows how far a Tantric ritual form could be separated from the Kaula content often associated with the word.

docs.title: 3.15 Tantric Vaiṣṇavism in Bengal: Sahajiyās and Bāuls
docs.text:
The Pāñcarātra and the Vaikhānasa are Vaiṣṇavisms of the temple. Eastern India also produced an esoteric and explicitly Tantric Vaiṣṇavism outside the temple, in which the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa became the model for a discipline of the body. Its antecedents include the songs of the Buddhist siddhas (Chapter 10), with their ideal of the “innate” (sahaja); its theology was shaped by the devotional movement of Caitanya (1486–1533) and by his followers, the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana, who analysed devotion in the categories of aesthetic savour (rasa) (Dimock 1966).

The Vaiṣṇava Sahajiyās, whose Bengali texts are mostly later than Caitanya, taught that Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā are present in every man and woman as their essential form (svarūpa) beneath the physical form (rūpa), and that the divine love of the pair can be realised by a man and a woman through a ritual of union learned from a guru and controlled by breath and the retention of seed. They took the love of a woman who is not one’s wife (parakīyā), like the cowherd women’s love for Kṛṣṇa, as the model of a passion indifferent to social convention, and they claimed as their own the poet Caṇḍīdāsa, whose legendary love for the washerwoman Rāmī became emblematic. Edward C. Dimock’s study remains the standard account (Dimock 1966). Orthodox Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas rejected this reading: for them the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa is to be entered through devotion and contemplation, not enacted.

The Bāuls, wandering singers of Bengal who may be of Hindu or Muslim background (the latter often called fakirs), reject temple, image and scripture; their songs seek the “man of the heart” (maner mānuṣ) within the body and mock caste, ritual and sectarian division. The most celebrated, Lālan Fakir (d. 1890), is revered in both Bangladesh and West Bengal, and Rabindranath Tagore admired and published Bāul songs. Behind the songs lies an esoteric practice, transmitted by gurus to initiates, that works with the body and its fluids in ways recalling both the Sahajiyās and older Tantric and Nātha yoga (Openshaw 2002). Related communities, such as the Kartābhajās of colonial Bengal, combined devotional egalitarianism with secrecy and esoteric ritual (Urban 2001). In 2005 UNESCO proclaimed the Bāul songs a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. These traditions show that Tantric ideas of the body and of transgressive love were not confined to Śaiva and Śākta milieus.

docs.title: Chapter 4: The Śākta Tantras: Traditions of the Goddess
docs.text:
Saundaryalaharī 1 (attributed by tradition to Śaṅkara)

śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api

Śiva, when united with Śakti, is able to create; otherwise the god cannot even stir.

docs.title: 4.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Śākta traditions worship the supreme reality as the Goddess (Devī, Mahādevī) or as Śakti, “Power”. Śākta Tantra is not a single school but a family of lineages — the Kaula traditions, the Kālī-centred Krama, the Kubjikā cult, Śrīvidyā, the worship of the Mahāvidyās, and the regional traditions of Bengal, Assam, Kerala and Nepal — most of which grew out of the goddess-centred scriptures of the Śaiva Bhairava tradition (Sanderson 1988; Goudriaan and Gupta 1981). For Śākta theologians, Śakti is the dynamic aspect of the absolute without which, as the opening verse of the Saundaryalaharī quoted above puts it, Śiva “cannot even stir”. The Brahmā hymn of the Devīmāhātmya addresses her as the power of whatever exists, real or unreal.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Antecedents
docs.text: Goddesses are present in the earliest Indian sources, though not yet as a supreme deity. Female terracotta figurines from Indus Civilisation sites have often been read as “mother goddesses”; the interpretation is possible but unproven, since the Harappan script is unread and continuity with later goddess cults cannot be demonstrated. The Ṛgveda praises Aditi, Uṣas (Dawn), Vāc (Speech), Pṛthivī (Earth), Rātrī (Night) and others, and the Śrīsūkta belongs to its later supplementary hymns, but goddesses are marginal in Vedic religion beside the gods. The Kena Upaniṣad has Umā Haimavatī reveal Brahman to the gods; the epics and early Purāṇas know Durgā, the slayer of the buffalo demon, and the fierce Mothers (mātṛs); and images of Mahiṣāsuramardinī survive from the Kuṣāṇa period.

docs.title: 4.2.2 The Devīmāhātmya
docs.text:
The Devīmāhātmya (also called Durgāsaptaśatī or Caṇḍī), composed around the fifth or sixth century and preserved in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, is the first Sanskrit text to present the Goddess as the supreme reality (Coburn 1984). Its thirteen chapters, traditionally counted as seven hundred verses, present her:

  1. as the supreme power, the source of all the gods’ energies;

  2. as the warrior goddess who destroys the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣa, and Śumbha and Niśumbha;

  3. as Mahāmāyā, the great delusion that binds beings, and simultaneously as the knowledge (mahāvidyā) that frees them.

Later appendices (the “secrets”, rahasyas) associate its three episodes with three forms, Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī. Its place in the Purāṇic corpus and its narrative are treated in Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa; what matters here is its afterlife in Śākta ritual. Tantric manuals turned the text into a liturgy: its recitation (pāṭha) is framed by preliminary hymns, by the placing of mantras on the reciter’s body and by the nine-syllable mantra of Cāmuṇḍā, and its verses are used as mantras in fire offerings. Bhāskararāya’s Guptavatī reads it through Śrīvidyā (Chapter 5), and the hymn to Nārāyaṇī in its eleventh chapter supplies some of the most widely recited prayers of goddess worship. Its recitation is the centre of the autumn Durgā worship throughout India (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 4.2.3 From Bhairava Tantras to Śākta Traditions
docs.text: The goddess-centred Śaiva scriptures of the Vidyāpīṭha — such as the Brahmayāmala (or Picumata), the Siddhayogeśvarīmata and the Jayadrathayāmala — centre on fierce goddesses and on the cult of the yoginīs, powerful female beings worshipped in cremation grounds. From these, between about the eighth and eleventh centuries, developed the Kaula traditions and the four “transmissions” (āmnāyas) in which later Śākta cults are organised: the Trika, the Kālī-centred Krama, the cult of Kubjikā, and the cult of Tripurasundarī that became Śrīvidyā (Sanderson 1988, 2009).

docs.title: 4.3 The Ten Mahāvidyās
docs.text:
The group of ten “Great Knowledges” (daśa mahāvidyā) is a relatively late development: the earliest lists appear in Purāṇas and Tantras of roughly the twelfth to sixteenth centuries, and the composition of the group varies (Kinsley 1997). The best-known list combines goddesses of very different character, from the beautiful Tripurasundarī to the self-decapitated Chinnamastā and the widowed Dhūmāvatī. Table 4.1 follows the most common list, which is usually headed by Kālī; Tripurasundarī is also called Ṣoḍaśī.

Table 4.1. The Ten Mahāvidyās Mahāvidyā Iconography and associations Kālī Dark, naked, garlanded with severed heads, standing on the corpse-like Śiva; time and death; in Bengali devotion also a loving mother Tārā Fierce blue goddess standing on a corpse; derived in part from the Buddhist Tārā, whose fierce forms (e.g. Ekajaṭā) were adopted by Hindu Śāktas; worshipped at Tārāpīṭh in Bengal Tripurasundarī “Beautiful in the three worlds”, also called Ṣoḍaśī and Lalitā; the goddess of Śrīvidyā (Chapter 5) Bhuvaneśvarī “Mistress of the worlds”; benign, associated with the manifest cosmos Bhairavī Fierce goddess, consort of Bhairava Chinnamastā Holds her own severed head, which drinks the blood spurting from her neck, while two attendants drink from the other streams; she stands on a copulating couple. Interpreted as self-sacrifice, as the cycle of life and death, and in yogic terms as the rising of kuṇḍalinī Dhūmāvatī “The smoky one”, an old widow riding a crow; inauspiciousness, poverty and misfortune Bagalāmukhī Pulls the tongue of a demon; associated with the power to paralyse (stambhana) enemies Mātaṅgī Associated with outcastes and with pollution (she accepts leftover food), and also with speech, music and learning Kamalā “She of the lotus”, a Tantric form of Lakṣmī; prosperity

Kinsley stresses that the group deliberately juxtaposes the auspicious and the inauspicious: it includes goddesses associated with death, pollution, social marginality and misfortune alongside goddesses of beauty and prosperity, expressing the Śākta conviction that the Goddess is present in the whole of reality, not only in its pleasant aspects (Kinsley 1997). Several of the goddesses are also invoked in rites for worldly ends — subjugation, paralysis of enemies and the like — which form part of the Tantric repertoire of “six acts” (ṣaṭkarmāṇi).

docs.title: 4.4 The Śākta Pīṭhas
docs.text:
The Śākta pīṭhas (“seats” of the Goddess) are sacred sites spread across South Asia. The best-known myth explaining them tells how Śiva carried the corpse of his wife Satī, who had immolated herself at her father Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and how Viṣṇu’s discus cut the body into pieces, which fell to earth at different places. Early Tantras know four principal pīṭhas (Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri and Kāmarūpa); later lists give 51, 52 or 108, and they differ in the sites and in the body-parts assigned to them (Table 4.2).

Table 4.2. Some Major Śākta Pīṭhas (assignments of body parts follow common later lists and vary) Pīṭha Location Body part Goddess Kāmākhyā Guwahati, Assam Yoni Kāmākhyā Vārāṇasī Uttar Pradesh Ear-ring Viśālākṣī Kālīghāṭ Kolkata Toes of the right foot Kālikā Jvālāmukhī Himachal Pradesh Tongue Jvālāmukhī (natural gas flames) Hiṅglāj Balochistan, Pakistan Crown of the head Koṭṭarī / Hiṅgulā Jaśoreśvarī Bangladesh Palms and soles Jaśoreśvarī

docs.title: 4.4.1 Kāmākhyā
docs.text: The temple of Kāmākhyā on Nīlācala hill in Guwahati is the most celebrated Śākta pīṭha. The sanctum contains no anthropomorphic image but a natural cleft in the rock, kept moist by a spring, worshipped as the yoni of the Goddess. The annual Ambubācī festival marks the Goddess’s menstruation: the temple is closed for three days and reopens with great celebration. Kāmākhyā was historically associated with animal sacrifice and with Kaula practice; its history, its royal patrons and the texts that describe it are treated in Section 13.4 (Urban 2010).

docs.title: 4.5.1 The Kulārṇava Tantra
docs.text: The Kulārṇava Tantra (“Ocean of the Kula”), in seventeen chapters (ullāsas), is probably a work of about the twelfth to fourteenth century and was widely influential in North and East India. It deals with the guru and initiation, the superiority of the Kula path, the Kaula ritual including its use of wine and meat, the conduct of initiates and the stages of attainment. Its second chapter ranks the paths in an ascending hierarchy: Vedic, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Siddhānta and, highest of all, Kaula. Like many Kaula texts it also insists that the Kaula ritual is for initiates only and condemns those who drink and indulge without the inner discipline it requires.

docs.title: 4.5.2 The Mahānirvāṇa Tantra: A Late Text
docs.text: The Mahānirvāṇa Tantra (“Tantra of the Great Liberation”) was the first Tantra to be widely known in English, through Arthur Avalon’s translation of 1913 (Avalon 1913). For Woodroffe and many readers after him it represented authentic, ancient Tantra in a socially progressive and philosophically Vedāntic form. Historical scholarship has shown it to be a late work. J. Duncan M. Derrett argued that it was composed in Bengal in the late eighteenth century, probably in the 1770s or 1780s, and that its legal chapters were shaped by the needs of the early British courts, which were then seeking “Hindu law”; it has been associated with the circle of Hariharānanda Bhāratī, the Tantric teacher of the reformer Rammohun Roy, who cited it (Derrett 1977; Urban 2003). Its rationalised ritual, its restriction of the transgressive elements and its monotheistic theology reflect that colonial setting. It is therefore valuable evidence for modern Bengali Tantra, not for the early history of the tradition.

docs.title: 4.5.3 Other Important Śākta Texts
docs.text:
Table 4.3 lists some other important Śākta texts.

Table 4.3. Some Important Śākta Texts Text Approximate date Content Brahmayāmala (Picumata) c. 7th–8th c. Vidyāpīṭha scripture of Kapālīśa Bhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kapālinī; yoginī cult (Hatley 2018) Kaulajñānanirṇaya c. 9th–11th c. Early Kaula text ascribed to Matsyendranātha Kubjikāmata c. 10th c. Scripture of the goddess Kubjikā Vāmakeśvarīmata / Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava c. 10th–11th c. Early scripture of the cult of Tripurasundarī Yoginīhṛdaya c. 10th–12th c. Inner doctrine of Śrīvidyā Śāradātilaka of Lakṣmaṇadeśika c. 11th c. Influential compendium of mantra and ritual Kālikā Purāṇa c. 10th–11th c. Goddess worship in Assam; Kāmākhyā; sacrifice Kulārṇava c. 12th–14th c. Kaula doctrine and ritual Tantrarāja c. 14th c. Śrīvidyā ritual Phetkāriṇī, Yoginī Tantra, Rudrayāmala (various texts so named) c. 14th–17th c. Bengali and Assamese Śākta works; the extant texts called Rudrayāmala are late Mantramahodadhi of Mahīdhara 1589 Compendium of mantras

docs.title: 4.6 The Kaula Tradition
docs.text: The word kula means “family” or “clan”. In the Kaula traditions it refers to the clans of goddesses, Mothers and yoginīs into which initiates are born by initiation, and, by extension, to the totality of powers that make up reality and the body. The Kaula traditions appear to have developed between the eighth and eleventh centuries from the cremation-ground cults of the Vidyāpīṭha, in a form that could be practised by householders (Sanderson 1988).

docs.title: 4.6.1 What the Kaula Sources Prescribe
docs.text:
The Kaula texts describe a ritual very different from the purity-centred worship of the Siddhānta or the Vaikhānasa. Their characteristic features include:

  1. Worship in the circle (cakra): the worship of the goddess and her retinue by a group of initiates, often at night, in which caste distinctions are suspended for the duration of the rite.

  2. Impure substances: offering and consuming alcohol and meat, substances forbidden to orthodox Brahmins, as sacraments.

  3. Sexual ritual: ritual union with a female partner (dūtī, śakti), who is worshipped as the goddess; in many sources the sexual fluids produced are themselves offered to the deities and consumed.

  4. Yoginīs: the belief that initiates could encounter, propitiate and gain powers from yoginīs, who were thought to possess human women and to fly.

  5. Secrecy and dual identity: the famous maxim that one should be “a Kaula inwardly, a Śaiva outwardly and a Vedic in social conduct” expresses the expectation that initiates would conceal their practice and observe orthodox norms in public.

docs.title: 4.6.2 Interpreting Kaula Ritual: Sanderson and White
docs.text:
Modern scholarship does not support either of the two popular images of Kaula Tantra: the colonial image of mere debauchery, or the apologetic image (from Woodroffe onwards) in which the “five Ms” were always purely symbolic. Both Alexis Sanderson and David Gordon White, despite their differences, treat the transgressive rites as real practices described in the texts.

Sanderson has shown that the Kaula ritual is a “domesticated” form of the Kāpālika cremation-ground cult. In the Kashmiri Trika, as expounded by Abhinavagupta in Tantrāloka 29, the secret Kaula ritual with a consort and with wine and meat is retained and literally performed, but it is interpreted in an “aestheticised” way: the intensified pleasure of the senses and the breaking of the inhibitions of purity (śaṅkā) are means of dissolving the limited self and realising the expansive bliss of consciousness that is Śiva. In Sanderson’s analysis the deliberate violation of Brahmanical purity rules is the heart of the matter: the initiate demonstrates that he is free from the contracted, purity-bound identity of the orthodox householder (Sanderson 1988).

White argues that the earliest Kaula practice was centred on the yoginīs and on the production, offering and consumption of sexual and other bodily fluids — the “clan fluid” (kuladravya) — through which initiates were thought to enter the family of the goddesses and gain their powers. On his reading, the high-caste exegetes of Kashmir later transformed this “hard-core” ritual into a semiotic and aesthetic discipline of consciousness, and later still the practice was further internalised or replaced by substitutes. White also emphasises that the modern Western notion of “Tantric sex” as a technique of erotic fulfilment has little to do with the medieval sources (White 2003).

Other scholars add qualifications. Christian Wedemeyer, writing on the Buddhist Yoginītantras, argues that the transgressive acts were tightly scripted ritual performances, carried out by relatively few initiates, whose meaning lay in their deliberate inversion of norms; they were not evidence of a marginal counter-culture (Wedemeyer 2013). Hugh Urban has traced how both European and Indian writers in the colonial period constructed “Tantra” as the dark other of a rational Hinduism, and how reformers such as Woodroffe responded by sanitising it (Urban 2003).

Scholarly Note: Literal, Substituted and Interiorised

Over time the Kaula rites were transformed in three ways, which coexisted. Some lineages continued to perform them literally. Others replaced the substances by substitutes (milk, ginger, sesame and the like for wine and meat; worship of the consort without intercourse). Others again, especially the “right-handed” (samayācāra) Śrīvidyā of South India, rejected external transgressive practice entirely and reinterpreted the rites as inner yoga. These developments are historical, and the later symbolic interpretations should not be read back into the earlier texts.

docs.title: 4.6.3 The “Five Ms”
docs.text:
Later Śākta sources sum up the Kaula sacraments as the “five Ms” (pañcamakāra): madya (wine), māṃsa (meat), matsya (fish), mudrā (parched grain, though in some texts the word may denote the female partner) and maithuna (sexual union). The table summarises the three ways in which they came to be treated.

Element Literal Substitutes (later texts) Interiorised reading (later texts) Madya Wine or spirits Milk, coconut water The nectar that flows from the crown in yoga Māṃsa Meat Ginger, sesame, pulses Restraint of speech; offering of merit and demerit Matsya Fish Radish, red sesame The two breaths moving in the left and right channels Mudrā Parched grain Rice or wheat Abandoning bad company; a state of inner absorption Maithuna Sexual union Offering of flowers; worship of the consort without union Union of kuṇḍalinī with Śiva at the crown

docs.title: 4.6.4 Dakṣiṇācāra and Vāmācāra
docs.text: Later Śākta texts sort practice into two orientations. “Right-hand” or “southern” conduct (dakṣiṇācāra) worships with pure offerings, mantra and meditation and conforms to orthodox purity rules; it is open to most initiates. “Left-hand” conduct (vāmācāra; vāmā also means “woman”) involves the five Ms, actual or substituted, and the worship of women, and the texts restrict it to advanced initiates under a guru. They treat it as powerful, dangerous and secret; some lineages practised it literally; its stated purpose was liberation and power through transcending the dualities of pure and impure; and the same sources condemn those who indulge without discipline.

docs.title: 4.7 Goddess Worship: Festivals and Regional Traditions
4.7.1 Navarātri and Durgā Pūjā
docs.text: The nine-night festival of Navarātri, celebrated in spring and, more importantly, in autumn, is the principal public festival of the Goddess. Its forms vary greatly: in Bengal it culminates in the Durgā Pūjā (Section 9.9); in Gujarat it is celebrated with communal dance; in much of South India dolls are displayed and the last three nights are associated with Durgā, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī in turn. The tenth day, Vijayādaśamī, celebrates the victory of the Goddess (and in North India of Rāma). Its royal form is described in Section 12.5.

docs.title: 4.7.2 Bengal
docs.text:
Bengal has been a heartland of Śākta worship since at least the later medieval period. Kālī is worshipped there as the supreme reality and, increasingly from the eighteenth century, as a loving mother, and her autumn festival is one of the great occasions of the Bengali year (Figure 4.1). The devotional songs (śākta padāvalī) of Rāmprasād Sen (18th century) and Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya (c. 1769–1821) turned Tantric themes into intimate devotion. Its great shrines include Kālīghāṭ in Kolkata, Tārāpīṭh with its cremation-ground ascetics, and Dakṣiṇeśvar, where Rāmakṛṣṇa (1836–1886) served as priest and practised Tantric discipline under a female guru (Section 4.14.3). Much Bengali goddess worship, all the same, is village and household religion only loosely connected with the Sanskrit Tantras (McDaniel 2004); the region’s digests, poets and patrons are described in Section 13.3.

Figure 4.1. A clay image of Kālī standing on the prostrate Śiva, in a worship shrine hung with a red curtain. Photo: UpasanaSen92, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 4.7.3 Village Goddesses
docs.text: Much goddess worship in India takes place outside the Sanskrit Tantric framework altogether. Every village has its goddesses (grāmadevatās) — in Tamil Nadu, for example, Māriyammaṉ, associated with rain and with epidemic diseases such as smallpox, and the many local “mothers” (ammaṉ) — who protect the community’s boundaries and are worshipped with festivals, processions, possession and, in many places, animal sacrifice, often by non-Brahmin priests. Over the centuries such goddesses were frequently identified with Durgā, Pārvatī or Kālī, and their temples sometimes brought under Brahmin priesthood and Āgamic ritual; but much village worship retains its own forms. The relation between the learned Śākta Tantras and this popular religion is one of continual exchange rather than of a single tradition (Kinsley 1997; McDaniel 2004).

docs.title: 4.7.4 Assam
docs.text: Besides Kāmākhyā, Assam produced two texts, the Kālikā Purāṇa and the Yoginī Tantra, which reflect its goddess worship, including blood sacrifice and the patronage of the Koch and Ahom kings (Section 13.4).

docs.title: 4.7.5 Kerala
docs.text: In Kerala the fierce goddess Bhadrakālī is worshipped in temples and in sacred groves (kāvu), often by non-Brahmin priests. In the teyyam of North Kerala, performers of low-status communities embody deities, including forms of the Goddess, and are worshipped by all castes for the duration of the performance. The Bhagavatī temple of Koṭuṅṅallūr is known for its Bharaṇi festival, with its ritual abuse and its former offerings of cocks, and at the annual Āṟṟukāl Poṅkala in Thiruvananthapuram very large numbers of women cook offerings for the Goddess. In the temples, meanwhile, Brahmin tantrīs worship her with the right-hand rites of the regional Tantrasamuccaya (Section 13.2).

docs.title: 4.7.6 Nepal
docs.text: In the Kathmandu Valley, Hindu and Buddhist Tantric traditions have coexisted for more than a millennium and preserve forms of worship that disappeared elsewhere. The Malla kings (13th–18th centuries) took as their tutelary deity Taleju, a goddess identified with Durgā, whose temples stand beside the old royal palaces of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur and whose inner shrines are closed to all but initiates. Newar Hindu Tantric ritual is performed by Rājopādhyāya Brahmins and by Karmācārya priests, and the cult of Kubjikā, otherwise largely extinct, survives among the Newars. The best-known Newar goddess cult is that of the Kumārī: a young girl of the Buddhist Śākya caste is chosen to serve as the living embodiment of the goddess, identified with Taleju, until she reaches puberty, and the royal Kumārī of Kathmandu presides over the festival of Indra Jātrā (Allen 1975; Gellner 1992). The Newar Buddhist Tantric tradition is described in Chapter 10, and further aspects of Newar Tantra in Section 13.6.

docs.title: 4.8 Śākta Mantra
docs.text: Śākta practice centres on mantras, especially monosyllabic “seed” (bīja) mantras, which are regarded as the goddess’s own sonic body: hrīṃ, the “Māyā” seed of Bhuvaneśvarī; krīṃ, the seed of Kālī; klīṃ, the seed of desire; aiṃ, the seed of speech; strīṃ, the seed of Tārā; and hlīṃ, associated with Bagalāmukhī and the power to paralyse. They are traditionally received only through initiation, and their associations are recorded here, and in Table 7.2, for information, not as instructions for practice.

docs.title: 4.9.1 Power and Consciousness
docs.text: Śākta theology inherits from the non-dual Śaiva traditions the doctrine that reality is consciousness endowed with power, and gives priority to the power. The three powers of will (icchā), knowledge (jñāna) and action (kriyā) are described as the Goddess’s own modes, and in Śrīvidyā they are correlated with the three sections of her mantra and the triangles of her diagram.

docs.title: 4.9.2 Māyā as the Goddess
docs.text: Whereas Advaita Vedānta treats māyā as the inexplicable ignorance that veils Brahman, Śākta theologians identify it with the creative power of the Goddess herself. The Devīmāhātmya calls her both Mahāmāyā, who deludes beings, and the knowledge that frees them. The world is accordingly not an illusion to be negated but the Goddess’s real manifestation and play (līlā), to be recognised as such. This is the basis of the Tantric combination of worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti).

docs.title: 4.9.3 The Body and Kuṇḍalinī
docs.text: Śākta traditions treat the body as a microcosm of the cosmos and of the Goddess’s diagram: the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad systematically identifies the parts of the human body with the enclosures of the Śrīcakra. The Goddess is also present in the body as kuṇḍalinī, the coiled power that, in the later yoga described in the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, sleeps at the base of the trunk, is awakened by yoga, rises through the cakras, and unites with Śiva at the crown (Avalon 1919).

docs.title: 4.10 The Yoginī Cult and Its Temples
docs.text:
The yoginīs — groups of fierce, often animal-headed female deities, frequently counted as sixty-four — were central to the Vidyāpīṭha and Kaula traditions. Between about the ninth and twelfth centuries kings and local rulers in central and eastern India built distinctive open-air temples for them, usually circular (Dehejia 1986):

Site Location Date (c.) Features Hirapur Odisha 9th–10th c. Small circular hypaethral temple with sixty-four yoginī images Ranipur-Jharial Odisha 9th–10th c. Large circular temple with sixty-four niches Khajuraho Madhya Pradesh late 9th c. Rectangular open-air yoginī temple, the earliest at Khajuraho Mitaoli (Morena) Madhya Pradesh 11th c. Large circular temple with sixty-four cells and a central shrine Bheraghat (Jabalpur) Madhya Pradesh 10th–11th c. Circular temple with eighty-one niches

docs.title: 4.10.1 Yoginīs in the Scriptures: The Brahmayāmala
docs.text:
The fullest early account of the yoginī cult is found in the Brahmayāmala or Picumata, the oldest surviving scripture of the Vidyāpīṭha (Section 2.5). In its surviving form it is a very large text of more than a hundred chapters, preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, the oldest of them copied in the eleventh century; the first volume of Shaman Hatley’s critical edition, together with his earlier study of the text, has opened the early yoginī cult to detailed study (Hatley 2007, 2018).

The Brahmayāmala addresses the sādhaka, the initiate who seeks supernatural powers. Having been initiated into the cult of Kapālīśabhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kapālinī, he undertakes a series of observances (vratas) of increasing intensity, many of them performed in cremation grounds and other places frequented by yoginīs, with offerings that include blood, meat and alcohol. The culmination of his practice is the “meeting” (melaka) with the yoginīs: if his practice is perfect, they appear to him and grant him powers, above all the power of flight and the status of a divine being who roams the sky with them; if it fails, the same goddesses may destroy him. The yoginīs are thus both the source of power and its greatest danger.

Initiation also places the initiate in a “clan” (kula, gotra). In the initiation ceremony the blindfolded candidate casts a flower onto the maṇḍala; the deity on which it falls determines the family of goddesses to which he belongs, and so the yoginīs who are his kin. Kaula and Vidyāpīṭha texts teach secret signs (chommā) — gestures and code words — by which initiates and yoginīs recognise one another. Hatley has also drawn attention to passages in which women appear as practitioners in their own right, a reminder that the word yoginī could denote human women as well as goddesses (Hatley 2007).

docs.title: 4.10.2 Who Were the Yoginīs?
docs.text:
The yoginīs drew together several older figures. One was the group of “Mothers” (mātṛ), female deities attested in sculpture from the Kuṣāṇa period and later standardised as the seven or eight Mothers who accompany Śiva or the Goddess in battle. Another was the host of female spirits — seizers (grahas) dangerous to children and pregnant women, and witches who feast on human flesh — feared in medical and narrative literature. A third was the human woman of power, the female ascetic or ritual partner. In the scriptures and in story literature such as Somadeva’s Kathāsaritsāgara (11th century), the yoginīs gather at night in cremation grounds, fly through the air, change shape and consume the vital essence of their victims; to the initiate who can master them they are protectresses and givers of power (White 2003; Keul 2013).

The number sixty-four (eight times eight) is a classificatory ideal rather than a fixed list. Vidya Dehejia’s comparison of the lists of yoginī names in texts and on temple images found that they rarely agree, and that each temple seems to have followed its own tradition (Dehejia 1986). Buddhist Tantra developed a parallel figure, the ḍākinī, who plays a similar role in the Yoginītantras (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 4.10.3 The Temples and Their Patrons
docs.text:
The open-air temples listed above translate the yoginī cult into architecture. Their circular plan reproduces the “circle” (cakra) of goddesses described in the scriptures, with the images set in niches around the inner face of the enclosing wall, facing a central shrine that housed, in several cases, a form of Bhairava or Śiva. The temples are roofless (hypaethral), and Dehejia related this to the yoginīs’ power of flight: the goddesses are imagined as descending into their circle from the sky (Dehejia 1986).

The images themselves are among the finest sculptures of their time. At Hirapur, near Bhubaneswar, the small stone yoginīs stand on their vehicles — animals, birds, demons, severed heads — some with animal faces, many with the graceful bodies and ornaments of court sculpture. At Bheraghat, on the Narmadā near Jabalpur, the larger seated images bear inscribed names on their pedestals, and a later shrine of Śiva and Pārvatī now stands in the courtyard.

Who built these temples, and for what purpose? Inscriptions are scarce, but the temples are associated with the ruling houses of their regions — the Kalacuris at Bheraghat, the Candellas at Khajuraho, the Kacchapaghātas in the Gwalior region, and the dynasties of early medieval Odisha. The scriptures promise that the yoginīs can grant victory and protection, and royal patronage of their cult is best understood in the light of the Śaiva services to kings discussed in Chapter 12: the circle of goddesses was a source of power that a king might wish to have at his disposal. Several temples now stand in ruins, and many images have been removed to museums or lost to theft; at Hirapur the yoginīs continue to receive worship from local devotees.

docs.title: 4.11 The Four Transmissions
docs.text:
Later Śākta and Kaula literature organises its cults into “transmissions” (āmnāyas) associated with the directions (Sanderson 1988; Goudriaan and Gupta 1981):

  • The Eastern transmission (pūrvāmnāya): associated with the Trika and the cult of the three goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā (Chapter 6).

  • The Northern transmission (uttarāmnāya): the cult of Kālī, systematised in the Krama of Kashmir, with its sequences of goddesses through which consciousness devours objectivity.

  • The Western transmission (paścimāmnāya): the cult of the hunchbacked goddess Kubjikā (see below).

  • The Southern transmission (dakṣiṇāmnāya): the cult of Tripurasundarī, which became Śrīvidyā (Chapter 5).

Later still, a fifth, “upper” transmission was added, and lists vary from text to text. The scheme shows how the various goddess cults came to see themselves as parts of one Kaula family.

docs.title: 4.11.1 The Western Transmission: Kubjikā
docs.text:
Of the four transmissions, the cult of Kubjikā, the “hunchbacked” or “crooked” goddess, is the least known outside Nepal, though its literature is large and comparatively well preserved. Its root scripture, the Kubjikāmata (also called the Kulālikāmnāya), probably of the tenth century, has been critically edited by Teun Goudriaan and Jan Schoterman (Goudriaan and Schoterman 1988); a large body of later works expands it, among them the Ṣaṭsāhasrasaṃhitā (“Collection of Six Thousand Verses”), whose opening chapters Schoterman edited (Schoterman 1982). Mark Dyczkowski’s survey of the canon shows how these texts place themselves in the “western house” of the Kaula system and rework the older scriptures of the Vidyāpīṭha and the Trika into a new system with its own deities, mantras, lineages and yoga (Dyczkowski 1988).

The goddess’s crooked form is read in the tradition as the coiled power within the body: Kubjikā is the power that lies curled at the base of the body and, straightened by yoga, rises to unite with Śiva above. Her cult therefore gave great weight to the yoga of the subtle body. Its texts map a series of centres (cakras) along the axis of the body, each with its deities and, in some texts, a sacred site of its own, so that the practitioner’s body becomes a map of sacred geography; scholars have traced to this tradition one of the earliest systems of six centres resembling the scheme that later became standard (Section 2.13.2) (Dyczkowski 1988; White 2003). The ritual of the cult, conducted in maṇḍalas of the goddess and her retinue, combines Kaula worship with a strong emphasis on the lineage of teachers through whom the teaching descends.

Almost extinct in India, the cult of Kubjikā survives among the Newars of the Kathmandu Valley, where her initiations are still given and her texts copied (Section 13.6). Its Nepalese manuscripts, which preserve both the root scripture and its many derivatives, are one reason why the later history of Kaula Tantra can now be studied in more detail than its earlier phases.

docs.title: 4.11.2 Kālī in Bengal
docs.text: The Kālī worship that is so prominent in Bengal today took its familiar form only in the early modern period. Bengali tradition credits Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa, compiler of the influential ritual digest Tantrasāra (late 16th or 17th century), with popularising the now standard image of Dakṣiṇakālī. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the patronage of landholders and the devotional songs of Rāmprasād Sen and Kamalākānta made her the object of an intimate, filial devotion, in which the terrifying goddess is addressed as a loving if unpredictable mother (McDaniel 2004; Kinsley 1997).
