In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries Kālī and Durgā also became symbols of the motherland in Bengali nationalist literature and politics (Urban 2003).

docs.title: 4.12 Blood Sacrifice
docs.text:
Animal sacrifice (bali) to the Goddess — most often of goats and buffaloes — is prescribed in many Śākta texts; the Kālikā Purāṇa contains a chapter on blood offerings that became an authority for later practice. It has been performed at major goddess shrines such as Kāmākhyā and in village goddess worship across India, and also during Durgā Pūjā in some households and temples.

Sacrifice has always been contested. Vaiṣṇava, Jain and Buddhist critics condemned it; many Śākta lineages, especially the Śrīvidyā of the South and the Bengali devotional traditions influenced by Vaiṣṇavism, replaced animals with pumpkins, sugarcane or other substitutes; and modern reformers campaigned against it. Several Indian states have legislated against animal sacrifice in temples — Kerala in 1968, for example — while elsewhere it continues, and courts and legislatures continue to debate how to balance religious freedom, animal welfare and public order.

docs.title: 4.13 Gender, Caste and the Śākta Traditions
docs.text: It is often claimed that because the Śākta traditions worship a supreme Goddess, they elevated the status of women. The evidence points in more than one direction (Kinsley 1997; White 2003). Many Kaula and Śākta texts command reverence for women as embodiments of the Goddess, forbid harming or insulting them and allow them to be initiated; some lineages recognised women as gurus, and female practitioners (sādhikās, bhairavīs) are attested in later centuries. Yet the same texts were composed by and for men. The female partner in Kaula ritual is often described primarily as a means to the male initiate’s attainment, and some texts prefer partners of low caste precisely because of their ritual impurity. Devotion to powerful goddesses has coexisted throughout Indian history with patriarchal social norms, and worship of the Goddess did not by itself bring social power to women. Caste shows a similar pattern: its suspension inside the ritual circle was combined with its observance outside, while in village India goddess worship has long been led by non-Brahmin priests and performers, as in the Kerala teyyam, and the Mahāvidyā Mātaṅgī and other figures give religious value to the socially marginal.

docs.title: 4.14 Women in the Tantric Traditions: Partners, Practitioners and Gurus
docs.text: Three kinds of evidence allow these generalisations to be tested: the prescriptions of the scriptures themselves, the scattered records of historical women who practised or taught, and the ethnography of the living traditions. Each has its limits. The scriptures are normative and often idealised, and they cannot be read as descriptions of society; the historical records are few; and the ethnography concerns the present. Read together, they show women in at least three different roles, whose relative weight changed over time.

docs.title: 4.14.1 The Early Śākta Scriptures
docs.text:
Judit Törzsök’s study of the earliest scriptures of the goddess cults, dated between the seventh and the ninth centuries — the Brahmayāmala, the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, the Tantrasadbhāva and the Jayadrathayāmala — distinguishes three ritual roles for women, which often overlap (Törzsök 2014).

The ritual partner. The female partner, called dūtī (“messenger”) or more often simply śakti (“power”), is required only in certain rites. The Brahmayāmala prescribes her for its most advanced class of practitioner and lists the qualities she should have: she should have received the guru’s instructions, have mastered the yogic postures, be steeped in the Tantras, be devoted to guru, deity and husband, and be free from greed. Yet in the rites themselves her role is largely instrumental: in the pre-Kaula cult the chief purpose of ritual union was to produce the mingled sexual fluids that were offered to the deities and consumed (Sanderson 1988), and the woman is the means or the support of that offering rather than its agent. The commentator Jayaratha later justified her presence by a Vedic analogy: as a Brahmin must sacrifice together with his wife, so the Kaula rite requires the dūtī (Törzsök 2014).

The human yoginī. The same texts teach that certain women belong by birth to the “clans” (kula) of the seven Mothers, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī and Cāmuṇḍā. The Brahmayāmala (chapter 74), the Siddhayogeśvarīmata and the Tantrasadbhāva describe how such a woman is to be recognised by her looks and behaviour — unrestrained laughter and anger are among the signs — and tested with secret hand gestures, to which she answers with a counter-gesture. Once recognised, she is to be worshipped, for she can grant powers and transmit teaching orally. The Siddhayogeśvarīmata adds that men are to be recognised in the same way, as “heroes” (vīra) fit to be partners of the yoginīs, which implies that women, too, sought out their partners (Törzsök 2014). These are the human counterparts of the divine yoginīs described in Section 4.10.

The female practitioner. Here the early Śākta scriptures differ most from the Śaiva mainstream. The Svacchandatantra (4.88) lists women, with children, the foolish, the old, kings and the sick, among those who may receive only the “seedless” initiation, which frees them from the duties of the initiate but also excludes them from the higher practice (Section 9.7). The goddess Tantras, by contrast, give women full initiation. In the Brahmayāmala initiates are divided not by caste but by sex, as “heroes” and “yoginīs”, and women receive initiation names ending in -śakti; in the Trika scriptures all initiates receive names ending in -śakti. The Siddhayogeśvarīmata prescribes its preparatory observances for “the male or female practitioner” (sādhaka, sādhakī) and allows women to undertake the propitiation of the goddess Aparā, with its fire offerings, alone or at home, exactly as men do. Of one mantra, the “Heart of the Yoginīs”, it says that it grants success chiefly to women and that it was handed down by women from mouth to mouth and not written in a book. Abhinavagupta, commenting on the Parātrīśikā, could still assume that a person initiated directly by the deity might be either a “hero” or a “yoginī” (Törzsök 2014).

The same texts also call women abalā, “the powerless”, and at times offer them easier rites as weaker practitioners. But they also promise that through practice the powerless woman becomes a powerful yoginī, just as the timid man becomes a hero. Törzsök found no explicit statement on whether women could attain final liberation by these means; since the texts treat liberation as one of the attainments of the practitioner, their silence need not imply exclusion. Literary evidence agrees with the scriptures: in Bhavabhūti’s Mālatīmādhava (early 8th century) two women, Kapālakuṇḍalā and Saudāminī, are shown as accomplished practitioners with the power of flight (Section 2.1.6).

docs.title: 4.14.2 The Later Kaula Texts
docs.text: A second body of evidence comes from the Sanskrit Tantras of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries, many of them associated with the Kālī-centred traditions of eastern India. Loriliai Biernacki has studied eight such texts and argued that they cannot be reduced either to a purely symbolic exaltation of “the feminine” or to the use of women’s bodies for male ends (Biernacki 2007). They prescribe rites in which women are honoured and worshipped as embodiments of the Goddess; they forbid the initiate to despise, strike or speak harshly to a woman; they treat women as practitioners and, in some passages, as gurus; and they attach particular power to women’s speech. At the same time Biernacki does not hide the elements that point the other way, above all the fact that the texts are still addressed mainly to men. Sanjukta Gupta had earlier surveyed the place of women in the Śaiva and Śākta ethos more broadly, including the women poets of these traditions (Gupta 1992).

docs.title: 4.14.3 Women Practitioners and Gurus in History
docs.text:
Historical records of women in the Tantric traditions are few, but they span the whole period covered in this volume.

  • A Pāśupata abbess. Although the Pāśupatasūtra restricts its observance to twice-born men, an inscription of the twelfth or thirteenth century from Mount Ābu names a woman Pāśupata ascetic, Yogeśvarī, as the head of a Śaiva monastery (Sanderson 2013).

  • Lallā of Kashmir. The fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lallā (Lal Ded), whose verses draw on the yoga and the non-dual theology of Kashmiri Śaivism (Section 6.14), is revered by Hindus and Muslims alike; her poetry is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

  • The Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī. The woman ascetic who arrived at the Kālī temple of Dakṣiṇeśvar in 1861 guided Rāmakṛṣṇa through a long series of Tantric disciplines over the following years (Section 14.3). She is the best-documented example of a female Tantric guru with a male disciple in modern India. In 1872 Rāmakṛṣṇa in turn worshipped his wife, Śāradā Devī, as the goddess Ṣoḍaśī; she later initiated many disciples herself and is revered by the Rāmakṛṣṇa movement as the Holy Mother.

  • Women tāntrikās in modern Bengal. June McDaniel’s fieldwork in West Bengal recorded women practitioners of several kinds: renunciant bhairavīs living at cremation grounds and goddess shrines such as Tārāpīṭh, women who became gurus after visions or possession by the Goddess, and householders who combined Tantric practice with family life (McDaniel 2004). Asking whether Tantric ritual empowers women, she found that renunciants could gain independence, authority and followers, while for women who remained in the household the gains were more limited (McDaniel 2007).

The worship of young girls as the Goddess (kumārīpūjā), prescribed in many Śākta texts and performed during Navarātri and Durgā Pūjā, belongs to a different register: the girl is honoured as the Goddess for the duration of the rite, and in the case of the royal Kumārī of Kathmandu for the years before puberty (Section 4.7). It shows the readiness of the traditions to see the divine in a human female, but it gives the girl a ritual status, not a role as practitioner or teacher.

docs.title: 4.14.4 The Modern Debate
docs.text:
Scholarly positions on women in Tantra range widely. One position, represented for Buddhist Tantra by Miranda Shaw (Section 10.10) and for the late Kaula texts by Biernacki, stresses that women were practitioners, teachers and objects of reverence, and that the texts’ exaltation of the feminine had real consequences. Another, represented by David Gordon White and, for the early scriptures, by much of the philological work, stresses that the texts were composed by men for male practitioners, that the women they describe are often instruments of male attainment, and that the partners preferred in some rites were women of low caste, valued for the very impurity that society attributed to them (White 2003). Törzsök’s analysis suggests that both are partly right for the early period: the same scriptures that use the dūtī as a means also grant women full initiation and the right to practise for their own ends (Törzsök 2014).

Two further cautions apply. First, the evidence is uneven in time and place: what holds for the Brahmayāmala need not hold for the Śaiva Siddhānta temple or for eighteenth-century Bengal, and the temple priesthoods governed by the Āgamas remained closed to women until very recent debates (Chapter 1). Second, modern interest in the “sacred feminine”, in India and abroad, has encouraged readings of Tantra that project present-day concerns onto the sources (Section 14.4), while the authority of the guru in secret traditions has also made women vulnerable to abuse by teachers claiming Tantric legitimacy (Section 14.2). What the evidence supports is a double conclusion: these traditions opened to women religious roles that the Vedic order denied them, and they did so within a social world that remained, for the most part, governed by men.

docs.title: 4.15 The Seven Ācāras
docs.text: The Kulārṇava’s ladder of seven “conducts” (ācāras), from Vedic to Kaula (Section 4.5), became standard in later Śākta texts. It is a hierarchy of religious paths with the Kaula path at its summit, not a historical description; texts disagree about the order of the higher stages, and some add further categories. Similarly the conventional number of sixty-four Śākta Tantras is ideal: the lists in different texts do not agree, and many of the works named in them are lost.

docs.title: 4.15.1 Purity and the Cremation Ground
docs.text: Śākta texts repeatedly relativise external purity, declaring that what matters is the purity of the mind and that the Goddess pervades the pure and the impure alike. The practice of worship in cremation grounds (śmaśānasādhanā), inherited from the Kāpālika and Vidyāpīṭha traditions and still followed by some ascetics at sites such as Tārāpīṭh and Kāmākhyā, dramatises this principle by confronting death and impurity directly.

docs.title: Chapter 5: The Śrīvidyā Tradition
docs.text:
Lalitāsahasranāma, opening names

śrīmātā śrīmahārājñī śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśvarī | cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā devakāryasamudyatā ||

The auspicious Mother, the great Queen, mistress of the glorious lion-throne, born from the fire-altar of consciousness, intent on accomplishing the work of the gods.

docs.title: 5.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Śrīvidyā (“auspicious wisdom”) is the tradition of worship of the goddess Lalitā Tripurasundarī through her mantra, the śrīvidyā itself, and her diagram, the Śrīcakra. It originated as one of the Kaula traditions: its earliest scripture, the Vāmakeśvarīmata (also known as the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava), was commented on in thirteenth-century Kashmir by Jayaratha, the commentator of the Tantrāloka. In South India, from about the fourteenth century, the tradition was progressively adopted by learned Brahmins and by the Advaita monasteries, and was reshaped in a more orthodox, Vedāntic direction (Brooks 1990, 1992; Sanderson 2009).

Three elements are central to it: the mantra, the fifteen-syllable pañcadaśī or its sixteen-syllable extension, the ṣoḍaśī; the diagram, the Śrīcakra or Śrīyantra; and the ritual in which the goddess and her retinue are worshipped in the nine enclosures of that diagram (navavaraṇapūjā).

docs.title: 5.2.1 The Goddess
docs.text:
Lalitā Tripurasundarī is the central deity of Śrīvidyā. The commentators explain her names as follows: she is Lalitā, “she who plays”, because the universe is her play (līlā); Tripurā, “of the three cities”, a name read as referring to the triads of creation, such as the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, the three powers of will, knowledge and action, and the three sections of her mantra; and Sundarī, “the beautiful”.

She is depicted as a beautiful sixteen-year-old goddess, red in colour, holding a noose, an elephant goad, a sugarcane bow and five flower arrows, and seated on a throne whose legs are the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara, with Sadāśiva as its seat. Figure 5.1 shows a Kangra painting of the goddess.

Figure 5.1. Tripurasundarī enthroned in a garden pavilion, seated on the couch of the gods, with attendant figures; Kangra school, eighteenth century (Museum of Kangra Art). Photo: SpeakingArch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.2.2 The Lalitāsahasranāma
docs.text: The Lalitāsahasranāma (“Thousand Names of Lalitā”), presented as part of the Lalitopākhyāna of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, is the most widely recited hymn of the tradition. Its names describe the goddess’s iconography, her victory over the demon Bhaṇḍa, her city and her abode in the Śrīcakra, her presence in the body as kuṇḍalinī, and her identity with the absolute. The standard commentary is Bhāskararāya’s Saubhāgyabhāskara (1728). The Lalitātriśatī, a hymn of three hundred names, is structured on the fifteen syllables of the pañcadaśī: each syllable begins twenty names.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Structure
docs.text:
The Śrīcakra is the most celebrated of Hindu yantras. At its centre is a point (bindu), the union of Śiva and Śakti. Around it nine large triangles interpenetrate, four with the apex upward (the “Śiva” triangles) and five with the apex downward (the “Śakti” triangles); their intersections produce forty-three smaller triangles, arranged as a central triangle surrounded by rings of eight, ten, ten and fourteen. The triangles are enclosed by a lotus of eight petals and a lotus of sixteen petals, then by three circles, and finally by a square enclosure (bhūpura) of three lines with a gate in each side. The tradition counts these elements as nine concentric enclosures (āvaraṇas), from the square to the point; Figure 5.2 shows them schematically, numbered as in Table 5.1.

Figure 5.2. Labelled schematic of the nine enclosures (āvaraṇas) of the Śrīcakra, numbered from the outside inwards as in Table 5.1. The four triangular enclosures are drawn here as separate rings so that their triangles (14, 10, 10 and 8, around the central triangle) can be counted. In the actual diagram they are not drawn separately: they are produced by the intersection of nine large triangles, four pointing upward and five downward, a construction this schematic does not attempt to show.

Drawing the nine triangles so that their lines meet exactly at common points is a genuinely difficult geometric problem, and traditional manuals and modern writers give different constructions (Bühnemann 2003; Khanna 2003). Popular claims that the figure encodes the golden ratio, fractals or other modern mathematics have no support in the classical texts.

The Śrīcakra may also be made in three dimensions, as a meru, in which the enclosures rise in tiers towards the central point like the cosmic mountain Meru (Figure 5.3).

Figure 5.3. A three-dimensional (meru) Śrīcakra in stone, with the lotus tiers rising to the interlocking triangles. Photo: Rashkesh, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.3.2 The Nine Enclosures (Āvaraṇas)
docs.text:
The Śrīcakra is understood as nine concentric “enclosures” (āvaraṇas or cakras), each with its presiding form of the goddess (cakreśvarī) and its class of attendant yoginīs. The standard names, found in the Vāmakeśvarīmata tradition and the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad, are (Table 5.1):

Table 5.1. The Nine Āvaraṇas of the Śrīcakra No. Name Figure Presiding goddess Class of yoginīs 1 Trailokyamohana Square enclosure Tripurā Prakaṭa (“manifest”) 2 Sarvāśāparipūraka Sixteen petals Tripureśī Gupta (“hidden”) 3 Sarvasaṁkṣobhaṇa Eight petals Tripurasundarī Guptatara (“more hidden”) 4 Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka Fourteen triangles Tripuravāsinī Sampradāya 5 Sarvārthasādhaka Outer ten triangles Tripurāśrī Kulottīrṇa 6 Sarvarakṣākara Inner ten triangles Tripuramālinī Nigarbha 7 Sarvarogahara Eight triangles Tripurāsiddhā Rahasya (“secret”) 8 Sarvasiddhiprada Central triangle Tripurāmbā Atirahasya (“most secret”) 9 Sarvānandamaya Central point Mahātripurasundarī Parāparāti­rahasya

The names describe a ritual progression from the “enchantment of the three worlds” at the outer enclosure to “complete bliss” at the centre. The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad identifies the enclosures with parts of the worshipper’s body and with elements of the cosmos, so that the external worship can be performed internally as meditation.

docs.title: 5.4.1 The Pañcadaśī
docs.text:
The central mantra is the pañcadaśī (“fifteen-syllabled”), divided into three sections called kūṭas (“peaks”). In its most common form, the “kādi” form attributed to the god Kāma, the sections have five, six and four syllables; another form, the “hādi” form, is attributed to the sage Lopāmudrā (Table 5.2).

Table 5.2. Structure of the Pañcadaśī Kūṭa Name Syllables Traditional correlations First Vāgbhava 5 Speech; power of knowledge; the head of the goddess Second Kāmarāja 6 Desire; power of action; her torso Third Śakti 4 Power; power of will; her lower body

The tradition holds that the mantra must be received through initiation; texts customarily encode its syllables rather than state them. The ṣoḍaśī adds a sixteenth syllable and is given at a higher stage of initiation.

docs.title: 5.5 The Two Schools
docs.text:
South Indian Śrīvidyā distinguishes two orientations (Table 5.3; Brooks 1992):

Table 5.3. Kaula and Samaya Orientations in Śrīvidyā Aspect Kaula Samaya Practice External worship of the drawn or metal Śrīcakra, with internal meditation; some lineages retain the Kaula sacraments, actual or substituted Rejects external worship of the yantra and all left-hand elements; worship is internal, in the cakras of the body Key authorities Vāmakeśvarīmata, Yoginīhṛdaya and their commentaries; Bhāskararāya Lakṣmīdhara’s commentary on the Saundaryalaharī; the Śubhagodaya and other works attributed by tradition to Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara Social setting Smārta Brahmin householders and other lineages Associated with the Advaita monasteries of Śṛṅgerī and Kāñcī

Both revere the same goddess, mantra and diagram. Brooks shows that the Samaya position represents a deliberate “brahmanisation” of a Kaula tradition, in which the transgressive elements were reinterpreted or excluded (Brooks 1992).

docs.title: 5.6 The Saundaryalaharī
docs.text:
The Saundaryalaharī (“Wave of Beauty”) is a hundred-verse hymn to the goddess, attributed by tradition to Śaṅkara. Modern scholars generally doubt the attribution to the author of the Advaita commentaries: the poem’s Tantric content and its first attested use point to a later date, and the tradition ascribes many devotional works to Śaṅkara (Brown 1958). The poem combines devotional poetry of great beauty with encoded Tantric doctrine, alluding to the Śrīcakra, the pañcadaśī and the cakras of the body, and it has been used in ritual, with later manuals assigning a yantra and a purpose to each verse.

It is traditionally divided into the Ānandalaharī (verses 1–41), more explicitly doctrinal, and the Saundaryalaharī proper (42–100), a description of the goddess from head to foot. Lakṣmīdhara’s commentary (probably 16th century) gives it the Samaya interpretation (Sastri and Ayyangar 1937). Its first verse, quoted at the head of Chapter 4, states the Śākta doctrine that Śiva without Śakti “cannot even stir”.

docs.title: 5.7 Key Authors of the Śrīvidyā Tradition
docs.text: The literature of Śrīvidyā runs from Kashmir to the Kaveri delta. In thirteenth-century Kashmir Jayaratha, the commentator of the Tantrāloka, also commented on the Vāmakeśvarīmata. Puṇyānanda and Amṛtānanda (c. 13th–14th century), authors respectively of the Kāmakalāvilāsa and of the Dīpikā commentary on the Yoginīhṛdaya, interpreted the tradition through Kashmiri non-dual theology. Tradition credits Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara with the Śubhagodaya, the Saundaryalaharī and the Prapañcasāra, but most historians do not accept these attributions. Lakṣmīdhara (c. 16th century) and Kaivalyāśrama, author of the Saubhāgyavardhinī, wrote the principal commentaries on the Saundaryalaharī, and the eighteenth-century Bhāskararāya, discussed below, gave the tradition its early modern form.

docs.title: 5.8 The Navavaraṇa Worship
docs.text:
The worship of the nine enclosures (navavaraṇapūjā) is the central ritual of Śrīvidyā. It proceeds through the enclosures of the Śrīcakra from the outer square to the central point, worshipping in each the presiding goddess, her attendant deities and yoginīs, with their mantras and hand gestures (mudrās; Figure 5.4). A full performance includes:

  1. Preliminary purifications: purification of the elements of the body (bhūtaśuddhi), breath control and the placing of mantras on the body (nyāsa), including in some lineages the elaborate “great sixfold” mahāṣoḍhānyāsa;

  2. Mental worship of the goddess and the Śrīcakra;

  3. Preparation of the special offering (viśeṣārghya), which in Kaula lineages may involve the sacraments discussed in Chapter 4;

  4. External worship of the goddess at the centre with the customary offerings;

  5. Worship of the nine enclosures in sequence;

  6. Recitation of the mantra and of hymns such as the Lalitāsahasranāma;

  7. Fire offering in elaborate performances, and concluding rites.

Figure 5.4. Worship of a large Śrīcakra drawn in coloured powders and surrounded by flowers and lamps. Photo: Quantumquark, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 5.9 Philosophy
docs.text: The theology of Śrīvidyā, especially as developed by Puṇyānanda, Amṛtānanda and Bhāskararāya, draws heavily on Kashmiri non-dual Śaivism (Chapter 6). Reality is the unity of luminous consciousness (prakāśa, Śiva) and its reflexive self-awareness (vimarśa, Śakti); the cosmos unfolds through the thirty-six tattvas of the Kashmiri scheme; worldly enjoyment and liberation (bhukti and mukti) are both offered and are not regarded as opposed; and the worshipper’s own body is understood as the Śrīcakra and the site of internal worship.

docs.title: 5.9.1 Sāmarasya
docs.text: The term sāmarasya (“sameness of savour”) denotes the non-dual state in which Śiva and Śakti, consciousness and its power, worshipper and deity, are realised to be of one nature. It is symbolised by the central point of the Śrīcakra and said to be realised when the mantra ceases to be an external recitation and becomes the worshipper’s own awareness.

docs.title: 5.9.2 Desire (Kāma)
docs.text: Śrīvidyā gives desire a positive theological value. The goddess is Kāmeśvarī, “Sovereign of Desire”, the consort of Kāmeśvara; she holds the sugarcane bow and flower arrows of the love-god; and the second section of her mantra is named after Kāma. The commentators distinguish desire as contracted, egoistic craving from desire as the universal creative impulse of the goddess, and treat practice as the transformation of the former into the latter.

docs.title: 5.10 The Yoginīhṛdaya
docs.text:
The Yoginīhṛdaya (“Heart of the Yoginī”), regarded as the second part of the Vāmakeśvarīmata, gives the inner, esoteric doctrine of the tradition in three “conventions” (saṁketas):

  1. Cakrasaṁketa: the Śrīcakra as the unfolding of consciousness and its correspondence with cosmos and body;

  2. Mantrasaṁketa: the meanings of the pañcadaśī, interpreted on several levels;

  3. Pūjāsaṁketa: the worship of the goddess, understood as the realisation of the identity of worshipper, deity, mantra and diagram.

Amṛtānanda’s Dīpikā commentary reads the text through the Pratyabhijñā philosophy.

docs.title: 5.11 Bhāskararāya
docs.text:
Bhāskararāya (Bhāsurānandanātha, 18th century), a Maharashtrian Brahmin who settled in the Kaveri delta under Marāṭhā patronage, is the most important Śrīvidyā author of the early modern period. A learned scholar of Vedic ritual, Mīmāṃsā and grammar as well as an initiate, he sought to show that Kaula Śrīvidyā was consistent with Vedic orthodoxy.

Work Type Significance Saubhāgyabhāskara Commentary on the Lalitāsahasranāma (1728) The standard commentary, explaining the names through mantra, yantra and doctrine Varivasyārahasya Independent treatise with auto-commentary On the meaning of the pañcadaśī and worship Setubandha Commentary on the Vāmakeśvarīmata / Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava Commentary on the root scripture Guptavatī Commentary on the Devīmāhātmya Influential Śākta reading of the text

His works remain standard references for South Indian Śrīvidyā practitioners, and his synthesis of Kaula practice with Vedic orthodoxy shaped the tradition’s modern form (Brooks 1992).

docs.title: 5.12 The Myth of Lalitā
docs.text:
The Lalitopākhyāna (“Tale of Lalitā”), presented as part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, gives Śrīvidyā its mythology. When Śiva burns Kāma, the god of love, with the fire of his third eye, a demon, Bhaṇḍa, is formed from the ashes and oppresses the worlds. The gods, led by Indra, perform a great sacrifice, and from the “fire-altar of consciousness” the goddess Lalitā arises, beautiful and armed with noose, goad, sugarcane bow and flower arrows. She marries Kāmeśvara, a form of Śiva, and with an army of goddesses — including her ministers Śyāmalā (Mātaṅgī) and Vārāhī, and the nityā goddesses of the lunar days — she destroys Bhaṇḍa and his sons in a great battle. She then dwells in her jewelled city, Śrīpura, on the summit of Mount Meru, whose concentric walls and palaces correspond to the enclosures of the Śrīcakra.

The myth expresses Śrīvidyā’s theology in narrative form: desire, burnt by asceticism, returns as demonic when separated from its divine source, and is restored only when it is reintegrated in the goddess who is herself the sovereign of desire. The names of the Lalitāsahasranāma follow the order of the tale.

docs.title: 5.13 The Kāma­kalā­vilāsa and the Bhāvanā Upa­niṣad
docs.text:
Two works illustrate how Śrīvidyā turned its ritual into contemplation.

Puṇyānanda’s Kāmakalāvilāsa, a short work in fifty-five verses with a commentary by Naṭānan­danātha, describes the emergence of the cosmos from the union of Śiva as light (prakāśa) and Śakti as reflexive awareness (vimarśa). Their union is visualised as the kāmakalā, a subtle triangle formed by a white point, a red point and a mixed point, which is the goddess’s most secret form and the seed of the Śrīcakra and of the mantra.

The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad, a late text attached to the Atharvaveda and commented on by Bhāskararāya, prescribes an “inner worship” in which every element of the Śrīcakra and of the worship is identified with an element of the worshipper’s body and mind: the nine enclosures with the nine apertures and the faculties, the attendant goddesses with the vital breaths and mental states, the offerings with attitudes of mind. The worshipper who knows these identities, the text says, is liberated while living. Such texts made it possible for the Samaya school to replace external ritual entirely by contemplation (Brooks 1990).

docs.title: 5.14 The Living Tradition
docs.text: Śrīvidyā remains alive in South India. The Advaita monasteries of Śṛṅgerī and Kāñcī maintain Śrīcakra worship; in the Kāmākṣī temple at Kāñcīpuram a Śrīcakra before the goddess, said by tradition to have been installed by Śaṅkara, receives worship, and Śrīcakras are worshipped in many other goddess temples. Smārta Brahmin families and numerous gurus in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka transmit the tradition, and since the twentieth century some teachers have initiated non-Brahmins, women and foreigners, a development criticised by conservatives (Brooks 1992).

docs.title: Chapter 6: Kashmir Śaivism: Trika, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā
docs.text:
Śivasūtra 1.1

caitanyam ātmā ||

The Self is consciousness.

docs.title: 6.1 Introduction
docs.text:
“Kashmir Śaivism” is a modern label for the non-dual Śaiva traditions that flourished in the Kashmir Valley between about the ninth and the twelfth centuries: the Trika (“Triad”), the Kālī-centred Krama (“Sequence”), and the philosophical schools of Spanda (“Vibration”) and Pratyabhijñā (“Recognition”). It is important to remember that Kashmir was also a major centre of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, whose exegetes debated with the non-dualists (Chapter 2) (Sanderson 1988; Dyczkowski 1987). The non-dual tradition culminated in the work of Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016 CE) and his pupil Kṣemarāja.

These traditions hold that the whole universe is the manifestation of a single absolute consciousness, Śiva, endowed with the power of free self-expression. Unlike the Advaita Vedānta of Śaṅkara, which treats the world as an appearance due to ignorance, they regard the world as a real expression of divine consciousness.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Scriptural and Foundational Texts
docs.text: The non-dual exegetes based themselves on the Śaiva Bhairava scriptures, especially the Mālinīvijayottara, the Svacchanda, the Netra and the Vijñānabhairava, and on a small number of foundational works of the ninth century. The seventy-seven aphorisms of the Śivasūtra, according to tradition, were found by Vasugupta inscribed on a rock on Mount Mahādeva after Śiva revealed their location in a dream. The verses of the Spandakārikā on “vibration” are attributed to Vasugupta or to his pupil Kallaṭa. The Vijñānabhairava, a short Bhairava scripture presenting some 112 contemplative techniques (dhāraṇās), was probably composed between the seventh and ninth centuries; its colophon assigns it to the Rudrayāmala.

docs.title: 6.2.2 The Principal Authors
docs.text:
Table 6.1 lists the principal authors of the tradition.

Table 6.1. Principal Authors of the Kashmiri Non-dual Śaiva Tradition Author Approximate date Key works Vasugupta c. 850–900 Received the Śivasūtra; Spandakārikā attributed to him or Kallaṭa Somānanda c. 900–950 Śivadṛṣṭi, the first Pratyabhijñā treatise Utpaladeva c. 925–975 Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with his own commentaries; devotional Śiva­stotrāvalī Abhinavagupta c. 950–1016 Tantrāloka; Tantrasāra; Parātriśikāvivaraṇa; commentaries on Utpaladeva; Abhinavabhāratī; Locana Kṣemarāja early 11th c. Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya; Śivasūtravimarśinī; Spandanirṇaya, Spandasandoha; commentaries on the Svacchanda and Netra Jayaratha early 13th c. Viveka commentary on the Tantrāloka

docs.title: 6.3 Abhinavagupta
docs.text: Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016 CE) is the most important figure of the tradition and one of the major thinkers of Indian intellectual history. The conventional dates are an estimate: the years of his birth and death are not recorded, and his dated works run from a hymn of 990/91 to his long commentary on Utpaladeva’s own commentary on the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, completed in 1014/15, so that his period of activity can be fixed more securely than his lifespan. At the end of the Tantrāloka he gives an account of his family and of his many teachers in grammar, logic, poetics, dramaturgy and the various Śaiva systems.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Major Works
docs.text:
1. Tantrāloka (“Light on the Tantras”): an encyclopaedic exposition in thirty-seven chapters (āhnikas) of the doctrine and ritual of the Trika, based on the Mālinīvijayottara and integrating Kaula and Krama teaching (see below).

  2. Tantrasāra (“Essence of the Tantras”): a prose summary of the Tantrāloka.

  3. Parātriśikāvivaraṇa: a commentary on a short Trika scripture, with a profound theology of the phonemes and the mantra sauh.

  4. Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and -vivṛtivimarśinī: commentaries on Utpaladeva’s verses and on Utpaladeva’s own (now largely lost) detailed commentary.

  5. Abhinavabhāratī and Dhvanyālokalocana: commentaries on Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra and Ānandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka, fundamental to Indian aesthetics.

docs.title: 6.4 The Thirty-Six Tattvas
docs.text: The Kashmiri non-dualists share the Śaiva scheme of thirty-six tattvas (Table 2.2) but interpret it as the stages by which a single consciousness manifests itself. In their presentation the principles fall into three “paths”: the pure (śuddhādhvan, 1–5), in which consciousness knows the universe as itself, the will, knowledge and action of Śiva unfolding as Sadāśiva, Īśvara and pure knowledge; the realm of māyā and its five “coverings” (kañcukas, 6–11), which contract consciousness’s infinite powers of agency, knowledge, contentment, eternity and pervasion; and the impure realm (12–36), headed by the limited subject (puruṣa) and comprising the world it experiences. The Siddhānta, as the note to the table explains, counts Puruṣa instead with Māyā and the coverings, so that the two schools draw the boundary between the middle and the lower level in different places. Māyā itself, for the non-dualists, is not illusion, as it is for Advaita Vedānta, but a real power of Śiva by which he freely limits himself: it lets Śiva appear as limited subjects and objects, the world it produces is real as his self-expression, and it is overcome not by knowledge of a changeless Brahman but by the recognition of one’s identity with Śiva.

docs.title: 6.5 The Pratyabhijñā (Recognition) Philosophy
docs.text:
The Pratyabhijñā school, founded by Somānanda and given its classic philosophical form by Utpaladeva, argues — in dialogue especially with the Buddhist epistemologists Dharmakīrti and his followers — that the self is a single, continuous, self-aware consciousness, the Lord (īśvara). Liberation is not the acquisition of something new but the recognition (pratyabhijñā) that one already is that Lord (Dyczkowski 1987). The modern study of the school rests above all on Raffaele Torella’s critical edition and annotated translation of Utpaladeva’s verses with the author’s own short commentary (Torella 2002), on John Nemec’s edition and study of the first chapters of Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi, the founding text of the school (Nemec 2011), and on Isabelle Ratié’s analysis of the Pratyabhijñā theory of the self and its debate with the Buddhist epistemologists (Ratié 2011).

Kṣemarāja’s Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya (“Heart of Recognition”), twenty short sūtras with his own commentary, is a concise introduction to the doctrine, drawing on Pratyabhijñā, Spanda and Krama sources (Singh 1963). Its first four sūtras are:

Sūtra Text Meaning 1 citiḥ svatantrā viśva­siddhi­hetuḥ Free consciousness is the cause of the manifestation of the universe 2 svecchayā svabhittau viśvam unmīlayati By her own will she unfolds the universe on her own screen 3 tan nānā anurūpa­grāhya­grāhaka­bhedāt That universe is manifold because of the differentiation of mutually corresponding objects and subjects 4 citisaṃkocātmā cetano ’pi saṃkucitaviśvamayaḥ The individual knower, whose nature is contracted consciousness, also contains the universe in contracted form

docs.title: 6.5.1 Utpaladeva’s Argument
docs.text:
Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā is a work of philosophical argument, not of revelation. Its opponent is above all the Buddhist epistemological school of Dharmakīrti, which held that reality consists of momentary, particular events and that the unified, enduring self is a conceptual construction. Utpaladeva replies that memory, the synthesis of cognitions in judgement, and the very possibility of relating one experience to another presuppose a single, continuous subject. That subject, moreover, must be self-aware: an unconscious light could not manifest anything. He therefore argues that the fundamental reality is a self-luminous consciousness that is also reflexively aware of itself (vimarśa), and that this consciousness, by virtue of its freedom, manifests the world of subjects and objects as its own content. The “Lord” (īśvara) of the title is this consciousness, and the work’s aim is that the reader should recognise himself as that Lord.

The work’s first verse states its purpose in devotional terms: the author, having attained the servitude of the Lord, wishes to make recognition possible for all people. The combination of rigorous argument with devotion — Utpaladeva was also the author of the hymns collected as the Śivastotrāvalī — is characteristic of the tradition.

docs.title: 6.5.2 Trika Ritual
docs.text: The non-dual Kashmiri tradition was not only a philosophy. Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka is largely a ritual handbook, prescribing initiation, daily worship and the secret Kaula rites for Trika initiates. Trika worship centres on the three goddesses on the prongs of the trident maṇḍala, with Bhairava, and on the “sacrificial vessel” filled with wine. Abhinavagupta reinterprets ritual as the expression of non-dual awareness, but he does not abolish it: for most initiates, he holds, ritual is the means by which insight is cultivated and expressed, and only the most advanced can dispense with it (Sanderson 1988).

docs.title: 6.6 The Spanda Doctrine
docs.text:
Spanda — “vibration”, “pulsation” — denotes the inherent dynamism of consciousness. Kṣemarāja defines it as “a slight movement” (kiñcic calanam): neither the inertness of an object nor physical motion, but the creative pulsation of awareness. The Spandakārikā opens:

Spandakārikā 1

yasyonmeṣanimeṣābhyāṃ jagataḥ pralayodayau | taṃ śakticakravibhavaprabhavaṃ śaṅkaraṃ stumaḥ ||

We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the glory of the wheel of powers, by whose opening and closing of the eyes the world dissolves and arises.

The Spanda teachers hold that every perception, thought and emotion is a pulsation of consciousness, and that the practitioner can become aware of spanda directly in moments of intensity and transition — at the junction of waking and sleep, in strong emotion, at the beginning and end of a thought (Singh 1980; Dyczkowski 1987). The three currents of Kashmiri non-dualism can thus be distinguished by their emphasis: the Spanda sees consciousness as dynamic pulsation and cultivates attention to that pulsation; the Pratyabhijñā sees it as the self-aware Lord and joins philosophical argument to contemplation; and the Krama (Section 6.9) sees each cognition as a cycle of phases, each a form of the goddess Kālī, to be worshipped and contemplated in sequence.

docs.title: 6.7 The Trika
docs.text:
The Trika takes its name from several triads. Its scriptural basis is the trio of the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, the Anāmakatantra (the “Nameless” Tantra) and the Mālinīvijayottara; its deities are the three goddesses Parā, Parāparā and Aparā, with Bhairava; and its doctrine distinguishes Śiva, Śakti and the individual (nara) (Table 6.2; Sanderson 1988).

Table 6.2. Some Triads of the Trika Level First Second Third Goddesses Parā (supreme) Parāparā (supreme-and-lower) Aparā (lower) Powers Will (icchā) Knowledge (jñāna) Action (kriyā) Realities Śiva Śakti Nara (the individual)

docs.title: 6.8.1 The Five Acts of Śiva
docs.text: Śiva performs five acts — emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhāra), concealment (tirodhāna) and grace (anugraha). Kṣemarāja (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 10–11) teaches that the individual performs them too, in every act of cognition: the arising, persistence and fading of a perception, the forgetting of one’s true nature and its recollection.

docs.title: 6.8.2 States of Consciousness
docs.text: The non-dualists also reworked the Upaniṣadic analysis of experience. They share with Vedānta the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep and a “fourth” (turīya) state of pure awareness, but they add a fifth, “beyond the fourth” (turīyātīta), in which the awareness of the fourth pervades the other three, so that waking, dream and sleep are themselves experienced as expressions of Śiva.

docs.title: 6.8.3 The Means to Liberation (Upāyas)
docs.text:
The Mālinīvijayottara teaches three means of realisation; Abhinavagupta adds a fourth, “no means”, above them. From the highest to the lowest they are:

  1. Anupāya (“no means”): immediate realisation through a single instruction or through grace alone.

  2. Śāmbhavopāya (the means of Śiva): sudden, thought-free intuition of one’s nature.

  3. Śāktopāya (the means of Śakti): the cultivation of pure, non-dual thoughts and contemplation.

  4. Āṇavopāya (the means of the individual): practices using the body, breath, mantra, visualisation and ritual.

docs.title: 6.8.4 Prakāśa and Vimarśa
docs.text:
Consciousness has two inseparable aspects: prakāśa, its luminosity or manifesting power, and vimarśa, its reflexive self-awareness, expressed as the “I” (aham). Without vimarśa, the Pratyabhijñā authors argue, prakāśa would be like a crystal that reflects objects without knowing it does so. Prakāśa is identified with Śiva, vimarśa with Śakti; the universe is the self-expression of consciousness aware of itself. The religious image of the inseparable couple Śiva and Pārvatī gives visual form to the same idea (Figure 6.1).

Figure 6.1. Śiva embracing Pārvatī (Umā-Maheśvara), bronze, Pāla period, Bihār, tenth century (Metropolitan Museum of Art). The inseparable divine couple became the theologians’ image for the unity of consciousness (prakāśa) and its power (vimarśa). Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.8.5 Svātantrya: Freedom
docs.text: The central attribute of consciousness is its freedom (svātantrya): its power to manifest as anything whatever without external cause. Bondage itself is a free self-limitation of consciousness; liberation is the recognition of one’s own freedom. Because the world is a free expression of consciousness, it is real.

docs.title: 6.9 The Krama
docs.text: The Krama (“Sequence”) is the Kālī-centred tradition that the Kashmiri authors regarded as the most esoteric. It analyses each act of cognition, and the cosmic process, as a cycle of phases: emanation (sṛṣṭi), persistence (sthiti), withdrawal (saṃhāra) and the “nameless” (anākhya) state of pure awareness in which the cycle is grounded; some sources add a fifth phase of radiance (bhāsā). Each phase is worshipped as a form of Kālī, the goddess who “devours” time and objectivity. Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka lists a sequence of twelve Kālīs, beginning with Sṛṣṭikālī, which are contemplated as the phases through which consciousness withdraws objectivity into itself. The Krama thus gives a Śākta inflection to the tradition: where the Pratyabhijñā stresses the self-aware subject, the Krama stresses the dynamic activity of cognition as the goddess (Sanderson 1988).

docs.title: 6.9.1 The Kālīkula and the Jayadrathayāmala
docs.text: The Krama grew out of a wider body of Kālī-centred scripture, the Kālīkula (“family of Kālī”), which belongs to the Śakti Tantras of the Vidyāpīṭha (Section 2.5). Its largest surviving work is the Jayadrathayāmala, a scripture in four books (ṣaṭkas), each in principle of six thousand verses, preserved, though not without gaps, in Nepalese manuscripts (Sanderson 1988, 2007). The first book centres on the goddess Kālasaṁkarṣaṇī, “she who draws in (and so destroys) time”, and the later books add a great profusion of Kālīs and other goddesses, each with her mantras, her retinue of yoginīs and her rites for the attainment of powers, many of them performed in cremation grounds. The text is later than the Brahmayāmala, whose cult of Kapālīśabhairava it presupposes, and earlier than the Kashmiri exegetes who quote it; it already reflects the ideas of the Krama and of the developing Trika. For a modern reader its interest lies less in doctrine than in its picture of a world of fierce goddesses, yoginīs and visionary practice from which the refined theology of the Kashmiri exegetes was later drawn.

docs.title: 6.9.2 The Krama Lineage
docs.text:
The Krama tradition presents itself as a lineage of teachers rather than a body of scripture. Its own accounts, preserved by Jayaratha and others, say that it was revealed by a yoginī to the master Jñānanetra, also called Śivānanda, in Uḍḍiyāna (Oḍḍiyāna, in the Swat valley), probably in the ninth century. Remarkably, the tradition then passed through women: Śivānanda’s three disciples were the yoginīs Keyūravatī, Madanikā and Kalyāṇikā, and they in turn initiated male disciples, among them Govindarāja, Bhānuka and Erakanātha, from whom the later Kashmiri lines descend (Sanderson 2007). Navjivan Rastogi’s study of the Krama’s sources remains the fullest account of its history in a single volume (Rastogi 1979). Women thus stand at the head of one of the most influential lineages of Kashmir, a fact that fits the evidence of the early goddess scriptures for women as initiates and transmitters of teaching (Section 4.14).

The Krama’s literature is small but varied. Beside short scriptures of the Kālīkula, it includes hymns, of which the most famous is a Kramastotra on which Abhinavagupta wrote a commentary, now lost; the Mahānayaprakāśa, a work in Old Kashmiri verse with a Sanskrit commentary, which is among the earliest surviving texts in the Kashmiri language; and the Mahārthamañjarī of Maheśvarānanda, composed in the Tamil country, which shows that the Krama, also known as the “Great Teaching” (mahānaya) or “Great Meaning” (mahārtha), travelled far beyond Kashmir (Section 6.14) (Sanderson 2007).

Practice. Krama practice centres on the worship and contemplation of a sequence (krama) of goddesses — in the most developed form the twelve Kālīs mentioned above — who stand for the successive phases of each act of awareness and of the cosmic cycle. The aim is not to master external objects but to see every perception as the goddess’s movement of projecting, holding and withdrawing the world, and so to rest in the “nameless” ground from which the cycle arises. Krama teachers therefore placed great value on direct, non-conceptual realisation and on the sudden “devouring” of duality, and they were correspondingly sparing with external ritual.

Integration into the Trika. Abhinavagupta absorbed the Krama into his synthesis. In his Trika the three goddesses of the Trika’s trident, Parā, Parāparā and Aparā, are surmounted by a fourth, Kālasaṁkarṣaṇī, the Kālī of the Krama, who represents consciousness in its all-devouring, transcendent aspect; and the fourth chapter of the Tantrāloka, above all, draws extensively on Krama teaching (Sanderson 1988). The Kālī of the Krama should be distinguished from the Kālī of later Bengali devotion (Section 4.11): the two share a name and a fierce iconography, but the Kashmiri goddess is above all a figure of cognition, the Bengali one a mother to be loved.

docs.title: 6.10 The Vijñānabhairava
docs.text:
The Vijñānabhairava, a dialogue between Bhairava and the goddess, presents some 112 contemplations through which the practitioner may realise the nature of consciousness. They include attention to the junction points of the breath; absorption in sound, music, taste or other sensations; the use of intense states — desire, anger, fear, joy — and of moments such as a sneeze or the edge of a precipice; contemplation of empty space, the sky or the interval between objects; and reflection on the “I” that underlies experience.

Its premise is that almost any experience, attended to with sufficient intensity, can open onto the ground of awareness. It has become widely known outside India through modern translations.

docs.title: 6.11 Aesthetics
docs.text: In his Abhinavabhāratī and Locana, Abhinavagupta developed, from the work of his predecessors, an influential theory of aesthetic experience (rasa). Rasa, he argued, is not the emotion of a character or of the spectator but a generalised, impersonal savouring of an emotion, in which the spectator’s ordinary self-interest is suspended. This savouring by the sensitive spectator (sahṛdaya) is a form of the self-aware bliss of consciousness and is “akin to” the bliss of realising Brahman — in his phrase, its “fellow-student” (sabrahmacārin; the better-known brahmāsvādasahodara is the fourteenth-century Viśvanātha’s) — though not identical with it, since it depends on the work of art and passes when the work ends. He also defended the tranquil (śānta) rasa as a distinct sentiment. The theory became standard in later Sanskrit poetics (see Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā).

docs.title: 6.12 The Tantrāloka
docs.text:
The Tantrāloka presents the whole of Trika doctrine and ritual. Its thirty-seven chapters may be grouped as follows:

Chapters Subject 1 Overview of the work: knowledge, ignorance and the means of liberation 2–5 The means: “no means”, and the means of Śiva, of Śakti and of the individual 6–12 Time and space: the paths (adhvans) of time, worlds, tattvas and other levels of the cosmos 13–14 The descent of grace (śaktipāta) and its concealment 15–24 Initiation in its many forms, consecration and funerary rites 25–28 Post-initiatory obligations and occasional rites 29 The secret Kaula ritual (kulaprakriyā) 30–32 Mantras, maṇḍalas and mudrās 33–35 The unity of the paths and the harmony of the scriptures 36–37 The transmission of the teaching and Abhinavagupta’s account of his lineage and teachers

Jayaratha’s Viveka commentary is indispensable for understanding the work; text and commentary were published in twelve volumes in the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (Abhinavagupta 1918–1938).

docs.title: 6.13 The Śivasūtra
docs.text:
The seventy-seven aphorisms of the Śivasūtra are divided, in Kṣemarāja’s commentary, into three sections corresponding to three means (Singh 1979):

Section First sūtra Focus 1: Śāmbhavopāya (22 sūtras) caitanyam ātmā (“The Self is consciousness”) Direct realisation of one’s nature as Śiva 2: Śāktopāya (10 sūtras) cittaṃ mantraḥ (“The mind is mantra”) Mantra and contemplation 3: Āṇavopāya (45 sūtras) ātmā cittam (“The [limited] self is the mind”) Practices of the individual: breath, concentration, yoga

Two further sūtras illustrate its style. Jñānaṃ bandhaḥ (1.2), “Knowledge is bondage”, is explained by Kṣemarāja as referring to limited, dualistic knowledge; udyamo bhairavaḥ (1.5), “The upsurge [of awareness] is Bhairava”, identifies the sudden emergence of intuitive awareness with the absolute.

docs.title: 6.14 Kashmir after Abhinavagupta
docs.text: The non-dual tradition did not end with Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja. Yogharāja, a pupil of Kṣemarāja, commented on Abhinavagupta’s Paramārthasāra; Maheśvarānanda’s Mahārthamañjarī (late 12th or early 13th century), written in the Tamil country, expounds the Krama; Jayaratha (early 13th century) wrote the great commentary on the Tantrāloka. In later centuries the Kashmiri Paṇḍits preserved texts and domestic ritual handbooks in which Trika, Krama and Siddhānta elements were combined, and devotional poetry in Kashmiri — above all the sayings of the fourteenth-century woman mystic Lal Ded (Lallā), which draw on Śaiva yoga — carried the tradition’s ideas into the vernacular. In the twentieth century Svāmī Lakṣmaṇ Jū (Lakshman Joo, 1907–1991), regarded by his followers as the last master of the oral Kashmiri lineage, taught the texts to Sanskritists from India and abroad, while the displacement of most Kashmiri Paṇḍits from the Valley in 1990 dispersed the community that had carried the tradition for centuries.

docs.title: 6.15 Legacy
docs.text: With the establishment of the Sultanate in Kashmir in the fourteenth century royal patronage of the Śaiva traditions ended, but their ideas lived on outside the Valley, above all in the Śrīvidyā of the South (Chapter 5). The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, from 1911, published most of the key texts, and modern scholarship has made the tradition accessible far beyond the Valley: K.C. Pandey’s study of Abhinavagupta (Pandey 1963), Lilian Silburn’s French translations and studies, including her work on kuṇḍalinī (Silburn 1988), Jaideva Singh’s English translations, and the work of André Padoux, Alexis Sanderson, Mark Dyczkowski, Paul Muller-Ortega, Raffaele Torella and others (Singh 1979; Muller-Ortega 1989; Pandit 1997). Philosophers have compared the Kashmiri doctrines of self-aware consciousness, freedom and perception with idealist and phenomenological positions in Western philosophy of mind, and with theories of pre-reflective self-awareness and of the lived body; such comparisons can be illuminating if treated as analogies and not as claims that the texts anticipated modern theories.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Mantraśāstra: The Theory and Practice of Mantra
7.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Mantras — formulae of sacred speech — are the most pervasive element of Tantric religion. The Sanskrit word combines the root man, “to think”, with the instrumental suffix -tra: a mantra is an “instrument of thought”. Tantric authors also give a devotional etymology, much quoted, according to which a mantra is so called because it “protects” (trāyate) through “reflection” (manana). In Tantric ritual nothing is done without mantras: they are the means by which deities are invoked and worshipped, the body is purified, initiation is conferred and powers are obtained (Padoux 1990; Alper 1989).

Tantric theologians regard the mantra not as a conventional sign but as the deity’s own form in sound. This view rests on a doctrine of the Word that the Tantras share in part with the Vedic tradition and with the grammarian Bhartṛhari.

docs.title: 7.2 The Word as Absolute
docs.text: The idea that ultimate reality has the nature of speech has deep roots. The Ṛgveda’s hymn of Vāc (ṚV 10.125) presents Speech as a goddess who pervades the worlds, and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.1.2) declares that speech is the highest Brahman (vāg vai samrāṭ paramaṃ brahma). The grammarian Bhartṛhari’s Vākyapadīya (5th century) teaches that Brahman is the eternal Word-principle (śabdatattva) from which the world unfolds, and that all cognition is permeated by language. Building on him, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta identified the supreme Word (parā vāc) with the self-awareness (vimarśa) of Śiva, so that consciousness itself is, at its root, linguistic; and in later yoga the contemplation of inner sound (nāda) became a path to realisation (Section 7.10).

docs.title: 7.2.1 The Levels of Speech
docs.text:
Bhartṛhari distinguished three levels of speech: paśyantī (“seeing”, the undivided intuition), madhyamā (“intermediate”, mental formulation) and vaikharī (articulated sound). The Kashmiri Śaivas added a fourth and highest level, parā (“supreme”), identified with Śiva’s consciousness (Figure 7.1). Later texts locate the levels in the body (Padoux 1990). Mantra practice reverses the descent of speech: recitation moves from the audible to the murmured and the mental, and finally to silent awareness.

Figure 7.1. The four levels of speech in Tantric theology, with the bodily locations assigned to them in later texts.

docs.title: 7.3 The Structure and Classification of Mantras
7.3.1 The Elements of a Mantra’s Use
docs.text:
In later ritual manuals the use (viniyoga) of a mantra is introduced by naming:

  1. its seer (ṛṣi), the sage who first received it;

  2. its metre (chandas);

  3. its deity (devatā);

  4. its seed (bīja), power (śakti) and “peg” (kīlaka), elements thought to contain, express and secure its power.

docs.title: 7.3.2 Classifications
docs.text:
Figure 7.2. Some traditional classifications of mantras. The “gender” of a mantra is determined in manuals such as the Śāradātilaka by its ending; mantras of female deities are called vidyā.

Mantras used for worldly ends (Figure 7.2) were grouped as the “six acts” (ṣaṭkarmāṇi): pacification (śānti) of illness and calamity, subjugation (vaśya), immobilisation (stambhana), causing dissension (vidveṣaṇa), driving away (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa). Their presence in the manuals is a reminder that Tantric ritual served practical and sometimes aggressive purposes as well as liberation.

docs.title: 7.3.3 The Six Acts in the Manuals
docs.text:
The lists vary. Some texts replace one of the six with “attraction” (ākarṣaṇa) or “bewitching” (mohana), and some add “increase” (puṣṭi) of wealth and health; the number six is, like many Tantric numbers, a classificatory ideal. What the lists share is the conviction that the same mantra-deity who grants liberation can be directed, by the right procedure, to any worldly end, and that each end requires its own ritual setting.

Gudrun Bühnemann’s study of the medieval digests, among them the Śāradātilaka (c. 11th century) and the Mantramahodadhi (1589), shows how elaborately that setting was specified (Bühnemann 2000). For each of the six acts the manuals prescribe a presiding goddess, a direction to face, a season and a time of day, a colour for the worshipper’s dress and for the flowers and substances offered, a posture and a kind of seat, a hand gesture, the material of the rosary, the shape of the fire-pit and the substances to be offered into the fire. Pacification, for instance, is associated with white, with calm postures and with auspicious substances, the destructive rites with black or dark colours, the south, inauspicious times and impure substances. A further variable is the way in which the name of the person to be affected is combined with the mantra: it may be placed before or after the mantra, enclosed by it on both sides, or interwoven with its syllables, each arrangement being suited to a different act. The system is a grammar of correspondences, in which the practitioner composes the rite for a desired effect much as a poet composes a verse for a desired sentiment.

The six acts were not confined to Hindu manuals. Jain mantra texts devoted to the goddesses Jvālāmālinī and Padmāvatī (Chapter 10) give rites of the same kind, and Buddhist Tantra developed a parallel and simpler scheme of four rites — pacifying, increasing, subjugating and fierce — performed in fire-pits that are respectively round, square, semicircular and triangular and associated with white, yellow, red and black. This fourfold fire ritual passed with Esoteric Buddhism to China and Japan, where it survives in the Shingon goma (Section 10.16).

The ethics of these rites troubled the traditions themselves. Many texts reserve the destructive acts for the protection of the king, the defence of the faith or the punishment of grave wrongdoers, impose expiations on the practitioner who performs them, and warn that a misdirected rite rebounds on its author; Buddhist authors justified the fierce rites as acts of compassion that free the victim from evil karma. Courts and kings, for their part, were among the main clients of such services (Chapter 12). In modern India the same repertoire survives in the advertisements of self-styled tāntriks offering to subdue rivals or win back a lover, and laws against superstition and fraud have been used to prosecute those who sell them (Section 14.3).

docs.title: 7.3.4 The Six “Limb” Mantras
docs.text:
One of the most widespread structures in Tantric mantra practice is the set of six “limb” mantras (aṅgamantras) that accompany a deity’s root mantra. Each is formed from the deity’s seed syllable with a characteristic ending (jāti), and each is placed on a part of the body in aṅganyāsa and karanyāsa (Table 7.1).

Table 7.1. The Six “Limb” Mantras (Aṅgamantras) Limb Placed on Ending Heart (hṛdaya) Heart namaḥ Head (śiras) Head svāhā Topknot (śikhā) Crown vaṣaṭ Armour (kavaca) Shoulders and chest hūṃ Eyes (netra) Eyes vauṣaṭ Weapon (astra) Around the body, with a clap or snap phaṭ

Several of these endings (svāhā, vaṣaṭ, vauṣaṭ) are exclamations of the Vedic sacrifice, showing again how Tantric ritual reworked Vedic materials. The “weapon” mantra ending in phaṭ is used throughout worship to expel obstacles and to seal the ritual space.

docs.title: 7.4 Seed Syllables (Bījas)
docs.text:
Monosyllabic “seed” mantras, usually ending in the nasal -ṃ, are regarded as the most concentrated form of a deity’s power. Many have no lexical meaning (Table 7.2).

Table 7.2. Some Common Bīja Mantras and Their Traditional Associations Bīja Name Deity / principle Traditional association oṃ Praṇava Brahman; Śiva; Viṣṇu Prefixed to most mantras hrīṃ Māyābīja Bhuvaneśvarī The Goddess as power of manifestation krīṃ Kālī’s seed Kālī klīṃ Kāmabīja Kāma; Kṛṣṇa; the Goddess Desire, attraction aiṃ Vāgbhava Sarasvatī Speech, learning śrīṃ Śrībīja Lakṣmī Prosperity hūṃ Varma / kūrca Fierce deities Protection, “armour” gaṃ Gaṇeśa’s seed Gaṇeśa Removal of obstacles hauṃ Prāsāda Sadāśiva The “palace” mantra of Śaiva worship strīṃ Vadhūbīja Tārā hlīṃ — Bagalāmukhī Paralysis (stambhana) of enemies

Commentators analyse each bīja into its components. A traditional analysis of krīṃ, for example, takes k as Kālī, r as fire (Brahman), ī as the Goddess’s power (Māyā), and the final nasal, written as a dot and crescent (bindu and nāda), as the transcendent resonance into which the sound dissolves.

docs.title: 7.5 The Alphabet as Divine Matrix (Mātṛkā)
docs.text: The Tantras regard the fifty (or fifty-one) phonemes of Sanskrit as the “matrix” (mātṛkā, “little mother”) from which all mantras, all language and the cosmos itself emerge. In the Trika, following the Mālinīvijayottara, the vowels are called the “seed” (bīja) and associated with Śiva, while the consonants are the “womb” (yoni) associated with Śakti; their union produces the world. The consonants from ka to ma are correlated with the twenty-five tattvas from earth to the limited soul, and the remaining phonemes with the higher principles. The Trika also worships the alphabet in a second, “mixed” order, beginning with na and ending with pha, personified as the goddess Mālinī. Abhinavagupta’s Parātriśikāvivaraṇa develops this phonematic theology into a meditation on the word ahaṃ (“I”), whose first and last letters, a and ha, embrace the whole alphabet and so the whole cosmos (Padoux 1990).

docs.title: 7.5.1 Placing the Alphabet on the Body
docs.text: In mātṛkānyāsa, one of the most common preparatory rites of Tantric worship, the worshipper places each phoneme, with the nasal -ṃ added, on a point of the body: the vowels on the head and face, the consonant groups on the arms, legs, sides, back and abdomen, the remaining letters on the heart and other centres. The body thereby becomes an image of the cosmos in sound.

docs.title: 7.6 Japa: Recitation
docs.text: Japa, the repeated recitation of a mantra, is the most widely practised form of mantra discipline. The manuals distinguish audible recitation (vācika); whispered recitation (upāṃśu), in which the lips move but the sound is barely audible; and purely mental recitation (mānasa), regarded as the most effective. Beyond these lies the “unrecited” mantra (ajapā) haṃsa, said to be repeated naturally with each breath (Section 7.12).

docs.title: 7.6.1 The Discipline of Recitation
docs.text: The mantra must be received from a qualified guru, and recitation is preceded by bathing, the purification of body and place, and nyāsa. It is performed regularly, at fixed times and places, and counted on a rosary (mālā), commonly of 108 beads of rudrākṣa, tulasī, crystal or other materials according to the deity, in fixed numbers of repetitions. Before a mantra can be used, a preliminary course of recitation (puraścaraṇa) — traditionally a hundred thousand repetitions for each syllable of the mantra, with accompanying fire offerings and observances — makes it “one’s own”.

docs.title: 7.7 How Mantras Work: The Tradition’s Account
docs.text:
The Tantric texts give a theological account of the efficacy of mantras. The mantra is the deity’s body in sound, so that to recite it is to make the deity present. For the Kashmiri Śaivas a mantra is effective only when the reciter’s awareness merges with the consciousness that the mantra embodies; without this “mantra-consciousness” (mantravīrya, mantracaitanya), recitation is mere sound. The guru, through initiation, is held to transmit the living power of the mantra, which is why a mantra read in a book is regarded as ineffective. And manuals such as the Śāradātilaka list numerous “defects” (doṣas) that render a mantra ineffective, with rites to remedy them.

These are claims of the tradition about ritual and religious efficacy. Modern scholars have approached mantras from linguistic, ritual and philosophical angles; some, such as Frits Staal, have even argued that many mantras are meaningless in the ordinary sense, a view contested by others (Alper 1989).

docs.title: 7.8 Mantras as Beings
docs.text: In the Śaiva Siddhānta, mantras are not only sounds but conscious beings. Among the souls that inhabit the pure levels of the cosmos are classes of liberated beings called Mantras, Mantreśvaras (“lords of mantras”) and Mantramaheśvaras, who act as Śiva’s agents. Above all stand the eight Vidyeśvaras — Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin — who are said to have received the scriptures from Śiva and to govern the lower creation on his behalf. When an initiate recites a mantra, he engages the power of such a being, ultimately the power of Śiva himself. Initiation into a mantra therefore establishes a relationship with a divine agent, and the rules surrounding mantras are rules of conduct towards a deity (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998).

docs.title: 7.8.1 Encoding Mantras
docs.text: Because mantras were secret and powerful, the scriptures often do not state them directly. Instead they “extract” (uddhāra) them by code: the phonemes are named by cryptic designations (“the first of the fifth group”, “the bright one”, “fire”) or located on a diagram of the alphabet (prastāra), so that only one who has been taught the key can assemble the mantra. Commentators and ritual manuals decode these extractions, and they form one of the most technical parts of the literature.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Śaiva Pañcākṣara
docs.text: The five-syllable mantra namaḥ śivāya (with the prefix oṃ, the six-syllable ṣaḍakṣara), already present in the Śatarudrīya of the Yajurveda, is the principal Śaiva mantra. Its syllables are correlated with the five elements, the five faces of Śiva and his five acts, and it is the subject of extended theological reflection in Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta.

docs.title: 7.9.2 The Vaiṣṇava Mantras
docs.text: The eight-syllable mantra oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya and the twelve-syllable mantra oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya are the principal Vaiṣṇava mantras; the latter is particularly associated with the Pāñcarātra and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. See Chapter 3 for the Śrīvaiṣṇava “three mantras”.

docs.title: 7.10 Inner Sound (Nāda)
docs.text: Later yoga texts such as the Haṭhapradīpikā (c. 15th century, chapter 4) and the Nādabindu Upaniṣad teach concentration on inner sounds (nāda) heard in meditation, compared to the roar of the ocean, thunder, kettledrums, a conch, a bell, a flute, a vīṇā and the humming of bees, progressing from louder to subtler sounds. The goal is absorption (laya) of the mind in the sound and beyond it.

docs.title: 7.11 Mantra in Āgamic Temple Worship
docs.text:
In Āgamic temple worship every ritual act is accompanied by its prescribed mantra. Mantras honour the door-guardians and remove obstacles as the priest enters the sanctum; they purify and divinise his body; they invoke the deity into the image; they consecrate the water, milk and other substances of the bath, and the food that is offered; they accompany the waving of lamps; and at the end of worship they dismiss the deity or ask it to remain.

The ritual manuals treat the mantra as the soul of the ritual act: an act performed without its mantra is defective and requires expiation (Davis 1991).

docs.title: 7.12 Haṃsa and the Nātha Tradition
docs.text: The Nātha yogis, who trace their lineage to Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha (c. 11th–13th centuries), developed a yoga in which mantra is closely linked with breath and the subtle body. Their texts, like many Tantras before them, teach the “unrecited” (ajapā) mantra haṃsa: the breath goes out with the sound ha and comes in with the sound sa, so that every living being repeats the mantra unawares — traditionally 21,600 times a day, a conventional figure based on fifteen breaths a minute. The yogin makes this recitation conscious; read in reverse, so ’ham (“I am He”), it becomes an affirmation of identity with the absolute. The emphasis falls differently in each tradition: the Śaiva Siddhānta treats its five- and six-syllable mantras, the five Brahma mantras and the six “limb” mantras as Śiva’s powers acting in ritual; Śrīvidyā stresses the identity of mantra, yantra and goddess; the Kashmiri Śaivas build a theology of consciousness on the phonemes and on mantras such as sauḥ and ahaṃ; the Nāthas join mantra to breath and the subtle body; and the Pāñcarātra centres its liturgy on the mantras of the vyūhas.

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction
docs.text:
If the mantra is the deity’s form in sound, the yantra and the maṇḍala are its form in space. Tantric worship takes place not only before an image but in and upon diagrams: drawn in coloured powders for initiation, engraved on metal plates for daily worship, laid out as the ground plan of a temple, or visualised in meditation (Bühnemann 2003; Khanna 2003).

The word yantra derives from the root yam, “to hold, restrain”, with the instrumental suffix -tra; it means any device or instrument, and in Tantric usage a diagram that “holds” the deity and the worshipper’s mind. Maṇḍala means “circle” or “disc”, and by extension a circular or square diagram in which a deity and its retinue are arranged around a centre. The two terms overlap; in general maṇḍala is used for larger, often temporary diagrams in which a whole pantheon is installed (especially for initiation), and yantra for smaller, usually permanent diagrams of a single deity, often inscribed with its mantras (Bühnemann 2003).

docs.title: 8.2 Geometric Elements
docs.text:
Yantras are built from a small repertoire of elements, to which the commentators assign symbolic meanings (Table 8.1 and Figure 8.1).

Table 8.1. Basic Elements of Yantras and Their Usual Interpretations Element Sanskrit Usual interpretation Point Bindu The source; undifferentiated consciousness; the deity’s seat Triangle, apex up Trikoṇa Śiva; fire Triangle, apex down Trikoṇa Śakti; the yoni Hexagram Ṣaṭkoṇa Union of Śiva and Śakti Circle Vṛtta Completeness; the cosmos Lotus petals Padma, dala Unfolding; seats for attendant deities Square with gates Bhūpura The earth; the enclosure separating sacred from profane space Figure 8.1. Basic geometric elements of yantras.

docs.title: 8.3 The Śrīcakra
docs.text: The Śrīcakra or Śrīyantra, the diagram of Tripurasundarī, is described in Chapter 5, together with its nine enclosures. It may be made in three forms: flat (bhūpṛṣṭha); slightly raised like the back of a tortoise (kūrmapṛṣṭha); and as a stepped, mountain-like solid (merupṛṣṭha, Figure 5.3). The difficulty of drawing it exactly is discussed in Section 5.3.

docs.title: 8.4 Other Yantras
docs.text:
Every deity has its own yantra, typically combining a central figure (triangle, hexagram, pentagon or circle) with lotus petals and a square enclosure, inscribed with the deity’s seed syllable and mantras. Forms vary between texts and lineages (Figure 8.2 and Table 8.2). A popular modern category is devoted to the nine “planets” (navagrahas) of Indian astrology, often in the form of magic squares of numbers, used to propitiate planets believed to be causing misfortune; these belong to popular astrology rather than to the classical Āgamas.

Figure 8.2. A schematic Gaṇeśa yantra: hexagram with the seed syllable gaṃ, within an eight-petalled lotus, circles and a square enclosure. Actual forms vary between texts. Table 8.2. Some Common Yantras Yantra Deity Typical features Śrīcakra Tripurasundarī Nine interlocking triangles; two lotuses; square enclosure Gaṇeśa yantra Gaṇeśa Often a hexagram or triangle with lotus Kālī yantra Kālī Nested downward triangles within a lotus Durgā yantra Durgā Triangle or hexagram, lotus and enclosure Sudarśana yantra Sudarśana (Viṣṇu’s discus) Hexagram within many-spoked wheel; Pāñcarātra Mahāmṛtyuñjaya yantra Śiva as conqueror of death Inscribed with the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra (ṚV 7.59.12)

Yantras, like mantras and amulets, are objects of devotion, and the claims made for them in the texts are claims about ritual efficacy. Many are now sold with promises that they cure disease or avert misfortune; such promises belong to the modern market rather than to the classical sources.

docs.title: 8.5 Maṇḍalas
docs.text: Maṇḍalas tend to be larger and more complex than yantras; they are often drawn for a particular rite, especially initiation and consecration, and then dismantled; and they map a deity’s entire retinue and realm. In Śaiva initiation the candidate, blindfolded, casts a flower onto the maṇḍala, and the deity on which it falls determines his initiatory name.

docs.title: 8.5.1 The Vāstupuruṣa Maṇḍala
docs.text:
The vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala is the diagram underlying the plan of temples and houses. It represents the “Person of the Site” lying face down within a square grid, his body pinned down by the deities who occupy its squares, with Brahmā at the centre (Figure 8.3). The texts on architecture describe a series of grids from one square (sakala) up to 1,024 (Table 8.3); temple plans most often use the 64-square (maṇḍūka) or 81-square (paramaśāyika) forms (Kramrisch 1946).

Figure 8.3. Schematic 81-square (paramaśāyika) vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, oriented with east at the top, showing Brahmā in the nine central squares and the guardians of the directions at the edges (simplified; the full diagram has forty-five deities). Table 8.3. Some Vāstu Grids Name Grid Squares Remarks Sakala 1\(\times\)1 1 Simplest; used in some rites Pecaka 2\(\times\)2 4 Pīṭha 3\(\times\)3 9 Mahāpīṭha 4\(\times\)4 16 Maṇḍūka 8\(\times\)8 64 Common for temples Paramaśāyika 9\(\times\)9 81 Common for temples and houses

Stella Kramrisch’s classic study showed how the Hindu temple is conceived as a three-dimensional elaboration of this diagram, with the sanctum over the centre of Brahmā and the superstructure rising as an image of the cosmic mountain (Kramrisch 1946). In this sense the temple is a maṇḍala in stone (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 8.5.2 Śaiva and Śākta Maṇḍalas
docs.text: The Śaiva scriptures prescribe maṇḍalas, drawn with coloured powders, for initiation: for example a central lotus for Śiva surrounded by enclosures for his attendant powers, the Vidyeśvaras, the guardians of the directions and their weapons. The Trika of Kashmir worshipped its three goddesses on the three prongs of a great trident rising from a lotus, the “trident-and-lotus maṇḍala” (triśūlābjamaṇḍala), whose structure expresses the identity of the goddesses with the powers of consciousness (Sanderson 1988). In Śrīvidyā the Śrīcakra functions as both yantra and maṇḍala.

docs.title: 8.5.3 Buddhist Maṇḍalas
docs.text: Buddhist Tantra developed the maṇḍala to an extraordinary degree, especially in Tibet (Chapter 10). A Buddhist maṇḍala depicts the celestial palace of a central deity, with walls, gates and directional deities, in symbolic colours; it may be painted, made of coloured sand and ritually dismantled, built in three dimensions, or visualised. Entry into the maṇḍala is the core of Buddhist initiation (abhiṣeka).

docs.title: 8.5.4 The Scale of Buddhist Maṇḍalas
docs.text: Buddhist maṇḍalas vary enormously in size. The Hevajra maṇḍala in its basic form has nine deities: Hevajra and Nairātmyā at the centre with eight yoginīs around them. The Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja worships a maṇḍala of thirty-two deities centred on Akṣobhyavajra; the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala includes concentric wheels of ḍākas and ḍākinīs associated with sacred sites; and the Kālacakra maṇḍala, with its several palaces of body, speech and mind, is traditionally said to contain over seven hundred deities. Such maṇḍalas are at once maps of a pantheon, of the cosmos and of the practitioner’s own body and mind.

docs.title: 8.6 Worshipping a Yantra
docs.text:
The worship of a yantra follows the general pattern of Tantric worship (Section 9.3). The diagram is first consecrated (pratiṣṭhā), with the ritual of “installing the life-breaths” (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) by which it becomes a seat of the deity. The deity is then invoked into it, mantras are placed on its parts, offerings are made to the deity and to the attendant deities of each enclosure, and the worshipper recites and meditates; a temporary diagram is finally dismantled after the deity has been dismissed (visarjana).

Permanent yantras are made of gold, silver or copper plates, or of stone or crystal; temporary ones are drawn on the ground with coloured powders or rice flour, or on birch bark, cloth or paper. Their consecration includes bathing with the “five nectars” (milk, curd, ghee, honey and sugar), offerings of sandal paste and flowers, and the installation of the life-breaths.

docs.title: 8.7 The Bindu
