docs.text: The point (bindu) at the centre of a yantra is geometrically dimensionless, yet in Tantric theology it is the most important element: the concentrated totality of consciousness from which the whole diagram unfolds and into which worship returns. In Śrīvidyā, Puṇyānanda’s Kāmakalāvilāsa describes a triad of bindus — white, red and mixed — forming a subtle triangle, interpreted as Śiva, Śakti and their union, and as the source of the three sections of the goddess’s mantra.

docs.title: 8.8 Yantra and Maṇḍala as Maps
docs.text:
A yantra functions as a map at several levels at once. It maps the cosmos, from the undifferentiated centre through successive enclosures to the manifest world at the square boundary; the deity’s realm, with its palace, attendants and powers; the body, whose cakras and parts correspond to its enclosures, as in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad; and the ritual, of which it is the ground plan.

Meditation on a yantra traditionally proceeds from gazing at the external diagram, through visualising it internally, to an identification of the meditator with the diagram and the deity, in which the form itself is finally transcended.

docs.title: 8.9 Maṇḍalas and Yantras in Southeast Asia
docs.text: Indian ritual diagrams travelled with Śaiva and Buddhist Tantra to Southeast Asia, where they took local forms. In Java the Śaiva temple complex of Prambanan (9th century), with its concentric courts of shrines, and the Buddhist Borobudur have both been read as three-dimensional maṇḍalas, though the interpretation of Borobudur is debated (Section 10.14.2). In Bali, where Śaiva priestly ritual survives, magical diagrams (rerajahan) are drawn on cloth or palm leaf for protection and healing. In Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, diagrams called yan (from yantra), including protective tattoos (sak yan), are used in a Buddhist setting; and the royal Śaiva temples of Cambodia and Champa are documented in Sanskrit inscriptions (Section 12.9).

docs.title: Chapter 9: Ritual: Worship, Fire Offering and the Ritual Body
9.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Āgamic and Tantric traditions developed one of the most elaborate bodies of ritual prescription in the history of religions. Ritual (kriyā) is the subject of the largest part of most Āgamas, and of a vast secondary literature of manuals (paddhatis) (Bhatt 1961–1988; Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998). This chapter describes the main components of Tantric ritual — worship, fire offering, the ritual purification and divinisation of the body, gestures, consecration and expiation — drawing on material common to Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta traditions. Initiation is treated in Chapter 2, the Kaula sacraments in Chapter 4, and temple worship in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 9.1.1 Why Ritual Works: Two Śaiva Views
docs.text:
The theologians disagreed about how ritual is effective. For the Śaiva Siddhānta, ritual is effective in its own right: since the soul’s bondage is a real substance, it can be removed only by a real act, and in initiation and worship it is Śiva himself who acts through the officiant and the mantras. For the Kashmiri non-dualists, ritual is an expression and support of insight; its efficacy depends on the officiant’s awareness, and for the most advanced it becomes unnecessary or is performed spontaneously (Sanderson 1988). Both positions agree that ritual performed without the prescribed mantras, or carelessly, is defective.

Ritual as Cosmic Process

Tantric authors often interpret a complete rite as a re-enactment of the cosmic process: invocation (āvāhana) corresponds to emanation, worship to maintenance, and dismissal (visarjana) to withdrawal. The worshipper thereby participates in the activity of the deity.

docs.title: 9.2 The Worshipper’s Body
docs.text: A distinctive feature of Tantric worship is that, before worshipping the deity, the worshipper ritually destroys his ordinary body and creates a divine one. This is summarised in the maxim nādevo devam arcayet, “one who is not a god should not worship a god”, and in the Śaiva injunction to worship Śiva having become Śiva.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Purification of the Elements (Bhūtaśuddhi)
docs.text:
In bhūtaśuddhi the worshipper visualises the dissolution of the elements of his body, each into the next subtler one, using their seed syllables: earth into water with the syllable laṃ, water into fire with vaṃ, fire into air with raṃ, air into space with yaṃ, and space into its source with haṃ.

The impure body, personified as a “person of sin” (pāpapuruṣa) in many manuals, is burnt away, and a pure body is then recreated in the reverse order.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Nyāsa
docs.text: Nyāsa (“placing”) then installs mantras on the new body, making it a body of mantras (Chapter 7). Its commonest forms are the placing of mantras on the fingers and palms (karanyāsa); the placing of the six “limb” mantras on the heart, head, topknot, chest (“armour”) and eyes, and around the body (“weapon”), with a snap of the fingers (aṅganyāsa; Table 7.1); and the placing of the fifty phonemes of the alphabet on points of the body (mātṛkānyāsa). In some rites the levels of the cosmos are mapped onto the body; the deity’s throne and its supports, or the goddess’s sacred sites, may be installed on it (pīṭhanyāsa); and Śrīvidyā uses an elaborate sixfold sequence of placements (ṣoḍhānyāsa).

docs.title: 9.3 Worship (Pūjā)
docs.text:
The core of Tantric worship treats the deity as a royal guest and offers a series of services (upacāras), in five, ten, sixteen or more steps; a common list of sixteen is given in Chapter 3 (Bühnemann 1988). Figure 9.1 sets out the general sequence.

Figure 9.1. The general sequence of Tantric worship (simplified).

docs.title: 9.3.1 Mental Worship (Mānasapūjā)
docs.text: All Tantric worship includes a phase of inner worship, in which the worshipper visualises the deity in the heart and offers all the services mentally. Many Tantras praise inner worship as superior to outer worship, and in some traditions — notably the Samaya school of Śrīvidyā — it replaces external worship altogether (Padoux 2017).

docs.title: 9.3.2 The Preparation of Space and Materials
docs.text: The place of worship is purified by sweeping, washing and sprinkling; the guardians of the directions are honoured; and a protective enclosure is “bound” with the weapon mantra (often ending in phaṭ) in each direction. Water, flowers, sandal paste, incense, lamps and food are each purified with specified mantras and gestures. Flowers should be fresh and whole, and particular flowers are prescribed for, or forbidden to, particular deities.

docs.title: 9.4 The Fire Offering (Homa)
docs.text:
The fire offering continues the Vedic sacrifice within a Tantric framework: the deity is worshipped in the fire, which is itself ritually “born” from the union of the god and goddess of speech, and oblations are offered with the deity’s mantra.

Rites are classified as obligatory daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika) and optional, for a specific desire (kāmya). Optional fire rites are commonly divided into pacifying (śāntika), nourishing or prospering (pauṣṭika) and aggressive (ābhicārika) types, for which the manuals prescribe different directions, colours, times, materials and shapes of fire-pit.

docs.title: 9.4.1 The Fire-Pit (Kuṇḍa)
docs.text: The manuals give detailed rules for constructing fire-pits of various shapes — square, circular, semicircular, triangular, lotus-shaped and others — according to purpose and direction. A standard pit for a single officiant measures one cubit (hasta, roughly 45 cm) a side, surrounded by three raised tiers (mekhalās), with a yoni-shaped projection on one side.

docs.title: 9.4.2 The Structure of a Homa
docs.text:
A homa begins with the construction and purification of the fire-pit and the materials and the purification of the officiant. The fire is then generated and consecrated (agnisaṃskāra) as if it were a child born of Śiva and Śakti, with the life-cycle rites of a child, and the deity is invoked into it. Oblations of ghee, sesame, grains or fuel-sticks follow, each with the deity’s mantra; the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) concludes the offering, and the rite ends with the dismissal of the deity and the distribution of ash and consecrated food.

Vedic mantras continue to be used alongside Tantric ones. One that is frequently recited in fire rites is Ṛgveda 1.189.1 (also Īśa Upaniṣad 18):

Ṛgveda 1.189.1

agne naya supathā rāye asmān viśvāni deva vayunāni vidvān | yuyodhy asmaj juhurāṇam eno bhūyiṣṭhāṃ te namaüktiṃ vidhema ||

Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O god who knows all ways. Keep from us the crooked sin; we would offer you the fullest words of homage.

docs.title: 9.5 Gestures (Mudrā)
docs.text:
Mudrās (“seals”) are hand gestures, and occasionally postures of the whole body, that accompany mantras in worship. They are understood both as forms of the deity and as means of acting upon the ritual substances (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Some Common Mudrās in Tantric Worship Mudrā Form Use Añjali Palms joined Salutation Dhenu (“cow”) Fingers interlocked to resemble a cow’s udder Making offerings and water into nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) Avaguṇṭhana (“veiling”) Hands circling the object Veiling and protecting consecrated substances Matsya (“fish”) One hand on the other, thumbs extended like fins Covering and consecrating water vessels Padma (“lotus”) Hands open like a lotus Offering a seat; invocation Yoni Fingers interlaced to form a triangle Śākta worship of the goddess Liṅga Hands clasped with one thumb raised Śaiva worship

The term mudrā has other meanings in Tantra: in Kaula usage it may denote the female partner or parched grain (Chapter 4), and in later yoga it denotes bodily techniques for controlling the breath and vital energies.

docs.title: 9.6 Consecration and Bathing (Abhiṣeka)
docs.text: The bathing (abhiṣeka) of an image is part of daily worship and, in elaborate form, of festivals and consecrations. The “five nectars” (pañcāmṛta) are milk, curd, ghee, honey and sugar; other substances commonly used include coconut water, sandal-water, turmeric water, sacred river water and water in which gold or gems have been placed.

docs.title: 9.6.1 Kumbhābhiṣeka
docs.text: The kumbhābhiṣeka (“consecration with pots”) is the great rite of consecration of a new temple or of reconsecration after renovation, conventionally about every twelve years. Over several days, deities are invoked into water-pots (kalaśas) installed in a pavilion with many fire-pits, worshipped with fire offerings and recitation, and finally the consecrated water is poured over the finials of the temple towers and onto the images, transferring the divine presence to them.

docs.title: 9.7 Initiation of Women, Children and the Dead
docs.text: Śaiva scriptures and manuals discuss whether initiation can be given to those who cannot fulfil the obligations of initiates. Many permit the initiation of women, of children and of the sick or aged in the “seedless” form that frees them from the burden of daily ritual, the form that also made Śaiva initiation acceptable to kings (Section 12.4). Some texts restrict women to this form, while the goddess scriptures and the Kaula sources allow them full initiation and even the role of guru (Section 4.14). Initiation also reached beyond death. Śaiva initiates receive their own funerary rites, and Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka (chapter 21) describes an “initiation in absence” (parokṣadīkṣā) for the dead, performed with an effigy or with the remains of the deceased, so that a relative who died uninitiated might still be liberated; the Kashmiri authors also describe a yogic departure from the body (utkrānti) by which an advanced practitioner may leave it at will (Sanderson 1988; Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998). These provisions show both the soteriological ambition of Śaiva initiation and the constraints of caste and gender within which it was usually given.

docs.title: 9.8 Expiation (Prāyaścitta)
docs.text: The Āgamas devote much attention to expiation for ritual faults and pollution, from minor errors in recitation to serious transgressions of the rules of initiates and damage to consecrated images. The remedy is graded to the fault. A minor error in a mantra or in the sequence of a rite is made good by additional recitation; an interrupted worship is begun again with purificatory rites; pollution of the sanctum requires purification and the reconsecration of the space; a breach of the rules of initiation calls for fire offerings, fasting or, in serious cases, re-initiation; and a damaged image must be repaired or replaced and consecrated anew.

docs.title: 9.9 Domestic and Festival Ritual: Two Examples
9.9.1 Durgā Pūjā in Bengal
docs.text:
The autumn worship of Durgā in Bengal shows Tantric ritual in a public, festive form. Over several days a clay image of the goddess slaying the buffalo demon, flanked by her children Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, is installed in a temporary pavilion. The rites, following Bengali manuals derived from Purāṇic and Tantric sources, begin with the awakening (bodhana) of the goddess, who in the myth was worshipped out of season by Rāma before his battle with Rāvaṇa. A bundle of “nine plants” (navapatrikā) is bathed at dawn and worshipped as the goddess, a survival of agricultural goddess worship; the image is consecrated by the installation of its life-breaths; and daily worship follows with the sixteen offerings, the recitation of the Devīmāhātmya and fire offerings. The “junction worship” (sandhipūjā) at the moment between the eighth and ninth lunar days, when the goddess is believed to have slain the demon, was formerly accompanied in many places by animal sacrifice and is now usually performed with vegetable offerings. On the tenth day the goddess is dismissed and the image immersed in a river or tank.

What was once largely a festival of landed households has become, since the nineteenth century, a great communal (sārbajanīn) celebration organised by neighbourhood committees, and in 2021 UNESCO inscribed Durgā Pūjā in Kolkata on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

docs.title: 9.9.2 Kerala Temple Ritual
docs.text: Kerala’s temples follow a regional Tantric tradition codified in the Tantrasamuccaya of Ceṉṉās Nārāyaṇaṉ Nampūtiri (15th century), which covers the installation and worship of seven deities (Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, Gaṇeśa, Śāstā, Subrahmaṇya and Śaṅkara-Nārāyaṇa). Each temple has a hereditary tantrī, a Nampūtiri Brahmin who holds supreme ritual authority over its consecrations and festivals, while daily worship is performed by other priests. The tantrīs’ authority has been central to modern disputes, such as those over the entry of women of menstruating age into the Śabarimala temple, where the Supreme Court of India ruled in 2018 that their exclusion was unconstitutional, a decision that provoked widespread protest and was referred to a larger bench in 2019. Kerala’s Tantric tradition is described more fully in Section 13.2.

docs.title: 9.10 The Material Culture of Tantric Ritual
docs.text: Tantric ritual is performed with things. The manuals specify not only words and gestures but vessels, lamps, bells, rosaries, seats, cloths and diagrams, the materials from which they are to be made (gold, silver, copper, bronze, clay, wood) and their dimensions. These objects are not neutral equipment: before use they are purified and consecrated with mantras, and several of them are themselves worshipped as seats or forms of deities.

docs.title: 9.10.1 Implements of Worship
docs.text:
Water-pots. The kalaśa or kumbha, a pot filled with water, wound with thread and crowned with leaves and often a coconut, serves as a temporary seat of the deity in consecrations, festivals and domestic rites (Section 9.6). In Śākta worship a special vessel of offering (viśeṣārghya), set on a tripod and itself worshipped, is the centre of the ritual; in Kaula forms it contains alcohol or a substitute.

The conch. In Vaiṣṇava and Śākta worship the conch (śaṅkha) is filled with water, worshipped and used to bathe the image; it is also blown at the opening of worship.

The bell. The hand-bell (ghaṇṭā) is rung at the bathing of the image and the offering of incense and lamp, to drive away obstructive beings and to summon the gods. Its handle is topped by the emblem of the deity: the bull Nandi for Śiva, Garuḍa or the discus for Viṣṇu. In Buddhist Tantra the bell is paired with the vajra, held in the left and right hands respectively, as symbols of wisdom (prajñā) and method (upāya).

Lamps. Single lamps burn before the deity; lamps of many wicks, sometimes tiered, are waved before it in the rite of ārati at the climax of worship.

The rosary. The japamālā or akṣamālā usually has 108 beads with a further “summit” bead (meru) that is not passed over: on reaching it the reciter turns the rosary back. Traditions prefer different materials — rudrākṣa for Śaivas, tulasī wood for Vaiṣṇavas, crystal, coral or lotus seeds for particular goddesses and purposes — and in Kāpālika and some Vajrayāna practice beads of human bone were used.

The guru’s sandals. The pādukās of the guru are worshipped as his presence; in Śrīvidyā the word also names the mantras of the lineage of teachers.

Diagrams. Engraved metal plates and three-dimensional merus serve as permanent seats of deities in domestic shrines and temples (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 9.10.2 Insignia of the Fierce Deities
docs.text: A distinct group of objects belongs to the fierce deities and to the ascetics who imitated them: the skull-bowl (kapāla); the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga); the hourglass-shaped drum (ḍamaru); the chopper or flaying knife (kartṛkā); the trident (triśūla); the noose (pāśa) and goad (aṅkuśa); garlands of heads and ornaments of bone. For the Kāpālika ascetics these were real possessions (Section 2.1.6); in the Hindu traditions today they appear mainly as attributes in images, though some Aghorī ascetics still carry skull-bowls. In Tibetan and Newar Buddhism many survive as ritual objects. The ritual dagger (kīla), which became central to Tibetan rites, derives from Indian rites of “nailing” (kīlana), in which pegs are driven into the ground to fix the boundaries of a ritual space and to pin down obstructive forces.

docs.title: 9.10.3 From Meditation Verse to Image
docs.text:
Each Tantric deity is described in a “meditation verse” (dhyāna), which gives its colour, faces, arms, attributes, posture, ornaments and mount. The worshipper visualises the deity according to this verse before invoking it, and the same verses guided sculptors and painters. Digests such as the Śāradātilaka and Kṛṣṇānanda’s Tantrasāra, and Buddhist collections of sādhanas, contain hundreds of such descriptions, and much of the iconography of medieval temples can be read through them (Bühnemann 2003).

The fierce deities have a recognisable visual language.

Bhairava appears naked or nearly so, smeared with ash, with fangs and flaming hair, holding a skull-bowl, trident, drum and sometimes a severed head, and accompanied by a dog. Eight Bhairavas — Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Kapāla, Bhīṣaṇa and Saṃhāra — guard the directions and the sacred sites.

Cāmuṇḍā, the most terrible of the Mothers, is emaciated, with sunken eyes and belly and visible ribs, often seated on a corpse and wearing a garland of skulls. In many temples the seven Mothers (saptamātṛkā) are carved in a row, flanked by Vīrabhadra or Śiva and by Gaṇeśa.

Kālī is dark, naked or clad in a tiger skin, with a lolling tongue, a garland of severed heads and a girdle of arms, standing on the prostrate Śiva (Figure 4.1).

Yoginīs, often animal-headed, stand or sit on their vehicles (Section 4.10); the Buddhist herukas and ḍākinīs share much of this repertoire (Chapter 10).

The general principles of Indian iconography and image-making are treated in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa. What is specific to the Tantric deities is that their terrifying features express their power over death, impurity and the forces of disorder — the same power that the practitioner seeks to make his own.

docs.title: 9.10.4 Painted Images and Diagrams
docs.text: Painting served Tantric ritual in several ways. Temporary maṇḍalas of coloured powder were drawn for initiations and erased afterwards (Chapter 8); painted scrolls served as permanent supports for visualisation and worship. In the Kathmandu Valley Newar painters produced scroll paintings (paubhā) of maṇḍalas and deities for both Hindu and Buddhist patrons, and Newar artists worked widely for Tibetan monasteries; the most famous of them, Anige (1245–1306), led a group of Newar craftsmen to Tibet and then to the court of Khubilai Khan, where he directed imperial workshops of painting and sculpture. Tibetan scroll paintings (thangka) developed from these Indian and Newar models. In India itself, painters of the Rajput and Pahari courts illustrated the goddesses of the Śākta tradition, including series of the ten Mahāvidyās, and painted cosmological and yogic diagrams for Tantric practitioners and their patrons, such as the Nāth paintings of Jodhpur (Section 13.8). These works were made to guide meditation or to be worshipped; their later display as “art” is a modern development (see below).

docs.title: 9.10.5 Manuscripts as Sacred Objects
docs.text: Tantric manuscripts were themselves ritual objects. Because the scriptures were restricted to initiates, manuscripts were kept within lineages and monasteries, worshipped and copied as acts of merit; the Śaiva Śivadharma literature describes the solemn gift of a manuscript to a temple or monastery as one of the greatest of donations (De Simini 2016). Palm-leaf manuscripts of Buddhist and Hindu Tantras from eastern India and Nepal were often protected by painted wooden covers depicting the deities of the text. This culture of reverent preservation, especially in Nepal, is the reason so many early Tantras survive at all (Section 1.7).

docs.title: 9.10.6 Tantric Objects in Museums and Modern Art
docs.text: In the twentieth century Tantric objects and paintings found a new audience as art. The collector and writer Ajit Mookerjee presented yantras and Rajasthani diagrammatic paintings as Tantra Art (Mookerjee 1966), and Philip Rawson’s exhibition “Tantra” at the Hayward Gallery in London in 1971, with his book The Art of Tantra, brought them to Western audiences, where their geometric abstraction appealed to modernist taste (Rawson 1973). Several Indian painters, among them G.R. Santosh, Biren De and S.H. Raza, drew on Tantric diagrams in what critics called a “neo-Tantric” style. The British Museum’s exhibition Tantra: Enlightenment to Revolution (2020) set such objects in a historical narrative that ran from early medieval scripture to colonial politics and the counterculture (Ramos 2020). Displays of this kind have done much to make the traditions visible; they also detach objects from the ritual contexts that give them meaning, and can reinforce the romantic image of Tantra that this volume has tried to correct (Section 14.4).

docs.title: 9.11 Vedic and Āgamic Ritual
docs.text:
Table 9.2 compares the two forms of ritual.

Table 9.2. Vedic and Āgamic Ritual Compared Feature Vedic śrauta ritual Āgamic ritual Central act Fire sacrifice (yajña) Worship of a deity in an image, diagram or fire (pūjā) Officiants Specialised priests (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahman) Initiated priest or the initiate himself Deities Many gods (Agni, Indra, Soma and others) A supreme deity with its retinue Mantras Vedic verses and formulae Āgamic mantras, including seed syllables, alongside Vedic ones Space Temporary altar Temple or domestic shrine; temporary diagrams Eligibility Twice-born men Initiates, in principle of any caste and sometimes women Body of the officiant Purified Purified and ritually divinised

Āgamic authors generally presented their ritual as continuous with the Vedic heritage and suited to the present age (kaliyuga), in which the great Vedic sacrifices had largely fallen out of use. Historically, temple and image worship did largely replace public Vedic sacrifice as the dominant form of Hindu religious practice in the first millennium CE, while the Vedic domestic rites continued alongside it.

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text:
From about the seventh century CE Indian Buddhism produced its own Tantric scriptures and practices, known as the Mantranaya (“way of mantras”) or Vajrayāna (“vehicle of the vajra”, the diamond-thunderbolt). Buddhist Tantra accepted the goals and philosophy of the Mahāyāna — the bodhisattva’s aspiration to awaken for the sake of all beings, and the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā) — but claimed to offer a swifter path to Buddhahood, through initiation, mantra, maṇḍala, deity yoga and the yoga of the subtle body (Snellgrove 1987; Davidson 2002).

The great monasteries of eastern India — Nālandā, Vikramaśīla, Odantapurī and others — became centres of Tantric as well as philosophical study. Scholars such as Nāropa and Atīśa combined philosophical learning with Tantric practice, while the wandering siddhas cultivated a more unconventional style. This chapter treats Buddhist Tantra, and then Jain Tantra (Section 10.19), in relation to the other Tantric traditions; their place within Buddhist and Jain history and institutions is treated in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā.

docs.title: 10.2 Historical Development
docs.text: Period Development c. 4th–6th century Protective and mnemonic formulae (dhāraṇīs) in Mahāyāna literature; early ritual texts c. 6th–7th century Ritual (“Kriyā”) Tantras such as the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Susiddhikara and Subāhupari­pṛcchā; the Mahāvairocana c. late 7th–8th century The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha and the Yoga Tantras; transmission to China c. 8th century The Guhyasamāja c. 9th–10th century The Yoginītantras (Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra); the siddha movement early 11th century The Kālacakra Tantra; the “later diffusion” to Tibet begins late 12th–13th century Destruction of the great monasteries; decline of Buddhism in most of India 13th century onward Preservation and systematisation in Tibet; continuity among the Newars of Nepal

docs.title: 10.3 Classifications of the Buddhist Tantras
docs.text:
Indian authors classified the Tantras in several ways. The fourfold scheme that became standard in the Tibetan “new” (Sarma) schools arranges them by the practitioner’s relation to the deity (Snellgrove 1987). The Kriyā (“action”) Tantras, such as the Susiddhikara, the Subāhupari­pṛcchā and many ritual texts, stress external ritual, purity and worship, and the practitioner relates to the deity as a servant to a lord. The Caryā (“performance”) Tantras, of which the Mahāvairocana is the chief, balance external ritual and inner meditation, approaching the deity as a friend. The Yoga Tantras, above all the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha, centre on meditative identification with the deity. And the Anuttarayoga (“unsurpassed yoga”) Tantras — the Guhyasamāja and the Yoginītantras such as the Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra and Kālacakra — add the yoga of the subtle body and, in their original form, sexual and transgressive rites.

The Tibetan Nyingma (“old”) school uses a different scheme, culminating in Mahāyoga, Anuyoga and Atiyoga (Dzogchen).

docs.title: 10.4.1 The Guhyasamāja
docs.text: The Guhyasamāja (“Secret Assembly”), probably composed in the eighth century (later in that century rather than earlier), is one of the earliest Tantras to adopt deliberately transgressive language and sexual imagery. Its two exegetical traditions (the Ārya school, which attributed its works to Nāgārjuna and others, and the Jñānapāda school) systematised the “generation” and “completion” stages of practice, including the attainment of the “illusory body” (māyādeha) and the “clear light”. It became especially central for the Tibetan Gelug school.

docs.title: 10.4.2 The Cakrasaṃvara
docs.text: The Cakrasaṃvara (or Laghuśaṃvara) centres on the fierce deity Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) in union with his consort Vajravārāhī, surrounded by yoginīs and ḍākinīs associated with sacred sites. Sanderson has shown that substantial passages of it were adapted from Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha scriptures (Sanderson 2009). It was especially important for the Kagyu and Sakya schools (Gray 2007). The consort became the object of an independent cult as Vajrayoginī, whose visualisations and rites Elizabeth English has studied from the Sanskrit sādhana literature (English 2002).

docs.title: 10.4.3 The Hevajra
docs.text: The Hevajra Tantra, in two parts of eleven and twelve chapters, centres on Hevajra and his consort Nairātmyā (“selflessness”) with a retinue of eight yoginīs. It teaches the yoga of the subtle body, the experience of four “joys” (ānandas) in sexual yoga, and the innate (sahaja) nature of awakened mind, and includes verses in Apabhraṃśa. The text itself explains the name: “He” signifies great compassion and “vajra” wisdom (Snellgrove 1959). Through the siddha Virūpa it is the basis of the Sakya school’s “Path and Fruit” (Tibetan lam ’bras) teaching, which holds that the fruit of practice is already implicit in the path.

docs.title: 10.4.4 The Kālacakra
docs.text: The Kālacakra (“Wheel of Time”) Tantra and its great commentary, the Vimalaprabhā, composed in the early eleventh century, are the last major Indian Buddhist Tantric works. The system has three levels: an “outer” Kālacakra of cosmology, astronomy and calendar; an “inner” Kālacakra of the human body and its channels, winds and drops; and an “other” (anya) Kālacakra, the path of initiation and yoga by which the outer and inner cycles are purified. Vesna Wallace’s study of the “inner” Kālacakra shows how the text reads the human body, with its channels, winds and drops, as a counterpart of the cosmos and its cycles of time (Wallace 2001). The text also contains an apocalyptic narrative of the kingdom of Śambhala and its conflict with invaders. In modern times the Dalai Lama has given the Kālacakra initiation to very large public gatherings.

docs.title: 10.5 The Subtle Body
docs.text:
The Yoginītantras teach a yoga of the subtle body that shares structural features with Śaiva and Śākta systems while interpreting them in Buddhist terms. It describes three channels, the central avadhūtī and the left lalanā and right rasanā; centres (cakras), most commonly four, at the navel, heart, throat and crown; the winds (prāṇa, vāyu) or vital currents that move in the channels; and the drops (bindu), subtle essences, above all the white drop at the crown and the red drop at the navel, whose melting produces bliss.

Centre Location Petals Associations Mahāsukha­cakra Crown 32 Great bliss Saṃbhoga­cakra Throat 16 Enjoyment body Dharma­cakra Heart 8 Dharma body Nirmāṇa­cakra Navel 64 Emanation body; the “fierce woman” (caṇḍālī) fire

docs.title: 10.5.1 Generation and Completion
docs.text:
Practice is divided into two stages. In the generation stage (utpattikrama) the practitioner, having meditated on emptiness, visualises the deity’s seed syllable, the protective circle and palace of the maṇḍala, and the deity and retinue, identifying with the central deity; the “wisdom being” (jñānasattva) is invited to merge with the visualised “pledge being” (samayasattva); mantras are recited; and the visualisation is finally dissolved. In the Nyingma tradition the process is preceded by three samādhis: of suchness, of universal illumination (compassion), and of the cause (the seed syllable).

In the completion stage (utpannakrama, sampannakrama) the practitioner works with the subtle body, drawing the winds into the central channel to produce the experiences of bliss and of the “clear light” (prabhāsvara), understood as the fundamental nature of mind. In the original Indian texts these practices included sexual yoga with a consort; later monastic traditions often performed them with a visualised consort.

docs.title: 10.5.2 The Six Doctrines of Nāropa
docs.text: The Kagyu school systematised the completion stage in the “six doctrines” associated with Nāropa: inner heat (caṇḍālī, Tibetan gtum mo), the illusory body, clear light, dream yoga, transference of consciousness at death (’pho ba) and the yoga of the intermediate state (bar do). The last two reflect the importance of the moment of death. Tibetan teachings derived from the Guhyasamāja describe dying as a sequence of dissolutions of the elements, each marked by an inner sign (a mirage, smoke, fireflies, a flickering flame), culminating in the dawning of the “clear light”, which the trained practitioner may recognise as the nature of mind.

docs.title: 10.6 The Five Buddha Families
docs.text:
Buddhist Tantra organises its pantheons and correspondences around five “families” (kulas) headed by five Buddhas (Table 10.1).

Table 10.1. The Five Buddha Families Family Buddha Colour Affliction transformed Wisdom Tathāgata Vairocana White Delusion Wisdom of the dharmadhātu Vajra Akṣobhya Blue Anger Mirror-like wisdom Ratna Ratnasambhava Yellow Pride Wisdom of equality Padma Amitābha Red Desire Discriminating wisdom Karma Amoghasiddhi Green Envy All-accomplishing wisdom

Correlations with the elements, directions and other categories vary between systems. The scheme expresses a central Tantric idea: the afflictions are not merely to be suppressed but transformed into their corresponding wisdoms.

docs.title: 10.7 Initiation (Abhiṣeka)
docs.text:
Initiation (abhiṣeka, “consecration”, often translated “empowerment”) by a qualified master is the gateway to Tantric practice. In the Anuttarayoga Tantras four consecrations are given (Table 10.2):

Table 10.2. The Four Consecrations of the Anuttarayoga Tantras Consecration Significance in later systematisations Vase (kalaśa) Purifies the body; authorises generation-stage practice Secret (guhya) Purifies speech; authorises practices with the channels and winds Wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna) Purifies mind; authorises the yoga of bliss and emptiness; originally involved union with a consort Fourth (caturtha) Introduces the nature of mind; authorises the highest meditations (Mahāmudrā, Dzogchen)

The secret and wisdom consecrations originally involved sexual rites with a consort and the consumption of sexual fluids. Their literal performance became controversial even in India, and in Tibetan monastic settings they were generally given symbolically (Snellgrove 1987; Davidson 2002).

docs.title: 10.7.1 Tantric Vows (Samaya)
docs.text: Initiates take vows (samaya): a standard list of fourteen “root downfalls” (mūlāpatti) forbids, among other things, disparaging the master, abandoning the aspiration to awakening (bodhicitta), abandoning love for beings, revealing secrets to the unprepared and despising women, who are regarded as embodiments of wisdom. The vows show that the antinomian language of the Tantras was framed by a demanding ethical discipline; scholars debate how far the transgressive rites were actually performed and by whom (Wedemeyer 2013). Jacob Dalton has traced how Tibetan Buddhists, from the early manuscripts of Dunhuang onwards, interpreted the violent rites of the Tantras as the “liberation” of hostile beings, and how that interpretation shaped Tibetan ideas of ritual violence and of the subjugation of demons (Dalton 2011).

docs.title: 10.8 The Maṇḍala
docs.text:
A Buddhist Tantric maṇḍala typically consists of an outer protective circle of fire and vajras; in the Yoginītantras, eight charnel grounds; a lotus circle; a square palace with four gates; inner circles of deities; and the principal deity at the centre (Figure 10.1). Maṇḍalas are painted, made of coloured powders and ritually dismantled (a practice publicly demonstrated by Tibetan monks today), built in three dimensions or visualised. The size of the assembly varies enormously (Section 8.5.3): the basic Hevajra maṇḍala has nine deities, while the Kālacakra maṇḍala is said to contain over seven hundred.

Figure 10.1. Schematic plan of a Buddhist Tantric maṇḍala, with east, as in painted maṇḍalas, at the bottom. The inner lotus shows the arrangement of the five Buddhas (Table 10.1) in the Vajradhātu maṇḍala; other maṇḍalas place other deities at the centre and in the directions, and the charnel grounds belong to the Yoginītantras.

docs.title: 10.9 The Mahāsiddhas
docs.text:
The mahāsiddhas (“great adepts”) were Tantric masters of roughly the eighth to twelfth centuries, active mainly in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Assam. A collection of the lives of eighty-four of them, attributed to Abhayadatta, survives in Tibetan. The hagiographies depict men and women of every class — kings and princesses, Brahmins, monks, fishermen, cobblers, weavers and prostitutes — who attained awakening through Tantric practice, often while living unconventionally in cremation grounds and forests. Their vernacular songs, the Caryāgīti and the dohās, are among the earliest literature in eastern Indo-Aryan languages and are claimed by Bengali, Odia, Assamese and Maithili literary history alike (Table 10.3).

Table 10.3. Some Mahāsiddhas Siddha Background in hagiography Associated teaching Saraha Brahmin who became an arrow-maker Songs (dohās) on the innate (sahaja) nature of mind Lūipā Royal renunciant who lived on fish entrails A Cakrasaṃvara lineage Virūpa Monk “Path and Fruit” teaching of the Hevajra Tilopā Sesame-pounder Teacher of Nāropa; Mahāmudrā Nāropā Scholar of Nālandā or Vikramaśīla The six doctrines; teacher of the Tibetan Marpa Lakṣmīṅkarā Princess A female siddha; teachings on the innate

docs.title: 10.10 Women in Buddhist Tantra
docs.text: The place of women in Buddhist Tantra is debated. The Yoginītantras exalt the feminine: wisdom is female, the central deities are often goddesses or deities in union with consorts, one of the root vows forbids despising women, and the hagiographies include female siddhas such as Lakṣmīṅkarā and teachers who instruct male disciples. Miranda Shaw has argued that women were full participants and sometimes leaders in the early Tantric movement (Shaw 2006). Other scholars, such as David Snellgrove and Ronald Davidson, read the same texts as written primarily from the point of view of male practitioners, for whom women were above all ritual partners, and note that in later Tibetan monastic institutions women’s opportunities for advanced practice and teaching were limited (Snellgrove 1987; Davidson 2002). Both readings find support in the sources, which were produced in varied settings over several centuries.

docs.title: 10.11 Tārā
docs.text:
Tārā (“she who carries across”), the female saviour, is the most popular goddess of Buddhist devotion. She appears in Indian Buddhist art and literature from about the sixth or seventh century, first as a companion of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (a later legend has her born from his tear of compassion) and then as an independent saviour who rescues devotees from the “eight great fears”. Her best-known forms are the green and white Tārās, and Tibetan tradition celebrates twenty-one forms. She is regarded as a bodhisattva and, in Tantric contexts, as a fully awakened Buddha (Shaw 2006).

The relation with the Hindu Mahāvidyā Tārā (Chapter 4) is not one of simple identity. The Hindu goddess, fierce and associated with the cremation ground, derives largely from fierce Buddhist forms such as Ekajaṭā and Ugratārā, and some Hindu Tantras openly acknowledge a “Chinese” (that is, Tibetan or Himalayan) mode of her worship. The gentle, compassionate saviour who dominates Buddhist devotion has no close Hindu counterpart. Tārā thus illustrates both the exchange between the traditions and their differences (Kinsley 1997; Shaw 2006).

docs.title: 10.12 Buddhist and Hindu Tantra
docs.text:
Hindu and Buddhist Tantra share a common vocabulary of practice: initiation (the Hindu dīkṣā, the Buddhist consecration or abhiṣeka); mantras and seed syllables, to which the Buddhists add the dhāraṇī; diagrams, the yantras and maṇḍalas of the Hindus and the maṇḍalas of the Buddhists; and a subtle body of channels and centres, in which the Hindu kuṇḍalinī has its Buddhist counterpart in the inner fire (caṇḍālī) and the winds and drops. The goals differ: realisation of identity with Śiva or the Goddess on the one side, Buddhahood as the union of emptiness and bliss on the other.

The parallels are real, but so are the differences. Buddhist Tantra reverses the gender symbolism of Hindu Śākta theology: the female principle is wisdom, the male compassionate activity. And the Buddhist systems interpret everything through the doctrine of emptiness rather than a theology of a supreme self. Historically, Sanderson has shown detailed textual borrowing from Śaiva scriptures into the Yoginītantras, while Buddhist goddesses such as Tārā passed into Hindu worship; the Pāla courts of eastern India patronised both religions (Sanderson 2009).

docs.title: 10.13 Dhāraṇīs
docs.text:
The dhāraṇī (“that which holds”) — a formula used for protection, for memory and for liberation — is found in Mahāyāna literature well before the Tantras and is one of their main sources. Many Mahāyāna sūtras contain such formulae, and whole texts were devoted to them. The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya (the “Heart Sūtra”) ends with the mantra gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā; the Uṣṇīṣavijayā dhāraṇī, recited for the purification of karma and protection from bad rebirth, was very widely disseminated in East Asia; the Sitātapatrā invokes the goddess of the White Parasol for protection; the five protective texts of the Pañcarakṣā, among them the Mahāpratisarā, came to be personified as five goddesses; and the Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra is the earliest source of Avalokiteśvara’s mantra oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ.

The early ritual Tantras later classed as Kriyā Tantras set such spells within a regulated ritual of worship. The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, a large and composite text, prescribes the painting of cloth images and the drawing of a maṇḍala of Mañjuśrī and his retinue, the conduct of the practitioner, the times, places and materials of mantra practice and rites for many worldly ends; one of its later chapters even contains a prophetic history of Indian kings. The Susiddhikara and the Subāhupari­pṛcchā regulate the recitation of mantras, the observances of the reciter and the fire offerings appropriate to different aims. These texts already sort their deities into “families” — the families of the Tathāgata, the Lotus and the Vajra — from which the later five-family scheme grew (Section 10.6). Their aims were largely practical — protection, rain, healing, success — but they placed them within the bodhisattva’s aspiration, and their ritual repertoire of purification, invocation, offering and recitation passed into all later Buddhist Tantra (Snellgrove 1987; Davidson 2002).

docs.title: 10.14.1 Tibet
docs.text:
Tibetan tradition distinguishes two diffusions of Buddhism. The “early diffusion” of the eighth and ninth centuries is associated with the Indian abbot Śāntarakṣita and the Tantric master Padmasambhava, invited by King Trisong Detsen; the Nyingma school traces its lineages to this period. The “later diffusion” began in the late tenth and eleventh centuries with translators such as Rinchen Zangpo (958–1055) and Marpa, and the arrival of Atīśa (982–1054) (Samuel 2008). Each of the main schools gave priority to particular Tantric systems: the Nyingma to Mahāyoga, Anuyoga and Atiyoga (Dzogchen, the “Great Perfection”); the Kagyu to Mahāmudrā and the six doctrines of Nāropa; the Sakya to the “Path and Fruit” based on the Hevajra; and the Gelug, founded by Tsongkhapa (1357–1419), to an integration of all four classes of Tantra with monastic discipline and scholastic study, with particular emphasis on the Guhyasamāja, Cakrasaṃvara and Kālacakra.

The Tibetan canon (Kangyur and Tengyur) preserves translations of thousands of Indian Tantric texts, many of which are lost in Sanskrit.

docs.title: 10.14.2 East and Southeast Asia
docs.text:
Table 10.4 summarises Tantric traditions beyond the subcontinent.

Table 10.4. Tantric Traditions Beyond the Subcontinent Region Period Evidence China and Japan 8th c. onward Esoteric Buddhism of Śubhakarasiṃha, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra in Tang China; Shingon and Tendai in Japan Cambodia 9th–13th c. Royal Śaiva initiation and the devarāja cult, described in the Sdok Kak Thom inscription as Śaiva; Buddhist Tantric deities such as Hevajra in Khmer art; the Buddhist temples of Jayavarman VII (late 12th century) Java 8th–15th c. Buddhist Borobudur and Śaiva Prambanan; Tantric Buddhist texts in Old Javanese; a syncretic Śiva–Buddha cult in East Java Bali To the present Śaiva and Buddhist (boda) priests (pedanda) serving a Hindu-Balinese community Nepal 5th c. to the present Newar Buddhist Vajrayāna alongside Hindu Tantra; many Sanskrit texts preserved

docs.title: 10.14.3 Borobudur
docs.text: Borobudur in Central Java (c. 800 CE) rises in nine terraces — six square and three circular — crowned by a central stūpa, with 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha images. It is often read as an ascent from the realm of desire through the realm of form to the formless, and sometimes as a three-dimensional maṇḍala; whether its programme is specifically Tantric or more broadly Mahāyāna is debated.

docs.title: 10.15 Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen
docs.text: Two Tibetan traditions present the culmination of Tantric practice as a direct recognition of the nature of mind. Mahāmudrā (“great seal”), a term that in the Indian Tantras denotes the final union of bliss and emptiness and is celebrated in the songs of Saraha and other siddhas, became in the Kagyu school the name of a contemplative path of resting in the luminous, empty nature of mind, taught both within and apart from Tantric initiation. Dzogchen (“great perfection”), the highest of the Nyingma vehicles, teaches that awareness is primordially pure and spontaneously present, so that realisation consists in recognising and abiding in it rather than in producing anything new. Both traditions were the subject of controversy in Tibet, where critics questioned their authenticity and their relation to the gradual path, and both have become widely known in the modern West (Samuel 2008).

docs.title: 10.16 Esoteric Buddhism in China and Japan
docs.text: In the eighth century three Indian masters — Śubhakarasiṃha (637–735), Vajrabodhi (671–741) and Amoghavajra (705–774) — brought the Mahāvairocana and Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha systems to Tang China, where they translated texts, performed rituals for the protection of the state and enjoyed imperial patronage. After the persecution of Buddhism in 845 the Chinese tradition declined, but it had already been transmitted to Japan. Kūkai (774–835) founded the Shingon school on the basis of the two great maṇḍalas of these texts, the “Womb Realm” and the “Diamond Realm”; the Tendai school also absorbed esoteric practice. In Japan, Sanskrit mantras and seed syllables were written in the Siddhaṃ script, which is still used there in ritual, and Indian deities such as Sarasvatī (Benzaiten) and Gaṇeśa (Kangiten) entered Japanese religion through esoteric Buddhism.

docs.title: 10.17 Newar Buddhism
docs.text: The Newars of the Kathmandu Valley preserve the only surviving Sanskrit-based Buddhist Tantric tradition of South Asia. Newar Buddhism has a married, hereditary clergy — the Vajrācāryas, who perform Tantric rites, and the Śākyas — living in courtyard monasteries (vihāras). Its rituals, conducted in Sanskrit from manuscript handbooks, include initiation into the maṇḍalas of Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī, fire offerings and life-cycle rites parallel to those of their Hindu neighbours, with whom the Newar Buddhists share festivals, deities and a caste organisation. Nepalese libraries also preserved many of the oldest manuscripts of Indian Buddhist and Śaiva Tantras (Gellner 1992; Samuel 2008).

docs.title: 10.18 The Decline of Buddhism in India
docs.text:
By the fourteenth century Buddhism, and with it Buddhist Tantra, had almost disappeared from the Indian plains, though it survived in the Himalaya, among the Newars of Nepal and in small pockets elsewhere. The decline was a long and uneven contraction rather than a single event: already in the seventh century Xuanzang found many monasteries deserted, and by the eleventh and twelfth centuries the main strongholds were the great monasteries of Bihar and Bengal under the Pālas, together with Kashmir and pockets in Odisha and the south. Historians agree that there was no single cause.

The great monasteries of Nālandā, Vikramaśīla and Odantapurī were sacked around 1200, during the campaigns of the Ghurid general Muhammad Bakhtiyār Khaljī in Bihar and Bengal (c. 1193–1205), and many monks fled to Nepal and Tibet. These campaigns also struck Brahmanical temples and the states that had protected the monasteries, but because Buddhist learning was concentrated in a few great institutions their loss was decisive. Activity did not cease at once: the Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin, who visited Bihar in 1234–1236, found Nālandā largely ruined but the aged master Rāhula Śrībhadra still teaching some seventy students there (see Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā). The destruction came on top of a longer loss of patronage. The large monasteries depended on land grants and royal favour; as most early medieval rulers turned their patronage to Brahmanical temples and grantees, and as the Pāla dynasty came to an end, they lost their resources, and their relatively weak lay support left them exposed. Hindu devotional and Tantric movements, meanwhile, competed successfully for lay allegiance, and some Buddhist deities and practices were absorbed into Śākta and Nātha traditions.

The relative weight of these factors is debated; most historians see a long process of decline that the destruction of the great monasteries brought to a close (Davidson 2002; Samuel 2008).

docs.title: 10.19 Jain Tantra
docs.text:
The Jains, who reject blood offerings and the transgressive elements of Kaula and Buddhist Tantra, nonetheless adopted much of the Tantric repertoire of mantra, diagram and goddess worship (Sanderson 2009). The central Jain formula, the “fivefold homage” (pañcanamaskāra), beginning ṇamo arahantāṇaṃ, is recited by all Jains and treated as a mantra of great power, and a secret sūrimantra is transmitted at the consecration of an ācārya. Among Śvetāmbara Jains the siddhacakra or navapada diagram, honouring the five supreme beings and the four virtues of right faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity, is worshipped especially during the biannual ōlī festival, and the ṛṣimaṇḍala is another important diagram. The attendant goddesses (śāsanadevatās, yakṣīs) of the Tīrthaṅkaras — above all Padmāvatī, Ambikā, Cakreśvarī and Jvālāmālinī — and the sixteen goddesses of knowledge (vidyādevīs) became objects of worship for worldly protection and prosperity. Handbooks such as Indranandi’s Jvālāmālinīkalpa (939) and Malliṣeṇa’s Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa (11th century) adapt mantra, diagram and even the “six acts” (Section 7.3.3) to Jain purposes.

Jain authors justified these practices as serving the welfare of the community and the protection of the teaching, while insisting that the liberated Tīrthaṅkaras themselves do not intervene in worldly affairs; it is their attendant deities who respond to worship.

docs.title: 10.19.1 Mantra and Monastic Authority
docs.text:
Among the image-worshipping Śvetāmbaras the most important mantra is the sūrimantra. It is conferred on a monk when he is raised to the rank of ācārya (sūri), transmitted orally and kept secret, and traced by tradition to Gautama Indrabhūti, the chief disciple of Mahāvīra. The ācārya periodically withdraws to propitiate it in retreat, and its power is regarded as the source of his authority. Only an ācārya who possesses it may perform the “eye-opening” consecration (añjanaśalākā) that turns a newly made image of a Jina into an object of worship. Paul Dundas has shown how the literature of the sūrimantra links the monk’s identity to that of Gautama, so that each new ācārya in a sense “becomes” the first disciple (Dundas 1998). Ellen Gough’s study of the sūrimantra, of the diagrams on which it is worshipped and of the meditations of present-day Śvetāmbara ācāryas goes further: drawing on texts and fieldwork, she argues that Tantric ritual is not a lay accretion to Jain asceticism but has long been part of the path of the renouncer himself (Gough 2021). Ritual manuals such as the Vidhimārgaprapā (1306) of Jinaprabhasūri, a Kharatara Gaccha monk who was also remembered for his mantra powers at the court of Muḥammad bin Tughluq, codified consecration, initiation and mantra rites for the community (Dundas 2002).

Among the Digambaras, image consecration was regulated by manuals such as the thirteenth-century Pratiṣṭhāsāroddhāra of the lay scholar Āśādhara, which prescribe nyāsa, mantras and homa in forms close to those of Śaiva manuals, and the bhaṭṭārakas — clerics who administered temples and lands — were the principal ritual specialists of the community for several centuries.

docs.title: 10.19.2 Protector Deities
docs.text:
Much Jain Tantric practice is directed to protector deities rather than to the Jinas themselves.

Padmāvatī, the snake-hooded attendant goddess of Pārśvanātha, is the most widely worshipped. Her principal Digambara centre is Humcha (Hombuja) in Karnataka, where, according to legend, the founder of the Śāntara dynasty received her favour, and where she remains the object of a major pilgrimage cult.

Ghaṇṭākarṇa Mahāvīra, a martial protector deity, has a popular shrine at Mahudi in Gujarat, founded by the Śvetāmbara monk Buddhisāgarasūri in the early twentieth century; devotees seek his help in worldly difficulties, and it is customary to eat the sweet offered to him within the precinct.

Bhairavas and field-guardians (kṣetrapālas) protect temples and pilgrimage sites; Nākoḍā Bhairava, at the Pārśvanātha shrine of Nākoḍā in Rajasthan, draws large numbers of pilgrims.

The Dādāgurus, four deceased ācāryas of the Kharatara Gaccha who lived between the twelfth and early seventeenth centuries, are worshipped in shrines (dādābāṛī) bearing their footprints. Their hagiographies tell how they overcame rival adepts and, in the case of Jinadattasūri, subdued the sixty-four yoginīs; devotees ask them for help in business, health and family matters (Laidlaw 1995).

docs.title: 10.19.3 Interpreting Jain Tantra
docs.text: Jain teachers have long been aware of a tension between these practices and the ascetic path to liberation. The standard justification is that the protector deities are beings of right faith (samyagdṛṣṭi) who serve the Jina’s teaching, and that worship of them for worldly ends is legitimate so long as it is not confused with the worship of the Jinas. John Cort has described Jain religious life as shaped by two value systems — the path to liberation (mokṣamārga) and a realm of well-being concerned with health, prosperity and the welfare of the community — and has argued that the second is not a corruption of the first but an integral part of Jain practice (Cort 2001). Reformers have taken a different view. The non-image-worshipping Śvetāmbara movements reject temple ritual altogether, and the Digambara Terāpanth, from the seventeenth century, rejected both the worship of protector deities and the authority of the bhaṭṭārakas. In historical perspective, the Jain adoption of mantra, consecration rites and protector cults is part of the wider Tantric transformation of Indian religion described in Chapter 12 (Dundas 2002; Sanderson 2009).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Temple Worship and Sacred Architecture
11.1 Introduction: The Temple as Cosmos
docs.text: In Āgamic thought the temple (ālaya, devālaya, prāsāda, vimāna) is not merely a building in which worship takes place. It is the dwelling and the body of the deity, a constructed image of the cosmos laid out on a sacred diagram, and the place in which the deity, installed by consecration, receives daily worship as a living presence. Much of the kriyāpāda of the Āgamas, and a large technical literature on architecture and image-making (vāstu- and śilpaśāstra, such as the Mayamata and Mānasāra), deals with temple building (Kramrisch 1946; Davis 1991).

docs.title: 11.2 The Vāstupuruṣa Maṇḍala
docs.text:
The plan of a temple is generated from the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, the square grid in which the “Person of the Site” lies face down, pinned by the deities of the grid, with Brahmā at the centre (Chapter 8). The sanctum is placed over the central “place of Brahmā” (brahmasthāna), and subsidiary shrines, halls and gates are related to the grid. The texts also associate the directions with particular functions: the main entrance is usually on the east, towards the rising sun; the north-east, the auspicious quarter of Īśāna, is the place for water; the south-east, the quarter of Agni, for fire and often the kitchen; the south-west for heavy structures and storage; and the north-west for subsidiary buildings.

Modern popular “vāstu” that claims magnetic or “energy” effects for these prescriptions goes well beyond the classical texts and has no scientific basis.

docs.title: 11.3 The Principal Parts of a Temple
docs.text:
A large South Indian temple consists of nested enclosures (prākāras) with the principal shrine at the centre (Figure 11.1). The main image or liṅga stands in a small, dark sanctum, the “womb-house” (garbhagṛha), which is reached through one or more vestibules (antarāla, ardhamaṇḍapa) from pillared halls (maṇḍapas) used for worship, music, dance and festivals. In South Indian usage the vimāna is the sanctum together with its superstructure, rising in tiers and crowned by a cupola (śikhara) and finial (stūpi); it is identified with the cosmic mountain Meru. Gateway towers (gopuras) pierce the enclosure walls, and from the twelfth century onwards in Tamil Nadu they came to dwarf the central vimāna. On the main axis before the sanctum stand the flag-staff (dhvajastambha) and the offering platform (balipīṭha), with the deity’s mount (in a Śiva temple, the bull Nandi) facing the shrine; the temple tank (puṣkariṇī) lies within or beside the enclosures.

Figure 11.1. Schematic plan of a South Indian Śaiva temple of the Āgamic type, with the main entrance on the east, at the bottom. The plan is not to scale and is not that of a particular temple: the number of enclosures and gateways, and the placing of the subsidiary shrines, the tank and the kitchen, vary from temple to temple.

docs.title: 11.4 Consecration (Pratiṣṭhā)
docs.text:
Through consecration the image is transformed from stone or metal into the seat of the deity. The rites extend over several days. The site, the image and the officiants are purified; the eyes of the image are “opened” (netronmīlana); the image is laid to “sleep” in water, in grain and on a couch (adhivāsa); fire offerings are made in a pavilion with several fire-pits; the deity’s mantras are installed on the image (nyāsa) and the deity is transferred into it from consecrated pots; and the rite culminates in a bathing with the consecrated water, the kumbhābhiṣeka described in Section 9.6.

Once consecrated, the image must receive regular worship; interruption of worship requires expiation and, in serious cases, reconsecration (Davis 1991).

docs.title: 11.5.1 Materials
docs.text: The fixed image in the sanctum is usually of stone (śilā) — granite in much of South India, sandstone in the North — while processional images are of metal (loha); the texts speak of “five metals” (pañcaloha), but South Indian “bronzes” are in practice mainly copper alloys. Some traditions use wood (dāru), notably for the images of Jagannātha at Purī, which are periodically renewed; small liṅgas and images may be of crystal or gems; and clay (mṛd) serves for temporary festival images, as in Bengal.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Proportional Systems (Tālamāna)
docs.text: The Āgamas and śilpa texts prescribe proportional systems for images, based on a module, the tāla (roughly the length of the face). Higher deities are made to longer proportions: the principal gods often to ten tālas, goddesses and lesser deities to nine or eight, human figures to fewer. Different texts give different schemes, and the measurements of surviving images vary (Rao 1914–1916). Defects in an image are held to make it unfit for worship.

docs.title: 11.6 Temple Plans and Types
docs.text:
The construction of a temple involves examination and choice of the site (bhūparīkṣā), for which the texts prescribe tests of the soil’s colour, smell and taste and of a refilled pit; orientation by means of a gnomon (śaṅku) and its shadows; drawing of the grid; and derivation of the dimensions of all parts from a basic module.

The South Indian texts distinguish three types of superstructure by the shape of its crowning element: square (nāgara), octagonal (drāviḍa) and circular or apsidal (vesara). Modern art historians use the same terms differently, for the North Indian temple with curvilinear tower (Nāgara), the South Indian temple with stepped pyramidal vimāna (Drāviḍa), and hybrid Deccan forms (Vesara).

The texts expect the architect-sculptor (sthapati) who translates the diagram into stone to be learned in the śāstras, skilled in drawing, mathematics and sculpture, and of good character; the craft has largely been transmitted in hereditary families of the Viśvakarma communities. In the twentieth century V. Ganapati Sthapati (1927–2011), who long headed the Government College of Architecture and Sculpture at Māmallapuram, was a leading figure in the revival of traditional temple architecture in South India and abroad.

Modern stylistic term Features and examples Nāgara Curvilinear tower (śikhara); North and East India; Khajurāho, Liṅgarāja at Bhubaneswar Drāviḍa Stepped pyramidal superstructure; South India; Bṛhadīśvara at Thanjavur Vesara Mixed forms of the Deccan; later Chālukya and Hoysaḷa temples Kerala Square, circular or apsidal shrines with tiered sloping roofs clad in copper or tiles

docs.title: 11.7 The Historical Development of the Temple
docs.text:
Freestanding stone temples appear in India from about the fifth century CE, in the Gupta period, roughly when the earliest surviving Tantric scriptures were composed. The growth of temple architecture over the following centuries parallels the rise of Āgamic worship:

Period Region and dynasty Examples and developments 5th–6th c. Gupta, North India Small flat-roofed shrines and early towered temples, such as the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh 6th–8th c. Chālukya, Deccan Experimental temples at Aihole, Bādāmi and Paṭṭadakal, in both northern and southern styles 7th–9th c. Pallava, Tamil country Rock-cut shrines and monolithic rathas at Māmallapuram; the Shore temple; the Kailāsanātha temple at Kāñcīpuram 8th c. Rāṣṭrakūṭa The Kailāsa temple at Ellora, carved from the living rock 10th–13th c. Chōḷa Bṛhadīśvara at Thanjavur (c. 1010) and Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḷapuram; classic bronzes; growth of enclosures and gateways 10th–13th c. North and East India Khajurāho; Bhubaneswar; Koṇārka 14th–17th c. Vijayanagara and Nāyaka Vast enclosures, halls and towering gopuras; much of Madurai and Śrīraṅgam in their present form

Many surviving South Indian Āgamas and architectural treatises, such as the Mayamata, are later than the earliest monuments they appear to describe; the relation between text and building is one of mutual influence rather than of buildings simply realising earlier blueprints. Nor did architecture follow the texts slavishly: each region and period developed its own forms within the shared framework.

docs.title: 11.8 Vaiṣṇava Temples
docs.text: Vaiṣṇava temples of South India are governed either by the Pāñcarātra (for example Śrīraṅgam, the Varadarāja temple at Kāñcīpuram and Melkote) or by the Vaikhānasa Āgama (for example Tirumala-Tirupati); see Chapter 3. In Śrīvaiṣṇava theology the consecrated image (arcā) is the most accessible of the Lord’s five modes of presence. Piḷḷai Lokācārya’s Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇa teaches that the qualities of the Lord’s love for devotees (vātsalya), lordship (svāmitva), gracious condescension (sauśīlya) and accessibility (saulabhya) are most fully manifest in the image, in which the Lord makes himself dependent on his worshippers.

docs.title: 11.9 Festivals (Utsava)
docs.text: The great festival (mahotsava, brahmotsava), usually of seven to eleven days, begins with the hoisting of the flag (dhvajārohaṇa), brings the deity out in daily processions on different mounts and culminates in a chariot procession and a ritual bath. In the chariot festival (rathotsava) the deity is drawn through the streets in a great wooden car, as at Purī and Tiruvārūr; in the float festival (teppotsava) it is floated on a raft in the temple tank; and in the divine marriage (kalyāṇotsava) it is wedded to its consort, as in the Cittirai festival of Mīnākṣī and Sundareśvara at Madurai.

docs.title: 11.9.1 Festivals and Social Conflict
docs.text: Temple festivals display the social order of the community that celebrates them: who pulls the chariot, who carries the image, who receives honours and consecrated food, and in what order, are matters of precedence, and they have often been contested. In colonial and modern South India, disputes between castes over the right to take part in processions, to have the deity’s chariot pass through their streets or to receive temple honours have repeatedly led to litigation and, at times, to violence; Dalit communities in particular have campaigned for the right to participate on equal terms. Arjun Appadurai, Fuller and others have shown that such conflicts are not aberrations but part of how temples have long functioned as arenas of status and authority (Appadurai 1981; Fuller 2003).

docs.title: 11.10.1 Qualifications, Heredity and Caste
docs.text: In South India, worship in Śaiva Āgamic temples is performed by hereditary ādiśaiva (Tamil civācāriyār) priests and in Vaiṣṇava temples by bhaṭṭācāryas of the Pāñcarātra or Vaikhānasa lineages. Priests are trained in the Āgamic manuals, Sanskrit and Vedic recitation, and receive the initiations and consecrations that entitle them to touch the image. The hereditary and caste-restricted character of the priesthood, though defended by many as an Āgamic requirement, is not found in the earliest scriptures, which open initiation more widely, and it has been challenged by legislation and litigation. Tamil Nadu legislated in 1970 and again in 2006 to allow trained persons of any caste to be appointed as temple priests; the Supreme Court in 2015 upheld the principle while requiring appointments to conform to the Āgamas of each temple, and the state began appointing non-Brahmin priests trained in its Āgama schools in 2021. The debate shows that “what the Āgamas say” about access is itself a matter of interpretation. C.J. Fuller’s classic ethnography of the priests of the Mīnākṣī temple at Madurai (Fuller 1984), and his later study of the reform of their training (Fuller 2003), describe how the status and education of the ādiśaiva priests changed in the twentieth century.

docs.title: 11.10.2 Music and Recitation
docs.text: Music is part of worship itself. In Tamil temples the nākasuram (nāgasvaram, a large double-reed instrument) and the tavil (barrel drum) are the auspicious instruments (maṅgalavādya) that accompany processions and the main services; particular rāgas are customarily associated with particular times of day, a convention of performers rather than a prescription of the Āgamas. In Kerala the pañcavādya (“five instruments”) ensembles play for processions, and sopāna singing is performed at the steps of the sanctum. Beside the Sanskrit liturgy, Tamil hymns are sung: the Āḻvār hymns are recited in Vaiṣṇava temples (Chapter 3), and in Śaiva temples hereditary singers (ōtuvārs) perform the Tēvāram, the hymns of the three principal Nāyaṉmār poets, Campantar, Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar) and Cuntarar, composed between the seventh and ninth centuries and set to Tamil melodic modes (paṇ). According to a later tradition, the hymns were recovered from a locked room in the Chidambaram temple by Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi at the behest of a Chōḷa king, often identified with Rājarāja I, whose inscriptions do record the endowment of hymn-singers at Thanjavur. The joining of vernacular devotional poetry to a Sanskrit Āgamic liturgy, which these singers embody, distinguishes the Tamil temples from most others in India (Peterson 1989).

docs.title: 11.10.3 Temple Women and Their Abolition
docs.text: Medieval inscriptions, such as those of Rājarāja I at Thanjavur, record large numbers of women attached to temples as dancers and ritual performers. In the colonial period the institution of “devadāsīs”, women dedicated to temple deities, came to be associated with concubinage and exploitation, and after a long reform campaign it was abolished in the Madras Presidency by the Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947. Recent scholarship stresses both the exploitation the system entailed and the loss of the women’s artistic heritage, much of which was appropriated in the twentieth-century reconstruction of dance as “Bharatanāṭyam”.

docs.title: 11.11.1 Chidambaram
docs.text: The Naṭarāja temple at Chidambaram is among the most sacred Śaiva sites of Tamil Nadu. Its hereditary priests, the Dīkṣitars, follow not the Śaiva Āgamas but a Vedic-style liturgy ascribed to Patañjali. The temple’s gateway towers bear reliefs of the 108 dance poses (karaṇas) of the Nāṭyaśāstra. Control of its administration has been contested between the Dīkṣitars and the Tamil Nadu government in a long series of court cases.

docs.title: 11.11.2 Tirumala-Tirupati
docs.text: The Veṅkaṭeśvara temple at Tirumala, one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in the world, follows the Vaikhānasa Āgama and is administered by the statutory Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.

docs.title: 11.11.3 Madurai
docs.text: The Mīnākṣī–Sundareśvara temple at Madurai, largely in its present form from the Nāyaka period (16th–17th centuries), has fourteen gateway towers, the tallest about fifty metres high, a hall of a thousand pillars and the tank of the golden lotus. Its annual Cittirai festival celebrates the marriage of the goddess and Śiva. Fuller’s studies of its priests are a classic account of a living Āgamic temple (Fuller 1984, 2003).

docs.title: 11.11.4 Śrīraṅgam
docs.text: The Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam, with its seven enclosures, is the principal seat of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition and was the base of Rāmānuja (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 11.11.5 North India and Kerala
docs.text:
The great temples of North and East India — Liṅgarāja at Bhubaneswar (11th century), the Khajurāho temples (10th–11th centuries), the Sun temple at Koṇārka (13th century) and the Jagannātha temple at Purī (12th century) — were not governed by the South Indian Āgamas. Their worship follows Purāṇic and regional ritual manuals and local priestly traditions; at many North Indian temples devotees may touch and themselves worship the image, which is unthinkable in a South Indian Āgamic sanctum.

Kerala, with its own Tantric temple ritual under hereditary tantrīs, is described in Section 13.2; its temple arts include the pañcavādya ensembles and the Pūram festivals with their processions of elephants.

docs.title: 11.12 The Temple as Body and Maṇḍala
docs.text: Texts and commentators describe the temple as a body: the sanctum is the womb or heart, the superstructure the head, the finial the crown; the doors are its mouth, the enclosure walls its skin. The temple is at the same time the cosmic person and the mountain at the centre of the world. Stella Kramrisch’s The Hindu Temple (1946) showed how this symbolism, rooted in Vedic conceptions of the sacrificial altar and the cosmic person, is built into the geometry of the plan and the elevation (Kramrisch 1946). The homology allows temple worship and internal meditation to be understood as parallel practices (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 11.13 The Temple Kitchen and the Tank
docs.text:
Food offered to the deity (naivedya) is prepared in the temple kitchen (Tamil maṭappaḷḷi) by ritually pure cooks, according to prescribed recipes and timings, and distributed after offering as prasāda, the deity’s grace. Many temples are famous for particular offerings, such as the laḍḍu of Tirupati.

The temple tank serves for ritual bathing, provides water for worship and is the scene of the float festival. It is often consecrated as embodying sacred rivers. The water that has bathed the image (tīrtha) is distributed to devotees, who sip it and touch it to the head.

docs.title: 11.14 Administration and the State
docs.text: Medieval temple inscriptions show temples managed by assemblies, trustees and royal officers, with large endowments of land and gold and staffs of priests, musicians, dancers, accountants, cooks, garland-makers and craftsmen (Sanderson 2009). Since the nineteenth century the administration of Hindu temples in much of South India has passed to the state: in Tamil Nadu the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department oversees tens of thousands of temples. State control has been defended as a safeguard against mismanagement and as a means of social reform, and criticised as interference in religion; its relation to the Āgamas remains a subject of litigation.

docs.title: 11.15 Renovation and Reconsecration
docs.text: The Āgamas prescribe the renovation (jīrṇoddhāra) of temples and their reconsecration, conventionally about every twelve years, and after damage, pollution or interruption of worship. During renovation the divine presence is transferred to a temporary seat and then reinstalled through the rites of kumbhābhiṣeka (Chapter 9).

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Śaiva Age: Tantra, Kingship and the Early Medieval State
12.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Tantric traditions are often imagined as marginal: secret lineages of ascetics and adepts working on the edges of society, in cremation grounds and mountain retreats. The historical record of the early medieval period shows something very different. From about the fifth to the thirteenth century initiatory Śaivism was patronised by kings across South Asia and much of Southeast Asia; its officiants consecrated rulers and temples, its monasteries held land and villages, and its ritual systems shaped the religious practice of competing traditions. Alexis Sanderson, who has done more than any other scholar to assemble the evidence, called this period the “Śaiva Age” (Sanderson 2009).

The “Śaiva Age” is, first of all, one scholar’s synthesis: Sanderson built it from his own reading of a very large body of scriptures, manuals and inscriptions, much of it unpublished, and it has since become the framework of much recent work on early medieval Śaivism. Chapter 1 introduced the thesis briefly (Section 1.8). This chapter examines it in more detail: the kinds of evidence on which it rests, the rites by which Śaiva preceptors served kings, the monastic networks through which Śaiva learning travelled, the response of Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical rivals, and the criticisms and qualifications that other historians have offered. The question matters beyond the history of Śaivism. If Sanderson is right, much of what is now regarded as ordinary Hindu, Buddhist and Jain practice — temple consecration, image worship with nyāsa and bīja mantras, initiation by a guru — took its form in competition for the patronage of early medieval courts.

docs.title: 12.2 The Thesis in Outline
docs.text:
Sanderson’s argument, set out in a long essay of 2009 and in a series of related studies, can be summarised in four propositions (Sanderson 2009, 2013).

  1. Dominance. Between about the fifth and the thirteenth centuries the Śaiva traditions — first the ascetic Atimārga, then above all the Mantramārga of initiation and mantra — received more royal patronage than any rival religion across most of the Indian subcontinent and in Cambodia, Champa and Java.

  2. The reason: service to kings. Śaivism succeeded because its officiants made themselves useful to rulers. They offered initiation in a form that a king could accept; rites of consecration, protection and victory; the foundation and consecration of royal temples; and an organisation of monasteries that could supply trained preceptors to courts far from their home regions.

  3. Accommodation. The Siddhānta, the most widely patronised form, made itself compatible with the Brahmanical social order. It taught that Śiva’s initiation liberates while leaving the initiate’s caste duties in the world intact, so that kings, whose office was to protect the order of the varṇas, could support it without contradiction.

  4. Imitation. Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Buddhist and Jain traditions, and Brahmanical householders, competing for the same patronage, adopted the Śaiva model: its form of initiation, its liturgy of worship, its rites of consecration and its techniques of mantra.

A fifth element concerns the end of the period. In Sanderson’s account the Śaiva Age closed in North India with the loss of royal patronage after the Turkic conquests of the late twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and with the rise of Vaiṣṇava devotion and of Brahmanical orders centred on Vedānta; it lasted longer in the South, where the Śaiva Siddhānta survived as the liturgy of the Tamil temples (Section 12.12).

The thesis is not simply that kings were pious. It is a claim about the mechanism by which a religion spread: through the practical value of its specialists to those who held power, and through the transfer of its institutions and rituals to new regions and to rival traditions.

docs.title: 12.3 The Evidence
docs.text:
The case rests on several kinds of source, each with its own limitations.

Inscriptions. Copper-plate charters and stone inscriptions record grants of land to temples, monasteries and preceptors, name the gurus of kings, and sometimes describe the religious affiliation of donors in technical terms. They are dated or datable and cover the whole region, but they record donations rather than belief, and the surviving corpus is uneven: some dynasties are richly documented, others hardly at all. Sanderson has argued that inscriptions also change how the scriptures themselves should be read, since they show which texts and lineages were actually patronised (Sanderson 2013).

Scriptures and manuals. The Śaiva scriptures and the ritual manuals (paddhatis) prescribe rites for kings and give rules for the conduct of royal preceptors. Their prescriptions show what officiants offered, though not how often these rites were performed.

Monuments and images. Royal temples, their liṅgas and their iconographic programmes are the most visible evidence of patronage. Their scale — from the Kailāsanātha at Kāñcīpuram to the Bṛhadīśvara at Thanjavur and the temple-mountains of Angkor — shows the resources that Śaiva cults could command.

Literature. Court literature, satire and chronicle give glimpses of Śaiva preceptors at work. Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (1148–49) records the religious foundations of the kings of Kashmir; the eleventh-century Kashmiri satirist Kṣemendra mocked self-serving Tantric gurus and their royal and mercantile clients.

Table 12.1 lists some of the best-documented cases. It is a sample, not a census, and several of its entries are discussed further below.
