docs.title: 12.4.1 A Form of Initiation for Rulers
docs.text:
The full Śaiva initiation imposed demanding obligations. The initiate had to perform daily worship of Śiva, observe the rules (samayas) of his grade, and in some cases undertake further disciplines for the rest of his life (Chapter 2). A king, occupied with government and war, could not be expected to do so. The Siddhānta solved the problem by distinguishing two forms of liberating initiation. In the initiation “with seed” (sabījā), the initiate’s capacity to observe the post-initiatory rules is presupposed and the rules are binding. In the “seedless” initiation (nirbījā) the guru, out of compassion, removes the obligation to observe them. The texts recommend the seedless form for those unable to bear the burden: children, the very old, the sick, women in some texts, and the ruler. Liberation at death was promised all the same; the king’s duty was reduced to devotion to Śiva and to his guru (Sanderson 2009; Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998).

This was a decisive innovation. It meant that Śaiva initiation, which had begun as the preserve of ascetics, could be offered to a king without asking him to change his way of life, and it gave the guru who conferred it a lasting claim on the king’s gratitude. Inscriptions accordingly speak of royal “initiation preceptors” (dīkṣāguru) alongside the royal chaplain (purohita).

docs.title: 12.4.2 The Rājaguru and the Rites of the Realm
docs.text:
The Śaiva royal preceptor (rājaguru) took over many of the functions that Brahmanical law assigned to the king’s purohita. Śaiva and Pāñcarātra texts give their own versions of the royal consecration (abhiṣeka), in which the king is bathed with water from pots charged with mantras and so empowered by the deity. They provide rites to protect the king and his kingdom against enemies, disease, epidemics and evil portents; rites of appeasement (śānti) and of increase (puṣṭi), performed at times of crisis, at the new year and before campaigns; and rites for success in war, sometimes involving the fierce forms of Śiva and the Goddess and, in the Bhairava and Kaula traditions, the propitiation of yoginīs (Section 4.10).

The Netratantra, commented on by the Kashmiri exegete Kṣemarāja in the eleventh century, gives particular attention to rites performed by a preceptor for the protection of the king, and Sanderson has argued that the ordinary Śaiva ritual of Kashmir, based on the Svacchandatantra and the Netratantra, was also the ritual of the royal court (Sanderson 2009). In this way the Mantramārga’s ancient pursuit of supernatural power (siddhi) was redirected towards the needs of the state.

docs.title: 12.4.3 A Literary Portrait: Puṣpabhūti and Bhairavācārya
docs.text: Court literature shows how such relationships were imagined. In the third chapter of Bāṇa’s Harṣacarita (7th century), the founder of King Harṣa’s dynasty, Puṣpabhūti, becomes the devotee of a Śaiva adept from the South named Bhairavācārya. At the adept’s request the king and three companions guard a night-time rite in a cremation ground, in which Bhairavācārya, seated on a corpse, seeks the status of a vidyādhara, a semi-divine being of the air. When a nāga disrupts the rite the king overcomes him, and a goddess rewards the king with the promise that he will found a great royal line. The story is a romance, not a record; but it shows a seventh-century court poet taking for granted that a king might serve a Śaiva adept, and that the adept’s power might serve the dynasty in return (Lorenzen 1972).

docs.title: 12.5 The Goddess and the King
docs.text:
The Śaiva preceptor was not the only Tantric specialist at court. From the early medieval period onwards, the Goddess in her martial forms became the guardian of kingship across much of India, and her autumn festival became the great royal ritual of the year. The frame story of the Devīmāhātmya already sets the pattern: King Suratha, driven from his kingdom, worships the Goddess on the advice of a sage and regains his throne (Section 4.2).

Later texts, among them the Kālikā Purāṇa, prescribe the autumn worship of Durgā as a duty of kings, performed for victory and the prosperity of the realm. Its royal form combined several elements: the worship of the Goddess in an image, a pot or a yantra over nine nights; the worship of the king’s weapons, horses, elephants and insignia (āyudhapūjā); blood sacrifice, above all of buffaloes, re-enacting the Goddess’s victory over the buffalo demon; and, on the tenth day, the lustration of the army (nīrājana) and a royal procession marking the start of the campaigning season (Fuller 1992). Bihani Sarkar has traced the growth of this martial cult of Durgā in Sanskrit literature and ritual texts from about the sixth century, and argues that a “heroic” Śāktism, centred on the warrior goddess and her blood offerings, became part of the very idea of early medieval kingship (Sarkar 2017). The household and festival forms of the same worship are described in Section 9.9.

The festival can be followed across many kingdoms. At Vijayanagara the Portuguese visitor Domingo Paes, writing about 1520, described the nine-day Mahānavamī at which the king received the homage of his nobles, reviewed his troops and witnessed the sacrifice of great numbers of buffaloes and sheep; the stone platform from which the kings watched it still stands at Hampi. The Woḍeyar kings of Mysore continued the Vijayanagara festival as the Mysore Dasarā, and in Nepal the Dasaĩ festival, centred on the royal goddess Taleju, kept its royal character, with sacrifices offered on the king’s behalf, until the abolition of the monarchy in 2008 (Section 4.7). The Marāṭhā king Śivājī took as his tutelary deity the goddess Bhavānī of Tuljapur, and the Rajput clans of the North-west each honoured a lineage goddess (kuladevī) as protector of their rule (Section 13.8).

Royal goddess worship did not usually require the king’s Tantric initiation, and much of it was conducted according to Purāṇic rather than Tantric texts. But it drew on the same repertoire of mantra, sacrifice and protective rites, its officiants were often Tantric specialists, and in Nepal, Assam and Bengal the royal cults of Taleju, Kāmākhyā and Durgā were explicitly Tantric (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 12.6.1 The Śaiva Monastery
docs.text:
The institution that carried Śaiva learning across the subcontinent was the monastery (maṭha). A Śaiva maṭha was headed by an ascetic ācārya who had received the highest consecration and could initiate others and consecrate temples; it housed his ascetic pupils, who were often given initiation names ending in -śiva or -śambhu; and it was usually attached to a temple whose worship its members performed or supervised. Endowed with land and villages by kings and local lords, monasteries became centres of learning, teaching not only Śaiva scripture but grammar, logic, literature and Mīmāṃsā, and they distributed food to ascetics and the poor (Sanderson 2009; Lorenzen 1972).

Succession passed from teacher to initiated pupil, not from father to son, so that a monastic lineage could found branches in distant regions without depending on a local kinship group. This mobility was central to the Śaiva Age. A king who wished to establish a royal temple could invite a preceptor from an established lineage, endow a new monastery for him, and so acquire a complete religious institution, with its texts, its rites and its trained personnel.

docs.title: 12.6.2 The Mattamayūra and Golakī Lineages
docs.text:
Two Siddhānta lineages of central India illustrate the pattern. The Mattamayūra lineage took its name from a place in the region of Gwalior, where its first known leaders were settled by a local king in the ninth century. An inscription at Ranod (ancient Raṇipadra) describes the ascetic Purandara, invited by the king to his capital, founding monasteries there and at Raṇipadra; his pupils and their pupils later served as preceptors to the Kalacuri kings of Tripūrī (near Jabalpur) and to other dynasties of central India. The Golakī lineage, also patronised by the Kalacuris, later extended into the Deccan and Andhra (Sanderson 2009).

The fullest single document of such a network is the Malkāpuram pillar inscription of 1261, in the Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh, issued in the reign of the Kākatīya queen Rudramadevī. It traces the Golakī lineage over several generations, and claims for its preceptors the respect of kings of several dynasties, including the Kalacuris, the Chōḷas and the rulers of Mālava. Its hero is Viśveśvaraśambhu, a Śaiva ascetic from Bengal who was the initiating guru of the Kākatīya king Gaṇapati (r. 1199–1262). The inscription records the gift of land on which he founded a Śaiva settlement: a temple, a monastery, a feeding house said to be open to all, a school with teachers of the Vedas, grammar, logic, literature and the Āgamas, a hospital and a maternity house, together with Brahmin households and the craftsmen needed to sustain them (Talbot 2001; Sanderson 2009). Whatever its rhetorical exaggerations, the inscription shows a Śaiva monastic foundation acting as an instrument of settlement and social provision in a frontier region.

docs.title: 12.6.3 Preceptors on the Move
docs.text:
The inscriptions repeatedly show Śaiva preceptors working far from their homelands. Viśveśvaraśambhu moved from Bengal to Andhra. Under the Chōḷas, an inscription of the reign of Rājendra I at Thanjavur provides for the support of the Śaiva preceptor of the royal temple, Sarvaśiva Paṇḍita, and of his pupils and their pupils from “Āryadeśa, Madhyadeśa and Gauḍadeśa”, that is, from northern and eastern India (Sanderson 2009). The Kashmiri Siddhānta exegesis of Rāmakaṇṭha and his predecessors reached the Tamil country in the same way, and was absorbed into the manuals of Aghoraśiva of Chidambaram in the twelfth century (Section 2.3). The Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta that survives today is thus, in part, the southern outcome of a network that once reached from Kashmir to Bengal and the Deccan.

The ascetic orders of the Atimārga formed similar networks. The Kālāmukhas of Karnataka ran temple-monasteries endowed by the Chālukya and Hoysaḷa kings and their feudatories, and Pāśupata and Lākula teachers appear in inscriptions from Gujarat to Nepal (Section 2.1.6).

docs.title: 12.7 Temples, Liṅgas and the Names of Kings
docs.text:
The royal temple was the most conspicuous product of the alliance between Śaiva preceptors and kings. Its consecration was a Śaiva rite, performed by the ācārya according to the kriyāpāda of the Āgamas and the manuals (Chapter 11). The liṅga of a royal foundation was often named after its founder: the Pallava Rājasiṃha’s temple at Kāñcīpuram enshrines Rājasiṃheśvara; Rājarāja I’s temple at Thanjavur, consecrated about 1010, is called Rājarājeśvara in its inscriptions; his son Rājendra I built Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḷeśvara at his new capital to commemorate his northern campaign. The king’s name joined to that of the Lord (īśvara) bound the ruler’s fame to the deity’s permanence, and the temple’s endowments made the king’s piety visible in the agrarian economy around it (Section 1.8).

The same pattern appears in Cambodia. In 881 the Khmer king Indravarman I consecrated a liṅga named Indreśvara in the temple-mountain of Bakong; his successor Yaśovarman I founded āśramas for ascetics of different communities, among them Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas and Buddhists, and inscribed their rules on steles. The Sdok Kak Thom inscription of 1052, from the present Thai–Cambodian border, is the most detailed single witness. It records that at the beginning of the ninth century a Brahmin named Hiraṇyadāma taught four Tantras — named as the Vināśikha, Nayottara, Sammoha and Śiraścheda — to the priest of King Jayavarman II, in connection with the royal cult, and it traces a single priestly family that served that cult for some two and a half centuries. The first of these Tantras is probably the Vīṇāśikha, the surviving scripture of the Vāma stream (Section 2.6). What that cult was — the devarāja or “god who is king” of the inscription’s Sanskrit, rendered in Khmer as the “lord of the world who is king” — is debated. The older view saw in it the deification of the king; Hermann Kulke argued instead that it was a movable image of a god that protected the king and accompanied the court, and Sanderson has related it to the Śaiva Tantras named in the inscription (Kulke 1993; Sanderson 2003–2004).

Royal temples did not only express legitimacy. They also absorbed local cults. A goddess of a hill tribe or a village liṅga could be installed within a Śaiva temple complex as a form or attendant of Śiva, given an Āgamic liturgy and a Brahmin priest, and so drawn into the religious order of the kingdom. Historians of the early medieval state, notably Hermann Kulke and B.D. Chattopadhyaya, have made this process of integration a central theme of their work (Kulke 1993; Chattopadhyaya 1994).

docs.title: 12.8 A Regional Case: Kashmir
docs.text:
Kashmir allows the Śaiva Age to be observed in unusual detail, because it has both a large Śaiva literature and a court chronicle, Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī. The chronicle shows kings founding temples of every persuasion. Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa (8th century) built the great Sun temple of Mārtaṇḍa as well as Vaiṣṇava and Buddhist foundations; Avantivarman (r. 855–883) founded the town of Avantipura with a Śiva temple named Avantīśvara and a Viṣṇu temple named Avantisvāmin, after himself, in the manner described above. Royal religion in Kashmir was thus plural; but the scholarly and ritual culture of its Brahmins was overwhelmingly Śaiva.

Abhinavagupta himself traced his family to this alliance of court and Śaiva learning: at the end of the Tantrāloka he records that his ancestor Atrigupta was brought to Kashmir from the Gangetic plain by Lalitāditya and settled there with an endowment. The Siddhānta exegetes Rāmakaṇṭha and his father were Kashmiri Brahmins of the same milieu. Sanderson has argued that the ordinary Śaiva ritual of the Valley — the initiation and worship prescribed by the Svacchandatantra and the Netratantra, performed by hereditary family preceptors — formed the religious practice of most Kashmiri Brahmins, including those at court, while the non-dual Trika and Krama were cultivated by a smaller circle of virtuosi (Sanderson 2009, 1988).

Kashmir also supplies the period’s sharpest internal criticism. Kṣemendra (11th century) satirised gurus who exploited the households and officials who patronised them, and Kalhaṇa (12th century) repeatedly censured kings who fell under the influence of self-interested preceptors. Such criticism, from within a Śaiva society, shows that the power of Tantric specialists at court was real enough to provoke resentment. Elements of this culture survive in the domestic religion of Kashmiri Pandits, whose festival of Śivarātri (Herath) includes the worship of Bhairava and of Śiva’s attendants in water-filled pots — a household rite whose structure is Tantric (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 12.9 Beyond India: Champa, Java, Sumatra and Bali
docs.text:
The reach of the Śaiva model is clearest in Southeast Asia, where Indian scriptures and rites were adopted by courts with no Indian population of any size. Apart from Cambodia (Section 12.7), the evidence comes from four regions.

In Champa, in present-day central Vietnam, the sanctuary of My Son housed the royal liṅga Bhadreśvara, named after an early king, Bhadravarman, and later re-established by his successors. The Cham kings were mostly Śaiva, though Indravarman II founded a great Buddhist monastery at Dong Duong in 875.

In Java the Śaiva temple complex of Prambanan, whose foundation is recorded in the Śivagṛha inscription of 856, stood close to the Buddhist Borobudur. A body of Śaiva literature in Sanskrit and Old Javanese, such as the Vṛhaspatitattva, expounds a doctrine of the tattvas, souls and liberation closely related to that of the Siddhānta. In the Majapahit period Mpu Tantular’s Old Javanese poem Sutasoma (14th century) declared that Śiva and the Buddha are one; a phrase from it, bhinneka tunggal ika (“different, yet one”), is now the national motto of Indonesia.

In Sumatra and East Java Tantric Buddhism was also a royal religion. The East Javanese king Kṛtanagara of Singhasari (r. 1268–1292) is remembered for his Tantric Buddhist observances, and a colossal statue from Sumatra is usually identified as the fourteenth-century ruler Ādityavarman in the form of a Buddhist Bhairava.

In Bali Śaiva ritual survives to the present. Balinese Brahmin priests (pedanda) of Śaiva and Buddhist lineages consecrate the holy water on which Balinese religion depends. The Śaiva priest’s daily rite of sūrya-sevana, in which he purifies himself, identifies himself with Śiva by mantra and nyāsa, and worships Śiva in the Sun, preserves in simplified form the structure of the Indian Siddhānta’s daily worship (Hooykaas 1966).

docs.title: 12.10.1 Vaiṣṇavas and Brahmins
docs.text: The Śaiva model did not go unchallenged. Vaiṣṇava kings and preceptors built an equivalent system on the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās, with their own initiation, temple liturgy and royal rites (Chapter 3); in Kashmir the Pāñcarātra had its own royal temples and exegetes, and in the Tamil country the great Vaiṣṇava temples followed the Pāñcarātra or Vaikhānasa liturgies. Brahmin householders of the Smārta tradition, for their part, absorbed Tantric elements into their own domestic and temple worship while keeping their Vedic identity: the worship of five deities (pañcāyatanapūjā), with its nyāsa, mantras and offerings, is Tantric in structure though Vedic in self-image. Sanderson sees in this “Tantricisation” of Brahmanical practice one of the most enduring effects of the Śaiva Age (Sanderson 2009; Bühnemann 1988).

docs.title: 12.10.2 Buddhists
docs.text: Buddhist monasteries had long enjoyed royal support. In eastern India the Pāla kings (8th–12th centuries) were the great patrons of Buddhist learning: Dharmapāla (r. c. 770–810) is credited with founding Vikramaśīla, which became a centre of Tantric study (Chapter 10). Even the Pālas, however, made grants to Brahmins and to Śaiva temples, and the Buddhist Tantras that flourished under them borrowed extensively from Śaiva scripture. Ronald Davidson has emphasised a further parallel. The central Buddhist Tantric rite, the abhiṣeka, takes its name and much of its form from royal consecration: the initiate is consecrated as a king of the maṇḍala, which is itself organised like a royal court, with the central deity surrounded by subordinate lords in the directions. In Davidson’s reading, esoteric Buddhism sacralised the political order of the period, in which overlords presided over circles of vassals (Davidson 2002).

docs.title: 12.10.3 Jains
docs.text: The Jains, a community of merchants and of royal ministers in western and southern India, also competed for and obtained royal favour — most famously at the court of the Caulukya king Kumārapāla of Gujarat (r. 1143–1172), the patron of the monk-scholar Hemacandra. Jain teachers adopted mantra rites, protective goddesses and image consecration in forms that parallel Śaiva practice while rejecting its sacrificial and transgressive elements (Section 10.19).

docs.title: 12.10.4 Lay Śaivism and the Gift
docs.text: Not all Śaiva patronage passed through initiation. A large literature addressed to uninitiated lay devotees, the Śivadharma corpus, taught the merit of building and maintaining temples, of feeding Śaiva ascetics, and of copying manuscripts of Śaiva scripture and presenting them in a solemn “gift of knowledge” (vidyādāna) to a monastery or temple library. Florinda De Simini has shown how these texts, widely copied in Nepal, made the production and donation of manuscripts a religious act in its own right (De Simini 2016). Such teachings gave kings, queens, ministers and merchants a way of earning Śiva’s favour without the obligations of initiation, and they help to explain the scale of Śaiva foundations.

docs.title: 12.10.5 Queens, Ministers and Merchants
docs.text: Patronage was not confined to reigning kings. Queens were among the most active founders. The Chōḷa queen Sembiyaṉ Mahādevī, widow of Gaṇḍarāditya, rebuilt a series of older brick shrines in stone in the later tenth century and endowed bronzes for them, and her foundations anticipate the great royal temples of the following generation. In central India an inscription of the Kalacuri queen Alhaṇadevī at Bheraghat (1155) records a temple of Śiva and a monastery placed in the charge of a Pāśupata ascetic; in Andhra, the Malkāpuram foundation was recorded in the name of the ruling queen Rudramadevī. Ministers, feudatories, merchant guilds and village assemblies endowed lamps, festivals and recitations in temples across the South, as the thousands of Tamil and Kannada temple inscriptions show. The Śaiva Age was thus sustained by a broad elite, not by kings alone.

docs.title: 12.11 Critics and Qualifications
docs.text:
Few scholars have published a sustained critique of the thesis as a whole. The qualifications gathered here come in two kinds. Some address the thesis directly: they question how much the inscriptions can show, or how far the Buddhist Tantras borrowed from the Śaiva. Others come from work on other questions — the Purāṇic religion of the period, the nature of the early medieval state, the politics of Sanskrit and of images — which bears on the thesis without having been written against it. The two should be kept apart.

The weight of the evidence. The first and most direct qualification concerns the sources. Inscriptions record what was given, and to whom; they do not measure what most people believed or practised. The early medieval record also contains abundant Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Buddhist and Jain patronage: the Gupta kings called themselves devotees of Viṣṇu (paramabhāgavata); the Pālas were Buddhists; great Sun temples were built from Multan to Koṇārka; and in Odisha the cult of Jagannātha eventually became the state cult. “Dominance” therefore describes a balance of patronage across a very wide region, not a monopoly in any one place.

Purāṇic and lay Śaivism. Work on other sources bears on the thesis without being directed against it. Hans Bakker’s study of the early Skandapurāṇa shows a Śaivism of the sixth and seventh centuries in northern India that is closely tied to Pāśupata ascetics and to kings, but is Purāṇic rather than Tantric in character (Bakker 2014). Together with the Śivadharma literature, this suggests that much royal and popular Śaivism was carried by devotional and Purāṇic forms in which the Mantramārga was one strand among several.

Feudalism, integration and legitimation. Sanderson’s account intersects with a long debate among historians about the early medieval state. One school, associated with R.S. Sharma, described the period as one of “Indian feudalism”, in which grants to Brahmins, temples and monasteries fragmented royal power; another, associated with Kulke and Chattopadhyaya, saw the same grants as instruments by which states expanded and integrated new regions (see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra). Davidson’s account of Buddhist Tantra builds on the first model; Sanderson’s account of Śaiva monasteries fits easily with the second (Davidson 2002; Chattopadhyaya 1994; Kulke 1993).

Beyond legitimation. Some historians are wary of explaining royal religion as a search for “legitimacy”. Neither of the two works cited here was written as a response to Sanderson, but both bear on his argument. Sheldon Pollock has argued that the political culture of the period expressed itself above all through Sanskrit literary forms common to rulers of every persuasion, so that a king’s choice of god did not by itself determine how his rule was represented (Pollock 2006). Richard Davis has shown that kings could also treat the images of their rivals’ gods as trophies of war, carrying them off to their own capitals; royal relations with the gods were a matter of competitive display as much as of legitimation (Davis 1997). Sanderson’s emphasis on the practical services of Śaiva officiants — protection, consecration, healing, the founding of settlements — partly answers this objection, since it does not depend on a single theory of legitimacy.

Who borrowed from whom? The second direct qualification concerns Buddhist Tantra. The claim that it borrowed from Śaiva scripture rests on detailed textual parallels, and few specialists now doubt that the Buddhist Yoginītantras redacted Śaiva material. Davidson and Samuel, however, emphasise the shared milieu of wandering adepts, goddess cults and local deities from which both drew, and caution against treating every parallel as a one-way loan (Davidson 2002; Samuel 2008).

What is not in dispute is the documentary core of the thesis: the inscriptions that name Śaiva preceptors of kings, the monastic lineages that can be followed across regions, and the ritual forms that passed from Śaiva scripture into other traditions. What remains open is how much weight that evidence can bear for the religion of the period as a whole, beyond the courts and monasteries that produced it.

docs.title: 12.12 The End of the Śaiva Age
docs.text:
From the late twelfth century the conquests of the Ghurids and the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate removed or weakened many of the Hindu dynasties that had patronised Śaiva monasteries in North India. The great endowed monasteries could not survive without their villages, and the lineages that had supplied preceptors to courts disappeared from the record. In Kashmir the Śaiva traditions continued under local rulers into the fourteenth century and survived thereafter in Brahmin families (Chapter 6).

Elsewhere the religious landscape shifted towards devotional Vaiṣṇavism and towards Brahmanical orders centred on Advaita Vedānta, such as the monastery of Śṛṅgerī, which enjoyed the patronage of the Vijayanagara kings from the fourteenth century. In the Tamil country the Śaiva Siddhānta survived as the liturgy of the temples, administered by hereditary ādiśaiva priests, and as a Tamil theology cultivated in the non-Brahmin ātīṉams (Chapter 2); in Nepal and Bali Śaiva ritual remained tied to the royal court and to priestly families until modern times. The Śaiva Age ended, but its ritual forms, absorbed into temple liturgy, Smārta worship and the practice of other traditions, did not.

docs.title: 12.13 After the Śaiva Age: Tantric Power at Later Courts
docs.text:
The decline of royal Śaiva monasticism did not end the interest of rulers in the powers that Tantric specialists claimed. Under the Vijayanagara kings and their successors the royal festival of the Goddess flourished (Section 12.5); in Assam the Ahom kings made Kāmākhyā a state cult; in Nepal the Malla and Shah kings maintained the secret worship of Taleju; and at Jodhpur a Rajput king handed his kingdom’s religious life to the Nāth yogis (Chapter 13).

Islamicate courts were not untouched. Persian translations and adaptations of yogic and Tantric material were made from the sixteenth century, and Sufis and Nāth yogis met and competed at shrines and courts (Section 13.12.1) (Ernst 2003). At Bijapur in the Deccan an illustrated encyclopaedia of the sciences, the Nujūm al-‘ulūm (1570), includes depictions of yoginīs among its treatments of astrology and magic, and Bijapur painters produced celebrated images of yoginīs as figures of beauty and power. The Mughal emperors, beginning with Akbar, issued grants to the Nāth yogis of Jakhbar in the Punjab, whose monastery preserved a series of imperial and later documents confirming its lands (Goswamy and Grewal 1967). None of this amounts to a “Tantric” state; but it shows that the yogi and the Tantric adept remained figures whom rulers of many faiths thought worth cultivating long after the Śaiva Age had passed.

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Tantric scriptures present themselves as universal revelation, but they were practised in particular places, in particular languages and under particular kings. Over the centuries each region of South Asia developed its own Tantric culture: its own manuals and digests, its own hereditary specialists, its own sacred geography and its own relation between Sanskrit ritual and local goddesses, spirits and performers. Much of what is now encountered as “Tantra” — the Kerala temple tantrī, the Bengali Kālī Pūjā, the menstruating goddess of Kāmākhyā, the masked goddesses of Bhaktapur — is regional in this sense.

This chapter surveys Kerala, Bengal, Assam, Odisha, Nepal, the goddess shrines of Kashmir and the north-western hills, Rajasthan and Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka, the Deccan centre of Śrīśailam, and the Tamil country, and ends with the orders of Nātha yogis and Siddhas that moved between all of them. Figure 13.1 locates the principal places named here and in the chapters on the Goddess and on the Śaiva Age. Kashmir, the home of the non-dual Śaiva exegetes, is treated in Chapter 6; the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta in Chapter 2; the Śrīvidyā of the South in Chapter 5; and Newar Buddhism in Chapter 10. Here the emphasis falls on what is distinctive in each region, with cross-references where a topic is treated elsewhere in the volume. Table 13.1 summarises the comparison.

Figure 13.1. Principal places named in this volume, above all in Chapters 4, 12 and 13. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude on the frame and simplified coastline used in Volume 12; islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, no political boundaries are shown, and places outside the frame (Kashmir, Swat, Vaiṣṇo Devī, Hiṅglāj) are indicated at its edge. docs.title: 13.2.1 Tantrīs and Temples
docs.text: Kerala has the most fully preserved regional system of Tantric temple ritual outside the Tamil country, and it differs from the Tamil system in important ways. There is no separate caste of Āgamic temple priests corresponding to the Tamil ādiśaivas. Instead, ritual authority over each major temple belongs to a family of Nampūtiri Brahmins who hold the hereditary right (tantram) to be its tantrī. The tantrī performs the great rites — consecration, reconsecration, the annual festival and expiations — and is the final authority on ritual questions; daily worship is performed by other Brahmin priests called śāntis, under a chief priest (mēlśānti) and assistants (kīḻśānti). The family of Ceṉṉās, to which the author of the Tantrasamuccaya belonged, holds the tantram of the Krishna temple at Guruvāyūr; other families hold it for other temples, and a single family may serve many temples (Section 9.9.2).

docs.title: 13.2.2 The Tantrasamuccaya and Its Predecessors
docs.text: The Tantrasamuccaya of Ceṉṉās Nārāyaṇaṉ Nampūtiri (15th century) became the standard authority for Kerala temple ritual. Written in Sanskrit verse, it covers the whole life of a temple for seven deities: the testing and preparation of the site, the making of the image, its installation (pratiṣṭhā), the daily and periodic worship, the annual festival, expiatory rites for the many kinds of pollution and accident that can befall a temple, and renovation (see Chapter 9 for its seven deities and its role in modern disputes). It drew on older Kerala manuals of Śaiva ritual, notably the Prayogamañjarī of Ravi and the encyclopaedic Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, probably also of Kerala origin, a compendium in four parts dealing with general matters, mantras, ritual and yoga, which preserves material from older Śaiva scriptures, some now lost. Through these manuals the Siddhānta ritual system was adapted to Kerala’s distinctive temple architecture and to its Nampūtiri priesthood.

docs.title: 13.2.3 Distinctive Features of Kerala Ritual
docs.text: Kerala temples have a characteristic layout: the shrine stands within a square cloister (nālambalam), around which are set the stones (balikkal) that represent the deity’s attendants and the guardians of the directions. Several times a day, in the rite called śrībhūtabali, a priest carries a portable image or a metal plate bearing the deity’s form (tiṭampu) around the shrine, while another offers cooked rice to each of these stones, so that the whole retinue of the deity is fed. Daily worship is divided into a series of services from before dawn to night. The annual festival (utsavam) opens with the hoisting of the flag on the temple’s flagstaff (koṭiyēṟṟam) and closes with the ritual bath of the deity in a river or tank (āṟāṭṭu); in between, the deity is carried in procession, in central Kerala often on caparisoned elephants with the tiṭampu mounted on the leading animal. Gilles Tarabout’s study of Kerala temple festivals shows how these Āgamic rites interlock with the performances and offerings of many non-Brahmin communities (Tarabout 1986).

docs.title: 13.2.4 The Goddess in Kerala
docs.text:
Alongside the Brahmin temple ritual, Kerala has rich traditions of goddess worship performed by non-Brahmin specialists. Bhadrakālī, the fierce goddess who in Kerala myth slays the demon Dārika, is worshipped in temples and sacred groves (kāvu) and in two forms of ritual art. In kaḷameḻuttu large floor drawings of the goddess are made in powders of five colours, prepared from rice flour, turmeric, burnt husk, green leaves and a red mixture of turmeric and lime; the drawing is worshipped with songs and lamps through the night and then ritually erased. Muṭiyēṟṟu, a ritual dance-drama performed in Bhadrakālī temples of central Kerala after the harvest, enacts the goddess’s battle with Dārika; it was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010.

Sarah Caldwell’s ethnography of Muṭiyēṟṟu shows how its performers, who embody the goddess, combine Tantric ideas of power with local understandings of heat, anger and female sexuality (Caldwell 1999). In North Kerala, teyyam performers of low-status communities embody goddesses and heroes in the same way (Section 4.7). Kerala also had a strong tradition of mantravāda, protective and exorcistic rites practised by both Brahmin and non-Brahmin families with manuals in Sanskrit and Malayalam.

docs.title: 13.2.5 Caste and Access
docs.text: The Nampūtiri monopoly of temple ritual was bound up with one of the most rigid caste orders in India, in which many communities could not enter or even approach temples. The Vaikom Satyagraha of 1924–25, for the right to use the roads around the Vaikom temple, the Guruvāyūr Satyagraha of 1931–32 and the Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 were landmarks in the struggle for access. In 1888 the reformer Nārāyaṇa Guru consecrated an image of Śiva at Aruvippuram, challenging the Brahmin claim to an exclusive right to perform consecration. In 2017 the Travancore Devaswom Board appointed non-Brahmin priests, including Dalits, to its temples after a qualifying examination in the ritual system — a development that, like the Tamil Nadu legislation discussed in Section 11.10, turns on who may be trained in the Āgamic tradition.

docs.title: 13.3 Bengal
docs.text: Bengal’s prominence in modern images of Tantra has a history. In the Buddhist period under the Pālas it was a centre of Tantric Buddhism (Chapter 10); from the sixteenth century it became the home of a distinctive Śākta culture in which learned digests, vernacular poetry, zamīndār patronage and village goddess worship were closely interwoven. The cult of Kālī, the Tantric Vaiṣṇavism of the Sahajiyās and Bāuls, and the nineteenth-century encounter with colonial critics are treated in Chapters 4, 3 and 14.

docs.title: 13.3.1 The Digests
docs.text:
The Bengali Tantric tradition is above all a tradition of compilation. Its authors collected passages from older Tantras, many of which survive only in these quotations, and arranged them as practical handbooks for initiates. Brahmānanda Giri (16th century) wrote the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī, a manual of Śākta practice, and the Tārārahasya on the worship of Tārā. Pūrṇānanda, by tradition his pupil, completed the Śrītattvacintāmaṇi in 1577; its sixth chapter, the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, is the source of the modern six-cakra system through Arthur Avalon’s The Serpent Power (Avalon 1919). Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa of Navadvīpa (late 16th or 17th century) compiled the Tantrasāra, a large compendium of the mantras, meditations and worship of the principal deities, which became the standard ritual handbook of Bengali Śāktas and remains in print (McDaniel 2004).

These works are learned, Brahmanical and, for the most part, right-handed in their public prescriptions; they present the Kaula rites, where they include them, within a framework of initiation and qualification.

docs.title: 13.3.2 Pīṭhas, Poets and Patrons
docs.text:
Bengal developed a dense sacred geography of goddess sites. Late lists of the fifty-one śāktapīṭhas, such as the Pīṭhanirṇaya, place a large number in Bengal and its borderlands, each with its goddess and her guardian Bhairava (Sircar 1973). Tārāpīṭh in Birbhum, with its cremation ground, became famous through the ascetic Vāmākṣepā (Bāmākhepā, 1837–1911), whose eccentric devotion to Tārā made him the model of the “mad” saint of Bengali Śāktism (McDaniel 2004).

Vernacular narrative poetry carried the goddesses to a wide audience. The maṅgalkābyas, long Bengali poems in praise of a deity, include Mukundarām Cakrabartī’s Caṇḍīmaṅgal (late 16th century), and Bhāratcandra Rāy’s Annadāmaṅgal (1752–53), written at the court of Mahārājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia (r. 1728–1782). Kṛṣṇacandra, the patron also of Rāmprasād Sen, is remembered as a promoter of Kālī and Jagaddhātrī worship. In the eighteenth century, as Rachel McDermott and June McDaniel have described, the goddess worship of the landholding elite and the devotional songs of Rāmprasād transformed the fierce Kālī of the Tantras into a mother to be loved (Section 4.11) (McDermott 2001; McDaniel 2004).

docs.title: 13.4.1 Kāmarūpa in Tantric Geography
docs.text: Kāmarūpa, the ancient name of western Assam, appears in early Kaula texts as one of the four principal seats of the Goddess (Section 4.4), and its temple of Kāmākhyā is today the most famous of the pīṭhas. On the Nīlācala hill around the main temple stand shrines of the ten Mahāvidyās, so that the hill as a whole forms a map of the later Śākta pantheon (Section 4.3).

docs.title: 13.4.2 The Kālikā Purāṇa and the Yoginī Tantra
docs.text: Two texts above all express the Tantric culture of Assam. The Kālikā Purāṇa (c. 10th–11th century), an upapurāṇa composed in the region, tells the story of Kāmākhyā, describes the sacred geography of Kāmarūpa, and gives detailed rules for goddess worship, including the worship of the Goddess by kings and the rules of blood sacrifice. Its chapter on blood offerings, translated into English at the end of the eighteenth century in the journal Asiatick Researches, became one of the most cited texts in colonial descriptions of Hindu “barbarism” and a staple of later polemics. The Yoginī Tantra (c. 16th–17th century) glorifies Kāmarūpa as the supreme sacred land, describes its pīṭhas and rivers, and includes legendary accounts of the region’s rulers (Urban 2010).

docs.title: 13.4.3 Kings, Priests and Their Critics
docs.text:
Kāmākhyā’s history is closely tied to royal power. The present temple was rebuilt in the sixteenth century under the Koch king Naranārāyaṇa, and its cult was later patronised by the Ahom kings. The Ahom kings, originally Tai rulers with their own religion, increasingly adopted Śākta Hinduism. Rudra Siṃha (r. 1696–1714) invited a Bengali Śākta Brahmin, Kṛṣṇarām Bhaṭṭācārya of Nadia, to his court, and under his son Śiva Siṃha (r. 1714–1744) the priest’s family received charge of the Nīlācala temples; their descendants were known as the “mountain” (Parbatiyā) Gosāīs. Śiva Siṃha’s queen Phuleśvarī, who governed in his name, is remembered in the Assamese chronicles for compelling the heads of Vaiṣṇava monasteries to take part in Śākta rites, a grievance that contributed to later unrest (Urban 2010).

The tensions had deep roots. In the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the Assamese saint Śaṅkaradeva (traditional dates 1449–1568) had founded a Vaiṣṇava devotional movement, the ekasaraṇa dharma (“religion of refuge in the One”), which rejected the worship of other deities and the blood sacrifices of the Śāktas, and organised its followers around monasteries (satras) and village prayer halls. Assam thus offers an unusually clear case of a devotional critique of Tantric goddess worship, institutionalised and sustained over centuries. Kāmākhyā itself remains a centre of living Śākta practice, with daily animal sacrifice and the annual Ambubācī festival, which now draws very large numbers of pilgrims and ascetics.

docs.title: 13.5.1 Śaiva and Śākta Bhubaneswar
docs.text: Odisha preserves a remarkable sequence of early medieval monuments that document the Tantric traditions in stone. At Bhubaneswar the Paraśurāmeśvara temple (c. 7th century) carries images of Lakulīśa, the founder of the Pāśupatas (Section 2.1.6). The Vaitāl Deul (8th century), with its barrel-vaulted roof, is a temple of the Goddess as Cāmuṇḍā: its sanctum image shows the emaciated goddess seated on a corpse, and its walls carry fierce mātṛkās and Bhairava forms. Odisha also has two of the finest yoginī temples, at Hirapur near Bhubaneswar and Ranipur-Jharial in the west (Section 4.10).

docs.title: 13.5.2 Buddhist Tantra in Odisha
docs.text: The monasteries of Ratnagiri, Lalitagiri and Udayagiri, in the Jajpur and Cuttack districts, flourished from about the seventh to the twelfth century, and Ratnagiri in particular has yielded a large body of Vajrayāna sculpture. Some scholars have identified Odisha with Oḍḍiyāna, the land celebrated in Buddhist Tantric literature as a source of revelation; most now locate Oḍḍiyāna in the Swat valley of present-day Pakistan, but the debate illustrates how important Odisha was to the eastern Indian Buddhist world (Davidson 2002).

docs.title: 13.5.3 Jagannātha and the Goddess
docs.text:
The cult of Jagannātha at Purī, which became the state cult of the Gaṅga and Gajapati kings, is primarily Vaiṣṇava, but it has strong Tantric and tribal elements (Eschmann et al. 1978). The wooden images are periodically replaced in the rite of navakalevara (“new body”), in which the sacred substance believed to dwell in the old image is transferred secretly to the new one by the daitās, servitors who trace their descent from the tribal Śabaras credited in the temple’s legend with first worshipping the god. The goddess Vimalā has a shrine within the temple compound; food offered to Jagannātha becomes the sacred mahāprasāda only after it has also been offered to her, and Purī appears in the Śākta lists of pīṭhas, with Jagannātha as the guardian Bhairava of the Goddess. Parts of the temple’s daily and festival liturgy, too, follow Tantric patterns of nyāsa, mantra and worship.

The essays collected by Anncharlott Eschmann, Hermann Kulke and Gaya Charan Tripathi showed how a tribal deity was progressively “Hinduised” and made the centre of a regional state; its political dimension is discussed in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra.

docs.title: 13.5.4 Vernacular Mysticism and Its Critics
docs.text: In the sixteenth century five Odia poets, remembered as the Pañcasakhā (“five friends”) — Balārāma Dāsa, Jagannātha Dāsa, Acyutānanda Dāsa, Ananta Dāsa and Yaśovanta Dāsa — created a body of devotional and esoteric literature in Odia. Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa became the most widely read religious book in the region. Alongside their devotion to Jagannātha, several of these poets taught a yoga of the body and a doctrine of the “void” (śūnya) as the ultimate reality, ideas that scholars have related to the region’s older Tantric Buddhist and Nāth traditions. In the nineteenth century the Mahimā Dharma, founded by Mahimā Gosāī and given voice by the poet Bhīma Bhoi, went further: it rejected image worship, the authority of the Brahmin priesthood and, explicitly, the worship of Jagannātha, in favour of devotion to a formless absolute. Odisha thus shows, within a single region, the full range from state-sponsored temple Tantra to its esoteric reinterpretation and its outright rejection.

docs.title: 13.6 Nepal
docs.text: The Kathmandu Valley is the one region of South Asia where the Śaiva, Śākta and Buddhist Tantric traditions of early medieval India have survived continuously in the practice of a single urban society, that of the Newars. Its royal goddess Taleju, the cult of the living Kumārī and the Kubjikā tradition are introduced in Section 4.7, and Newar Buddhism in Section 10.17.

docs.title: 13.6.1 Paśupati and the Śaiva Kingdom
docs.text: The temple of Paśupati near Kathmandu has been the principal Śaiva shrine of Nepal since at least the Licchavi period, when kings described themselves in their inscriptions as favoured by the god (Section 12.3). By long-standing custom its chief priests are Brahmins from South India, from Karnataka, rather than local Brahmins. The adjacent shrine of Guhyeśvarī, regarded as a pīṭha of the Goddess, makes the site a meeting place of Śaiva and Śākta worship.

docs.title: 13.6.2 Secret Shrines and Lineage Deities
docs.text: Among the Newars, Tantric initiation is a family and caste matter. High-caste Hindu Newars, served by Rājopādhyāya Brahmins and Karmācārya Tantric priests, receive initiation into the worship of a lineage deity — often a form of the Goddess — whose image is kept in a secret shrine, the āgaṃ (from āgama), which only initiated members of the lineage may enter. Buddhist Newars have equivalent āgaṃ shrines of Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī, served by Vajrācārya priests. The public face of temple worship and the esoteric face of the lineage shrine thus coexist within the same households (Gellner 1992; Levy 1990).

docs.title: 13.6.3 The Navadurgā of Bhaktapur
docs.text: Robert Levy’s study of Bhaktapur showed how an entire city could be organised as a Tantric “mesocosm”, a structured world mediating between the individual and the cosmos. The city’s boundaries are guarded by shrines of the eight mother goddesses (aṣṭamātṛkā) set around it in the directions, with a ninth at the centre, so that the city is laid out as a maṇḍala. Each year a troupe of masked dancers from a caste of gardeners embodies the Navadurgā — nine goddesses with Gaṇeśa, Bhairava and other figures — and tours the city, receiving offerings, including blood offerings, and performing dramas. The masks are made anew each year and, at the end of the cycle, ritually disposed of, as if the goddesses had lived a life and died (Levy 1990).

docs.title: 13.6.4 Kubjikā and the Survival of Texts
docs.text: The Western Transmission of the hunchbacked goddess Kubjikā (Section 4.11), almost extinct in India, survives in Newar initiatory practice, and its scriptures are preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. Mark Dyczkowski’s study of the Kubjikā corpus showed how these texts reorganised earlier Śaiva and Kaula material into a new system with its own yoga, mantras and ritual (Dyczkowski 1988). Nepal’s libraries, which preserve the oldest manuscripts of the Niśvāsa, the Brahmayāmala and many other Tantras (Section 1.7), have made the Valley the single most important source for the recovery of the early Tantric literature.

docs.title: 13.7 Kashmir and the North-western Hills
docs.text:
The philosophy and ritual of the Kashmiri Śaivas are treated in Chapter 6. Less often noticed are the goddess shrines of Kashmir and the neighbouring hills, which give the Śākta side of the region’s Tantric culture a living geography.

Kashmir. Three goddess sites have been central to Kashmiri Pandit religion. On the hill of Hari Parbat in Srinagar the goddess Śārikā is worshipped in the form of a rock regarded as a self-manifested Śrīcakra. At Tulamulla, the goddess Rāgñā (Khīr Bhavānī) is worshipped at a spring whose changing colours are read as omens. Farther north, in the Neelum valley in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, lie the ruins of the temple of Śāradā, a renowned seat of the Goddess and of learning, after whom the Śāradā script of Kashmir is named. Kashmiri Pandit families continue to worship these goddesses with rites that draw on the Tantric literature of the Valley, and the annual festival at Tulamulla has become a focus of the displaced Pandit community since 1990.

The hills of Jammu, Himachal and Punjab. A circuit of goddess shrines in the Siwalik hills — among them Vaiṣṇo Devī near Jammu, Jvālāmukhī with its natural flames, Kangra’s Vajreśvarī, Cintapūrṇī and Nainā Devī — draws millions of pilgrims from northern India. At Vaiṣṇo Devī the goddess is worshipped in a cave as three natural rock forms (piṇḍīs) identified with Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī, the three forms of the Devīmāhātmya. Kathleen Erndl’s study of these cults showed how a Śākta theology derived from the Devīmāhātmya and the pīṭha myths combines with popular practices such as possession by the goddess (khelnā, “playing”), most often experienced by women, which gives them a religious authority otherwise rarely available to them (Erndl 1993). Most of this worship is vegetarian and Vaiṣṇava in tone, though some shrines retained animal sacrifice; the Tantric element lies less in Kaula ritual than in the shared vocabulary of pīṭha, śakti and the Goddess’s power to enter and act through human bodies.

docs.title: 13.8 Rajasthan and Gujarat
docs.text: In western India Tantric religion took two characteristic forms: the cult of lineage goddesses closely tied to Rajput kingship, and the patronage of Nāth yogis.

docs.title: 13.8.1 Lineage Goddesses and Their Shrines
docs.text: Each Rajput clan honours a lineage goddess (kuladevī) as the protector of its land and rule, worshipped at the clan’s principal shrine and in the household, above all at Navarātri. Lindsey Harlan’s study of Rajput women showed how this goddess, who protects the lineage in war, is also the model and guardian of the women who maintain the household’s ritual life (Harlan 1992). Several goddess shrines of the region are distinctive. Karṇī Mātā at Deshnok near Bikaner, a deified woman of the Cāraṇ community of bards, is the patron goddess of the Rāṭhōṛ rulers of Bikaner; her temple is famous for the rats that live in it, which are regarded as members of her family. Śilā Devī, the goddess of the Kachvāhā rulers of Amber, is said to have been brought from eastern Bengal by Mān Siṃh I about 1600, together with Bengali priests — an instance of the movement of Tantric specialists between regions. Ambājī, in the Aravalli hills on the Gujarat–Rajasthan border, one of the great goddess shrines of western India, has no anthropomorphic image in its sanctum: a yantra is worshipped in its place. And Bahucarā Mātā, near Mehsana in Gujarat, is the patron goddess of the hijrā communities, whose members regard their renunciation of male identity as service to her.

docs.title: 13.8.2 The Nāths at Jodhpur
docs.text: The Nāth yogis (Section 13.12) were influential at several Rajput courts. At Jodhpur, Mahārājā Mān Siṃh (r. 1803–1843), who believed he owed his throne to the prophecy of a Nāth guru, made the Nāths the dominant religious power of his kingdom, building their monastery (Mahāmandir) and granting them great estates. The court painters he patronised produced a remarkable series of paintings of Nāth cosmology, yoga and hagiography, including images of the absolute as a field of pure colour, which are among the most original works of Indian Tantric art (Diamond et al. 2008). After Mān Siṃh’s death the Nāths’ power was curtailed, under British pressure, by his successor.

docs.title: 13.9 Maharashtra and Karnataka
docs.text: The western Deccan has no single Tantric scripture of its own, but it shows with unusual clarity how Nātha yoga, goddess worship and Āgamic temple ritual were absorbed into regional devotional religion.

docs.title: 13.9.1 Nāthas, Dattātreya and the Marathi Saints
docs.text:
The Marathi devotional tradition traces its origin to the Nāthas. Jñāneśvar (Jñānadev), whose Marathi commentary on the Bhagavadgītā, the Jñāneśvarī, is dated 1290, gives his own lineage at its close as running from Ādinātha through Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha to Gahinīnātha, and from him to his elder brother and guru Nivṛttinātha. In its sixth chapter, on meditation, the work describes the awakening of kuṇḍalinī and its ascent through the body in some of the most celebrated passages of Marathi literature. Yet the same poet became the founding figure of the Vārkarī devotion to Viṭhṭhal of Pandharpur, which values the singing of the divine name above yogic technique; the Nātha inheritance was thus remembered as a lineage and reinterpreted as devotion (see Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā, for the poetry).

A second strand is the cult of Dattātreya, the ascetic sage regarded as a combined form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva and as the guru of gurus. Dattātreya appears in the Purāṇas as a teacher of yoga who behaves like an intoxicated, unconventional avadhūta and enjoys wine and women without being touched by them — a figure with clear affinities to the Tantric adept. He was claimed by the Nāthas, by the Mahānubhāvas founded by Cakradhar in the thirteenth century, and by the Datta tradition proper, whose Gurucaritra recounts the lives of the saints Śrīpāda Śrīvallabha and Narasiṃha Sarasvatī, the latter associated with the pilgrimage centre of Gāṇagāpur. A haṭha-yoga text, the Dattātreyayogaśāstra (Section 13.12), is presented as his teaching. Antonio Rigopoulos has traced how the unconventional yogin of the early sources became the gentle, three-headed guru of modern Maharashtrian devotion (Rigopoulos 1998).

docs.title: 13.9.2 The Goddesses of the Western Deccan
docs.text:
Maharashtrian tradition counts “three and a half” seats of the Goddess: Mahālakṣmī (Ambābāī) at Kolhapur, Bhavānī at Tuljapur, Reṇukā at Mahur, and, as the “half” seat, Saptaśṛṅgī at Vani. Tuljapur’s role as the lineage goddess of Śivājī is discussed in Section 12.5. Their worship includes the gondhaḷ, an all-night ritual performance of songs and narratives for the goddess (see Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya), and the offerings of hereditary priests rather than the elaborate Āgamic liturgy of the Tamil temples.

The goddess Reṇukā, worshipped as Yellamma at Saundatti in northern Karnataka, shows both the power and the social cost of such cults. Her myth makes her the mother of Paraśurāma, beheaded at the command of her husband Jamadagni and restored to life, and she is often worshipped in the form of a head. Her cult was long associated with the dedication of girls, mostly of Dalit families, as jogatis or devadāsīs, bound to the goddess and frequently drawn into sexual exploitation. Karnataka prohibited such dedication by law in 1982, and Maharashtra later passed similar legislation, but reports of continuing dedications show that law alone has not ended the practice. The case belongs to the wider history of temple women and its abolition (Section 11.10.3).

docs.title: 13.9.3 Karnataka: Monasteries and the Udupi Rotation
docs.text: Karnataka was the home of the Kālāmukha monasteries and of the Vīraśaivas, whose rejection of temple ritual was described in Chapter 2. It also produced a distinctive Vaiṣṇava ritual tradition. Madhva (c. 1238–1317; traditionally 1199–1278), the founder of the dualist (Dvaita) school of Vedānta, wrote a ritual digest, the Tantrasārasaṅgraha, which regulates mantra, worship and temple ritual for his followers, and he installed the image of Kṛṣṇa at Udupi. The worship there has been conducted ever since by the heads of eight monasteries in rotation (paryāya), each now holding office for two years (a period fixed, according to tradition, in the sixteenth century), so that a group of renunciant śāstric scholars rather than a hereditary priestly caste controls the temple ritual. On the coast, the same region preserves the worship of bhūtas, local spirit-deities who are embodied by non-Brahmin performers in the night-long bhūta kola, alongside the Brahmanical temples — another instance of the coexistence of learned and local religion observed in Kerala and Odisha.

docs.title: 13.10 Andhra and the Deccan: Śrīśailam
docs.text:
Śrīśailam (Śrīparvata), in the forested hills above the Krishna river, is one of the oldest and most varied Tantric centres of the Deccan. Its temple of Mallikārjuna is one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas of Śiva, and its goddess Bhramarāmbā is counted among the Śākta pīṭhas. Literary sources associate the mountain with Kāpālikas and other Tantric adepts: in Bhavabhūti’s Mālatīmādhava, for instance, the female adept Saudāminī has gained her powers at Śrīparvata (Section 2.1.6). Later tradition made it a haunt of Siddhas and alchemists, and legends of the alchemist Nāgārjuna (distinct from the Buddhist philosopher) were attached to the region. In the later medieval period it became a major Vīraśaiva centre, one of the five seats (pīṭhas) of the Vīraśaiva teachers, and it received the patronage of the Kākatīyas, Reḍḍis and Vijayanagara kings. The Golakī foundation at Malkāpuram (Section 12.6) lay in the same region of the Krishna valley.
