docs.title: 13.11 The Tamil Country: The Tirumantiram and the Siddhas
docs.text:
The Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta, the Nāyaṉmārs and the later Siddha poets are treated in Chapter 2 and below. One text, however, stands between Sanskrit Tantra and Tamil devotion and deserves separate notice: the Tirumantiram (“Sacred Mantra”), ascribed to Tirumūlar and placed as the tenth book of the Śaiva canon, the Tirumuṟai (Zvelebil 1975).

The legend and the date. According to the Periyapurāṇam, Tirumūlar was a yogi from Kailāsa who, travelling in the Tamil country, entered the body of a dead cowherd named Mūlaṉ out of pity for his grieving cows, and remained in it to compose the work, at the rate of one verse a year. Tradition therefore makes the text very old. Modern estimates range from about the sixth to the twelfth century. The work’s familiarity with developed Tantric doctrine — the Āgamas by name, the categories of the Siddhānta, a yoga of cakras and kuṇḍalinī, diagrams made of syllables, and the worship of a goddess in forms close to those of the Śākta Tantras — has led many scholars to favour a date late in this range, and the text as we have it may be composite (Zvelebil 1975).

Contents. The Tirumantiram consists of about three thousand quatrains in nine books (tantiram), a structure that itself recalls the Sanskrit scriptures. It treats Śiva, souls and bonds; morality and the dangers of attachment; a yoga of eight limbs that includes breath control and the raising of inner power; mantras and their diagrams (cakkaram); the grace of Śiva and the guru; and the states of the liberated. Several of its verses are among the most quoted in Tamil religious literature. One declares that love and Śiva are not two; another, that those who let the body perish lose the soul as well, and that the poet learnt to preserve the body and so preserved the soul; another, that the heart is the great shrine and the body of flesh the temple; and a much-quoted line proclaims that humanity is one family and God is one.

Significance. The Tirumantiram shows that the Sanskrit Tantric world view — initiation, mantra, yoga of the subtle body, the identification of body and temple — was rendered into Tamil verse and absorbed into the Tamil Śaiva canon. It became an authority both for the Siddhānta theologians and for the Siddha poets who rejected temple ritual, and it remains a point of reference for modern Tamil Śaivism.

docs.title: 13.11.1 The Tamil Siddhas
docs.text:
The Tamil country has its own tradition of cittar (from Sanskrit siddha), poet-yogis whose verses are among the most radical in Indian religious literature. Tradition counts eighteen Siddhas (patiṉeṇ cittar), but the lists differ, and the poems collected under the names of figures such as Civavākkiyar, Pāmpāṭṭi Cittar, Iṭaikkāṭar, Akappēy Cittar and Paṭṭiṉattār are difficult to date; most are probably late medieval or early modern, though Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram is often regarded as their precursor (Zvelebil 1973).

Written in plain, colloquial Tamil, the Siddha poems ridicule image worship, temple ritual, pilgrimage, the authority of the Vedas and the claims of caste and of the Brahmin priesthood, and they locate the divine within the body, to be realised through yoga, breath control and the raising of kuṇḍalinī. Many Siddhas are also credited with alchemy and medicine. The Tamil Siddha system of medicine (citta maruttuvam), now one of the officially recognised systems of medicine in India, traces itself to them and uses mineral and metallic as well as herbal preparations, and legend credits the Siddha Pōkar with making the image of Murukaṉ at Paḻaṉi. The Siddhas thus share the Nāthas’ concern with the perfected body, while their critique of caste and ritual recalls that of the Vīraśaiva poets (Section 2.10). The safety note in Section 13.12.2 applies equally to Siddha mineral preparations.

docs.title: 13.12 Orders across the Regions: The Nātha Yogis
docs.text: The Nātha or Kānphatā yogis, who trace their lineage to Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha (probably 11th–13th centuries), are an order of Śaiva ascetics whose traditions bridge Kaula Tantra and haṭha yoga. Matsyendranātha is honoured as the founder of a Kaula tradition, and a Kaulajñānanirṇaya is ascribed to him. The Nāthas became the principal exponents of haṭha yoga, with its techniques of posture, breath control, “seals” (mudrās) and “locks” (bandhas) aimed at the raising of kuṇḍalinī and the preservation of vital fluid, and with a goal of bodily immortality and powers. Recent research has shown, however, that the earliest haṭha texts, such as the Amṛtasiddhi (11th century) and the Dattātreyayogaśāstra (13th century), arose in Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava as well as Śaiva milieus; the Haṭhapradīpikā of Svātmārāma (15th century) compiled these earlier teachings (Mallinson and Singleton 2017); see Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī, for haṭha yoga itself. The Nāthas were open to men of all castes and attracted a large popular following, and the lists of the “nine Nāthas” vary from region to region.

docs.title: 13.12.1 Nāthas, Sufis and Sants
docs.text:
From the thirteenth century the Nāthas were among the most visible religious figures of North India, and their ideas crossed religious boundaries. A treatise on yoga called the Amṛtakuṇḍa (“Pool of Nectar”), now lost in its original form, was translated into Arabic and Persian; the Persian version, the Baḥr al-ḥayāt (“Ocean of Life”) of the Shaṭṭārī Sufi Muḥammad Ghawth Gwāliyārī (d. 1563), describes yogic postures, breath control and the recitation of mantras alongside the Sufi practice of remembrance (dhikr). Carl Ernst has shown how these translations recast yoga in Islamic terms while preserving much of its technical content (Ernst 2003). In the same milieu the songs of Kabīr and other Sants drew on Nātha vocabulary — the “unstruck” sound, the central channel, the inner nectar — while rejecting the ritual of both Hindus and Muslims, and Nāth yogis appear frequently in Persian chronicles and in Mughal painting. These exchanges are a reminder that the yogic and Tantric traditions were never confined to a single religious community.

The Sikh scripture preserves the most direct record of such an exchange. The Siddh Goṣṭ (“Discourse with the Siddhas”), a long composition of Guru Nānak (1469–1539) in the section of the Ādi Granth devoted to the rāga Rāmkalī, presents a dialogue in verse between Nānak and Nāth yogis, in which the yogis question him about his path and he answers that liberation comes not from the yogi’s earrings, ash, patched coat and bodily disciplines, nor from withdrawal from the world, but from the divine Name and the Word received through the Guru, by one who lives as a householder. Nānak’s hymns elsewhere take over and reinterpret Nāth vocabulary — the “unstruck” sound, the “tenth door” at the crown of the head, the “innate” state (sahaj). W.H. McLeod showed how the Nāth tradition formed both the background and the foil of Nānak’s teaching (McLeod 1968); the Sikh tradition as a whole lies outside the scope of this volume.

docs.title: 13.12.2 Tantra and Alchemy
docs.text:
Indian alchemy (rasaśāstra, “the science of mercury”) developed in close association with the Tantric and Nātha traditions from about the tenth century. Works such as the Rasahṛdayatantra of Govinda and the Rasārṇava present alchemy as a path to liberation in a perfected, immortal body: mercury is identified with the semen of Śiva and sulphur with the menstrual blood of the Goddess, and the alchemist’s “killing” and “binding” of mercury parallels the yogin’s mastery of breath and seed. David Gordon White has described this “alchemical body” as a meeting point of Tantra, haṭha yoga and medicine (White 1996). Rasaśāstra later became part of Āyurvedic pharmacy, where mercurial and other metallic preparations (bhasmas) are still made.

Health and Safety Note

Classical alchemical and rasaśāstra preparations contain mercury, lead, arsenic and other toxic metals. Studies of Āyurvedic products sold in the United States and over the internet found detectable heavy metals in about a fifth of those tested, in some cases at levels exceeding safety limits, and products containing rasa ingredients were especially likely to be contaminated (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). No recipe in the alchemical texts should be prepared or taken; the account here is historical only.

docs.title: 13.13 Regional Patterns
docs.text:
Table 13.1 compares the regional traditions surveyed in this chapter.

Four patterns stand out. First, everywhere the Sanskrit Tantric system was adapted to a regional priesthood and to regional kings: the Nampūtiri tantrī, the Bengali digest-writer, the Kāmākhyā priest and the Newar Rājopādhyāya are all local specialists in a pan-Indian discipline. Second, in every region learned Tantric ritual coexists with non-Brahmin performers and local deities — teyyam and muṭiyēṟṟu dancers, the daitās of Purī, the masked Navadurgā — who embody the gods in ways the Sanskrit texts only partly control. Third, regional traditions generated their own critics: the Ekasaraṇa movement of Assam, the Bengali Vaiṣṇavas, the Tamil Siddhas and the modern temple-entry movements of Kerala all contested the claims of Tantric ritual specialists. Fourth, the regions were never sealed off from each other: Nātha yogis, Siddhas, Śaiva preceptors and Bengali priests carried texts, practices and deities between them, and a goddess or a lineage could travel from one end of the subcontinent to the other.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Interpreting Tantra: Ethics, Reception and Scholarship
14.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Tantric traditions have seldom been described without being judged. Their own authors ranked them above the Veda; Brahmanical critics called them heretical; colonial missionaries saw in them the worst of Hinduism; Indian reformers disowned them or reinterpreted them; and modern Western readers have made them, by turns, a scandal, a philosophy and a technique of pleasure. The preceding chapters have described the traditions themselves. This one turns to the questions that their judges have asked. It considers first what the traditions prescribe about conduct and how they justified their transgressions; then the history of how “Tantra” has been condemned, defended, marketed and studied since the late eighteenth century; and finally how scholars now define the subject, and what remains of the traditions as living religions.

docs.title: 14.2 The Ethics of Tantra
docs.text:
The Āgamas bind their initiates with detailed rules (samayas): devotion to the guru and the deity, regular worship, truthfulness, purity, secrecy and the avoidance of harm, with expiations for every breach (Section 9.8). The Siddhānta, the most widely followed form of Tantric Śaivism, largely accepted the norms of Brahmanical society, and its manuals read in many places like codes of householder discipline. The Bhairava and Kaula traditions, and the Buddhist Yoginītantras, prescribed rites that deliberately violated those norms: the consumption of meat and alcohol, sexual ritual and the use of impure substances (Chapter 4). Their stated rationale was that the conventional distinction of pure and impure is itself a form of bondage, and that its ritual transcendence frees the initiate from the limited self (Sanderson 1988; White 2003). The same texts confined these rites to qualified initiates and condemned those who used them for indulgence, and the Buddhist vows required the practitioner never to abandon compassion for beings (Section 10.7.1).

Two further elements belong to the historical record as much as the philosophy does. The manuals contain rites for subjugating, paralysing, driving away and even killing enemies, the “six acts” (Section 7.3.3), whose ethics troubled the traditions themselves; and many Āgamic and Śākta traditions practised animal sacrifice (Section 4.12). On caste and gender, the earlier chapters have shown that Tantric openness to initiates of all castes and to women was real but limited: caste distinctions were often suspended in the ritual and retained in social life, priesthood became hereditary and caste-bound, and texts composed by men frequently treated women as means to male attainment (Sections 1.8 and 4.14). The debates over temple priesthood discussed in Section 11.10 show that these questions remain open.

docs.title: 14.3 Tantra in Modern Hindu Movements
docs.text:
Modern Hindu attitudes to Tantra have been ambivalent. Rāmakṛṣṇa (1836–1886) practised a series of Tantric disciplines under a female teacher at Dakṣiṇeśvar (Section 4.14.3), yet his disciple Vivekānanda, while revering the Goddess, criticised the left-hand rites and presented Vedānta as the core of Hinduism. In Bengal, scholars such as Atal Bihari Ghose worked with Woodroffe on the Tantrik Texts, and Gopinath Kaviraj (1887–1976) devoted a lifetime of scholarship and practice to Tantric traditions. Sri Aurobindo drew on the Tantric affirmation of the world and of Śakti in his integral yoga. In Kashmir, Svāmī Lakṣmaṇ Jū taught the Trika, and in South India Śrīvidyā gurus initiated growing circles of urban disciples (Urban 2003; Brooks 1992).

At the same time, the word “tāntrik” retains, in much of India, connotations of black magic, and self-styled tantriks offering exorcism, love charms or cures have been prosecuted under laws against superstition and fraud, such as Maharashtra’s anti-superstition act of 2013. The gap between the learned traditions described in this volume and the popular image of the “tantrik” remains wide.

docs.title: 14.4 “Tantra” in Colonial and Modern Perception
docs.text: The modern image of Tantra was made in two stages. In the nineteenth century missionaries, orientalists and many Hindu reformers described “Tantrism” as the degenerate underside of Hinduism, and Sir John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon) and his Indian collaborators answered by presenting it as a profound and ethically respectable philosophy. In the twentieth century Western teachers and writers reinvented it as a technique of sexual fulfilment and spiritual self-development. Hugh Urban has shown how the condemnation, the rehabilitation and the reinvention each constructed “Tantra” as a category in response to the concerns of its own time (Urban 2003). Each stage left its mark on how the traditions are still perceived.

docs.title: 14.4.1 Missionaries, Orientalists and Reformers
docs.text: The first detailed European accounts of Tantric worship came from Bengal, where missionaries and East India Company scholars met the Śākta religion of the region at first hand. The Baptist missionary William Ward of Serampore, whose account of the Hindus (first published in 1811 and enlarged in later editions) was widely read in Britain, described the left-hand rites as the extreme point of Hindu idolatry and moral corruption; Horace Hayman Wilson’s survey of the Hindu sects (1828–1832) treated the Śāktas more soberly but still as a degenerate late development, and Monier Monier-Williams later wrote in the same vein. Urban has shown how such accounts made “Tantrism” the convenient image of everything that colonial rule claimed to reform: secret, sexual, irrational and, through blood sacrifice, violent (Urban 2003). Many Bengali reformers accepted the diagnosis. Some, as the case of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra shows (Section 4.5), sought a purified Tantra compatible with monotheism and law; others, like the Brāhmo leaders, rejected Tantric worship altogether, and the word “tāntrik” acquired the pejorative sense that it still has in much of India.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Woodroffe and His Collaborators
docs.text: The rehabilitation of Tantra in English is associated above all with Sir John Woodroffe (1865–1936), a judge of the Calcutta High Court who published, under the name Arthur Avalon, translations and studies that included The Serpent Power (1919), the work that introduced the six-cakra system of Pūrṇānanda to Western readers (Avalon 1913, 1919). Kathleen Taylor’s study has shown that “Arthur Avalon” was in large part a collaborative identity: much of the Sanskrit work was done by Woodroffe’s Bengali associates, above all Atal Bihari Ghose, whose role was obscured by the pseudonym (Taylor 2001). Woodroffe’s own contribution was to present Tantra as a coherent, philosophically serious Śāstra, continuous with the Veda and suited to the present age, and to explain its transgressive rites as symbolic or as reserved for a small qualified elite. This apologetic reading answered the missionary caricature, but it also gave the late Bengali Tantras, and the Mahānirvāṇa above all, a representative status that historical scholarship has since qualified (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 14.4.3 The Goddess and Bengali Nationalism
docs.text: In the decades around 1900 the Goddess of the Bengali Śāktas became a symbol of the nation. Bankimcandra Chattopadhyay’s novel Ānandamaṭh (1882), with its hymn Vande Mātaram, presented the motherland as a goddess to be served by ascetic warriors, and the pamphlet Bhavānī Mandir (1905), associated with Aurobindo Ghose, proposed a temple to the Goddess as the power (śakti) of India, served by a dedicated order. Some members of the revolutionary societies of Bengal took vows before images of Kālī. Colonial officials, for their part, read the revolutionary violence of these years through the old image of Tantric blood sacrifice. Urban has traced how the Goddess and the language of sacrifice served both as a nationalist idiom and as a colonial explanation of “terrorism” (Urban 2003). The episode shows that the meanings attached to Tantra were never only religious.

docs.title: 14.4.4 Pierre Bernard and the American “Tantriks”
docs.text: In the United States the word “Tantra” was first popularised by Pierre Arnold Bernard (born Perry Baker, 1875 or 1876–1955), who founded a “Tantrik Order” in the first decade of the twentieth century, attracted newspaper notoriety as “Oom the Omnipotent”, and later ran a country club at Nyack, New York, where wealthy clients practised haṭha yoga. Bernard had some genuine knowledge of yoga, and his nephew Theos Bernard became a serious student of Tibetan Buddhism; but the “Tantra” he offered combined physical culture, secret initiation and sexual frankness in a form that had little to do with the Indian traditions (Love 2010; Urban 2003). The pattern of a Western teacher presenting himself as the holder of an exotic secret, and of a press presenting Tantra as scandal, was set for the rest of the century.

docs.title: 14.4.5 Neo-Tantra
docs.text:
From the 1960s Tantra became, in Western popular culture, a name for sacred sexuality. Mircea Eliade’s influential studies of yoga had already presented it as an archaic Indian spirituality of the body, and the counter-culture, popular writers and teachers such as Rajneesh (Osho) promoted it as sexual liberation and self-realisation. Urban has shown that this “neo-Tantra” drew less on Indian sources than on a Western tradition of sexual magic and erotic mysticism, which he traces from Paschal Beverly Randolph in nineteenth-century America through Aleister Crowley and Julius Evola, and which was later merged with Indian vocabulary by Rajneesh and by a large self-help literature (Urban 2006). Its themes — liberation through pleasure, the body as sacred, the rejection of repression — were those of the counter-culture, not of the medieval texts, whose sexual rites served the production of ritual substances, the gaining of powers or the realisation of non-duality within a demanding discipline of initiation (Chapter 4). White’s Kiss of the Yoginī was written in part to correct this picture (White 2003). Tibetan teachers in exile, meanwhile, introduced Buddhist Tantric practice to Western students in more traditional forms. The global market for “Tantra” workshops nevertheless continues to shape what many people, in India as well as abroad, imagine the word to mean, and Western ideas in turn influence how Tantra is presented in India today.

The secrecy of the teaching, the authority of the guru and the sexual elements of some traditions have also, in modern times, been used to justify abuse, in India and abroad, by teachers who claimed Tantric legitimacy. Traditional authorities and scholars alike have condemned such misuse, and the medieval texts themselves warn against teachers who exploit their pupils (Section 1.6).

docs.title: 14.4.6 Rāmakṛṣṇa and the Kālī’s Child Controversy
docs.text: The tensions between academic and devotional readings came to a head in the debate over Jeffrey Kripal’s Kālī’s Child (1995), a study of Rāmakṛṣṇa that read the saint’s mystical experiences, and his ambivalence towards the Tantric rites in which a woman ascetic had trained him, in terms of homoerotic desire (Kripal 1995). The book was praised by some reviewers and strongly contested by others, especially within the Rāmakṛṣṇa Order. Swami Tyagananda and Pravrajika Vrajaprana later published a detailed critique arguing that the book’s argument depended on mistranslations and selective readings of the Bengali sources (Swami Tyagananda and Pravrajika Vrajaprana 2010). The controversy raised questions that remain central to the study of Tantra: who may interpret a living tradition’s saints and secrets, what weight psychoanalytic readings can bear, and how the sexual elements of Tantric practice can be discussed in a way that both scholars and practitioners can recognise as accurate.

docs.title: 14.5 Tantra and Modern Science
docs.text: Modern presentations of Tantra often claim that its doctrines anticipated modern science: that spanda is the vibration of quantum fields, that mantras work through acoustic “frequencies”, that the cakras are endocrine glands, or that yantras channel measurable “energy”. Such claims find no support in the Sanskrit sources, which speak in the categories of their own theology, and they misrepresent both the texts and modern science. The Kashmiri doctrine of consciousness can be compared with modern philosophy of mind as a philosophical position, and contemplative practices derived from Tantric and Buddhist traditions have been studied by psychologists and neuroscientists; but such research concerns meditation as a human practice, not the truth of the cosmological claims of the texts. The traditions deserve to be understood on their own terms, as religious and philosophical systems, without being made to borrow authority from physics or medicine.

docs.title: 14.6 The Academic Study of Tantra
docs.text:
The academic study of Tantra has passed through four overlapping phases. The colonial period offered condemnation and selective description. The first half of the twentieth century brought rehabilitation: Woodroffe and his collaborators, Gopinath Kaviraj in Varanasi, the editors of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, K.C. Pandey’s study of Abhinavagupta (Pandey 1963) and Lilian Silburn’s translations and studies (Silburn 1988). From the 1960s philology and history took the lead: the editions of N.R. Bhatt and Hélène Brunner at Pondicherry, André Padoux’s studies of the Word, the surveys of Teun Goudriaan and Sanjukta Gupta, the dictionary of technical terms begun in Vienna (Brunner et al. 2000), Alexis Sanderson’s reconstruction of the history of Śaivism, and the editions of early scriptures by Dominic Goodall and his colleagues (Gupta et al. 1979; Goudriaan and Gupta 1981; Padoux 1990; Goodall et al. 2015). Alongside them, ethnographers and social historians have studied living temple priesthoods, goddess worship and Tantric practitioners (Fuller, McDaniel) and the social history of Tantra (Davidson, White, Urban, Samuel) (Fuller 2003; McDaniel 2004; Davidson 2002; Samuel 2008).

Of these, Sanderson’s work has done most to set the present agenda. His thesis of a “Śaiva Age” (Chapter 12), his demonstration that the Buddhist Yoginītantras borrowed from Śaiva scriptures, and his tracing of Śaiva ritual forms in Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, Jain and Smārta practice place the Tantric traditions at the centre, not the margin, of medieval Indian religion (Sanderson 1988, 2009). This volume follows his framework in many places, and the reader should bear in mind that much of it rests on one scholar’s reading of a vast and still largely unpublished body of sources, which younger scholars are now testing text by text.

docs.title: 14.7 What Is “Tantrism”?
docs.text: The reception history has also made scholars cautious about the category itself. The Sanskrit sources speak of tantras as texts and distinguish what is tāntrika from what is vaidika, but “Tantrism” as the name of a single religious phenomenon is a nineteenth-century Western coinage. André Padoux argued that it is best treated as a scholarly construct, useful for grouping traditions that share features such as initiation, mantra, ritual diagrams, the deification of the body and the pursuit of both liberation and power, but not to be mistaken for an indigenous self-description (Padoux 2002). Douglas Brooks proposed a list of characteristics none of which is necessary on its own (Brooks 1990), and Urban has emphasised how the category was formed in exchanges between Indian and Western authors (Urban 2003). The approach of Sanderson and his colleagues, followed in this volume, sidesteps the problem by starting from the scriptures: a tradition is “Tantric” when it takes the Tantras or Āgamas as its authority (Section 1.1).

docs.title: 14.8 The Living Traditions Today
docs.text: The traditions described in this volume are not only objects of study. The great Āgamic temples of South India draw very large numbers of pilgrims and remain centres of ritual, music and community life, and traditional schools and state-run Āgama schools train their priests; the opening of that training to non-Brahmins, and debates over the participation of women, are changing the priesthood. Tibetan Buddhism, in exile communities in India and worldwide, maintains Indian Buddhist Tantric lineages, and the Kālacakra initiation has been given by the Dalai Lama to very large audiences. Goddess worship, from Kāmākhyā to the village shrines of the Tamil country, continues in forms that the Sanskrit texts only partly describe. Thousands of Āgamic and Tantric manuscripts remain unedited, and digitisation projects in India, Nepal and Europe are making them more accessible; and the collaboration of traditional scholars with academic researchers, as at Pondicherry, has brought priests and philologists to the same texts.

docs.title: 14.9 Conclusion
docs.text:
What emerges from this volume is not a single “Tantra” but a family of traditions that, from about the fifth century CE, transformed Indian religion. They created the temple liturgies that still govern much Hindu worship and much of the ritual of Buddhists and Jains; they offered initiation, at least in principle, beyond the limits of the Vedic order; they produced philosophies of consciousness, language and aesthetic experience of lasting importance; and, in some lineages, they pursued liberation and power through the deliberate transgression of social and ritual norms.

These elements belong together. The philosopher Abhinavagupta was also the author of a ritual handbook that included the secret Kaula rites; the temple priest who performs the daily worship of Śiva follows manuals that also prescribe rites for kings; and the traditions that opened initiation to women and to the low-born also reproduced the hierarchies of their world. The living temples of South India, the Tibetan monastic traditions and the many lineages of goddess worship show that this inheritance remains a living and contested part of the present.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Abhiṣeka Consecration by sprinkling or bathing; in Buddhism, Tantric initiation Ācāra “Conduct”; in Śākta texts, a mode of practice (Vedic, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Kaula etc.) Ācārya Preceptor; in Śaivism, an initiate consecrated to initiate others and perform consecrations Adhikāra Entitlement or qualification for a practice Adhvan “Path”; the six levels of the cosmos purified in Śaiva initiation Ādiśaiva Hereditary priest of Tamil Śaiva Āgamic temples Āgaṃ Newar secret shrine of a lineage’s Tantric deity, open only to initiates Āgama “That which has come down”; revealed scripture, especially of the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions Ajapā The “unrecited” mantra haṃsa, identified with the breath Āmnāya “Transmission”; one of the directional families (eastern, northern, western, southern and upper) into which later Kaula and Śākta traditions group their cults Āṇavamala Innate impurity that limits the soul (Śaiva Siddhānta) Anugraha Grace; the fifth of Śiva’s five acts Arcā The consecrated image as a mode of the deity’s presence Atimārga The early ascetic Śaiva orders (Pāśupata, Lākula, Kāpālika) Āvaraṇa Enclosure of a maṇḍala or yantra, with its deities Bhūtaśuddhi Ritual purification of the elements of the worshipper’s body Bhūta Tantra Scripture of the western stream of the Mantramārga, on possessing spirits and their exorcism Bīja “Seed”; a monosyllabic mantra Bindu “Point”; the centre of a yantra; a drop of vital essence Cakra “Wheel”; a centre in the subtle body; a ritual circle; a diagram Caryāpāda Section of an Āgama on conduct Ḍākinī In Buddhist Tantra, a female deity or human practitioner who embodies wisdom and grants or guards the teaching; in Hindu sources, a class of dangerous female spirits Dakṣiṇācāra “Right-hand” practice conforming to purity rules Dhāraṇā “Fixation”; a limb of yoga; in the Śaiva scriptures, especially the fixation of the mind on the elements and the levels of the cosmos Dhāraṇī Buddhist protective or mnemonic formula Dhruva The fixed principal image in the sanctum of a Vaikhānasa temple Dīkṣā Initiation Dūtī Female ritual partner in Kaula rites Gāruḍa Tantra Scripture of the eastern stream of the Mantramārga, on the treatment of snakebite and poison Heruka Fierce male deity of the Buddhist Yoginītantras, such as Cakrasaṃvara or Hevajra Homa Fire offering Japa Repeated recitation of a mantra Jñānapāda Doctrinal section of an Āgama (also vidyāpāda) Kaḷameḻuttu Kerala floor drawing of a deity, especially Bhadrakālī, in coloured powders Kālasaṁkarṣaṇī “She who draws in time”; docs.title: Guide to Further Reading
docs.text:
The following works, all listed in the bibliography, are recommended starting points. For the technical vocabulary of the Hindu Tantras, the Tāntrikābhidhānakośa (Brunner et al. 2000), a dictionary of terms with references to the sources, is the standard reference work.

Editions and translations of primary texts. Among the primary sources discussed in this volume, the following are available in editions or translations listed in the bibliography: the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā (Goodall et al. 2015); the Brahmayāmala (Hatley 2018); the Kiraṇavṛtti of Rāmakaṇṭha (Goodall 1998); the Rauravāgama (Bhatt 1961–1988); Somaśambhu’s manual (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998); the yogic chapters of the Mālinīvijayottara (Vasudeva 2004); the Vīṇāśikhatantra (Goudriaan 1985); the Kubjikāmata (Goudriaan and Schoterman 1988) and the opening chapters of the Ṣaṭsāhasrasaṃhitā (Schoterman 1982); the early Pāñcarātra works edited by Acharya (Acharya 2015); Yāmuna’s Āgamaprāmāṇya (van Buitenen 1971); the Haribhaktivilāsa (Broo 2023); the Kulārṇava Tantra (Vidyāratna 1917); the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra in translation (Avalon 1913); the Saundaryalaharī with Lakṣmīdhara’s commentary (Sastri and Ayyangar 1937); the Tantrāloka with Jayaratha’s commentary (Abhinavagupta 1918–1938); Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā (Torella 2002); Somānanda’s Śivadṛṣṭi, chapters 1–3 (Nemec 2011); the Śivasūtra, Spandakārikā and Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya in translation (Singh 1979, 1980, 1963); and the Hevajra Tantra (Snellgrove 1959).

General introductions. André Padoux’s The Hindu Tantric World (Padoux 2017) and Gavin Flood’s The Tantric Body (Flood 2006) are reliable overviews. Teun Goudriaan and Sanjukta Gupta’s Hindu Tantric and Śākta Literature (Goudriaan and Gupta 1981) and Hindu Tantrism (Gupta et al. 1979) survey the texts. David Gordon White’s anthology Tantra in Practice (White 2000) offers translations with introductions.

History. Alexis Sanderson’s “Śaivism and the Tantric Traditions” (Sanderson 1988) is the classic short history; his “The Śaiva Age” (Sanderson 2009) presents the evidence for royal patronage in detail. Geoffrey Samuel’s The Origins of Yoga and Tantra (Samuel 2008) sets Tantra in a long history of Indic religion; Ronald Davidson’s Indian Esoteric Buddhism (Davidson 2002) gives a social history of Buddhist Tantra.

Śaiva Siddhānta and temple ritual. Richard Davis’s Ritual in an Oscillating Universe (Davis 1991) and A Priest’s Guide for the Great Festival (Davis 2010); Hélène Brunner’s edition of Somaśambhu’s manual (Brunner-Lachaux 1963–1998); C.J. Fuller’s Servants of the Goddess (Fuller 1984) and The Renewal of the Priesthood (Fuller 2003); Stella Kramrisch’s The Hindu Temple (Kramrisch 1946). For the early scriptures, Goodall’s editions of the Kiraṇa commentary and the Niśvāsa (Goodall 1998; Goodall et al. 2015).

Vaiṣṇava traditions. Schrader’s Introduction to the Pāñcarātra (Schrader 1916), Matsubara’s Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās and Early Vaiṣṇava Theology (Matsubara 1994) and van Buitenen’s translation of Yāmuna (van Buitenen 1971). Acharya’s edition of the earliest Pāñcarātra texts (Acharya 2015), Rastelli on the Pārameśvara (Rastelli 2006), Colas on Vaikhānasa images and fires (Colas 1996) and Broo’s edition of the Haribhaktivilāsa (Broo 2023) take the subject further. On the Tantric Vaiṣṇavism of Bengal, Dimock’s The Place of the Hidden Moon (Dimock 1966), Openshaw’s Seeking Bāuls of Bengal (Openshaw 2002) and Urban’s The Economics of Ecstasy (Urban 2001).

Śākta traditions. Thomas Coburn on the Devīmāhātmya (Coburn 1984); David Kinsley on the Mahāvidyās (Kinsley 1997); Douglas Brooks on Śrīvidyā (Brooks 1990, 1992); June McDaniel on Bengal (McDaniel 2004); Vidya Dehejia on yoginī temples (Dehejia 1986); and, on the Kaula traditions and their interpretation, David Gordon White’s Kiss of the Yoginī (White 2003) and Hugh Urban’s Tantra (Urban 2003). On women in the Tantric traditions, Törzsök on the early Śākta scriptures (Törzsök 2014), Biernacki on the late Kaula texts (Biernacki 2007), Gupta’s survey (Gupta 1992) and McDaniel on women tāntrikās in Bengal (McDaniel 2007).

Healing, possession and the lesser streams. Slouber’s Early Tantric Medicine (Slouber 2017); Goudriaan’s edition of the Vīṇāśikhatantra (Goudriaan 1985); Frederick Smith’s The Self Possessed (Smith 2006).

Kingship and the Śaiva Age. Sanderson’s “The Śaiva Age” (Sanderson 2009) with his studies of the Khmers and of inscriptions (Sanderson 2003–2004, 2013); Hermann Kulke’s Kings and Cults (Kulke 1993); B.D. Chattopadhyaya’s The Making of Early Medieval India (Chattopadhyaya 1994); Hans Bakker’s The World of the Skandapurāṇa (Bakker 2014); Florinda De Simini’s Of Gods and Books (De Simini 2016); and, for wider perspectives, Davis’s Lives of Indian Images (Davis 1997), Pollock’s The Language of the Gods in the World of Men (Pollock 2006), Talbot on medieval Andhra (Talbot 2001), Fuller on Navarātri and royal ritual (Fuller 1992) and Sarkar on the royal cult of Durgā (Sarkar 2017). On ascetic orders, Lorenzen’s The Kāpālikas and Kālāmukhas (Lorenzen 1972); on the yoginīs, Hatley’s study and edition of the Brahmayāmala (Hatley 2007, 2018) and the essays edited by Keul (Keul 2013).

Regional traditions. For Kerala, Tarabout (Tarabout 1986) and Caldwell (Caldwell 1999); for Bengal, McDermott (McDermott 2001) and Sircar on the pīṭhas (Sircar 1973); for Assam, Urban (Urban 2010); for Odisha, Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (Eschmann et al. 1978); for Nepal, Levy’s Mesocosm (Levy 1990) and Dyczkowski on Kubjikā (Dyczkowski 1988); for the goddesses of the north-western hills, Erndl (Erndl 1993); for Rajasthan, Harlan (Harlan 1992) and the Jodhpur catalogue Garden and Cosmos (Diamond et al. 2008); for the Tamil Tirumantiram, Zvelebil (Zvelebil 1975); for Bali, Hooykaas (Hooykaas 1966).

Jain, Saura and Gāṇapatya traditions. Dundas’s The Jains (Dundas 2002) and his essay on the sūrimantra (Dundas 1998); Gough’s Making a Mantra (Gough 2021); Cort’s Jains in the World (Cort 2001); Laidlaw’s Riches and Renunciation (Laidlaw 1995); von Stietencron on the Sun priests (Stietencron 1966); Courtright on Gaṇeśa (Courtright 1985).

Kashmiri Śaivism. Mark Dyczkowski’s The Doctrine of Vibration (Dyczkowski 1987); Paul Muller-Ortega’s The Triadic Heart of Śiva (Muller-Ortega 1989); Jaideva Singh’s translations of the Śivasūtra and Spandakārikā (Singh 1979, 1980). For the Pratyabhijñā, Torella’s edition of Utpaladeva (Torella 2002), Nemec on Somānanda (Nemec 2011) and Ratié on the self (Ratié 2011); for the older scholarship, Pandey’s Abhinavagupta (Pandey 1963) and Silburn (Silburn 1988). For the Krama, Rastogi’s The Krama Tantricism of Kashmir (Rastogi 1979), and for the history of Kashmiri exegesis, Sanderson’s “The Śaiva Exegesis of Kashmir” (Sanderson 2007). On the yoga of the Śaiva scriptures, Vasudeva’s study of the Mālinīvijayottara (Vasudeva 2004).

Reception. Taylor on Woodroffe and his collaborators (Taylor 2001); Urban on colonial and Western constructions of Tantra and on modern sexual magic (Urban 2003, 2006); Love on Pierre Bernard (Love 2010); Padoux on the category “Tantrism” (Padoux 2002); and, for the Kālī’s Child debate, Kripal and his critics (Kripal 1995; Swami Tyagananda and Pravrajika Vrajaprana 2010).

Mantra, yantra and the Word. Padoux’s Vāc (Padoux 1990); Alper’s Understanding Mantras (Alper 1989); Bühnemann’s Maṇḍalas and Yantras (Bühnemann 2003) and Pūjā (Bühnemann 1988). On Tantric art and its modern reception, Rawson’s The Art of Tantra (Rawson 1973), Mookerjee’s Tantra Art (Mookerjee 1966) and the British Museum catalogue Tantra: Enlightenment to Revolution (Ramos 2020).

Buddhist Tantra. Snellgrove’s Indo-Tibetan Buddhism (Snellgrove 1987) and his edition of the Hevajra (Snellgrove 1959); Gray’s Cakrasaṃvara (Gray 2007); Wedemeyer’s Making Sense of Tantric Buddhism (Wedemeyer 2013); Miranda Shaw’s Buddhist Goddesses of India (Shaw 2006); English on Vajrayoginī (English 2002); Wallace on the “inner” Kālacakra (Wallace 2001); and Dalton on violence and liberation in Tibetan Buddhism (Dalton 2011).

Yoga and alchemy. Mallinson and Singleton’s Roots of Yoga (Mallinson and Singleton 2017); White’s The Alchemical Body (White 1996); Zvelebil’s The Poets of the Powers on the Tamil Siddhas (Zvelebil 1973); Ernst on the Persian and Arabic translations of yoga (Ernst 2003); and McLeod on Guru Nānak and the Nāths (McLeod 1968).
